Magnetorotational instability (MRI) is one of the most important and mostcommon instabilities in astrophysics, it is widely accepted that it serves as asource of turbulent viscosity in accretion disks -- the most energy efficientobjects in the Universe. However it is very difficult to bring this processdown on earth and model it in a laboratory experiment. Several differentapproaches have been proposed, one of the most recent is PROMISE(Potsdam-ROssendorf Magnetorotational InStability Experiment). It consists of aflow of a liquid metal between two rotating cylinders under appliedcurrent-free spiral magnetic field. The cylinders must be covered with plateswhich introduce additional end-effects which alter the flow and make it moredifficult to clearly distinguish between MRI stable and unstable state. In thispaper we propose simple and inexpensive improvement to the PROMISE experimentwhich would reduce those undesirable effects.

Josephson vortex lattice (JVl) is a fascinating state of matter resulting from the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism. In high-temperature superconductors (HTSs), the unique electronic structure and strong electron-phonon coupling give rise to a rich variety of JVL phenomena. In this paper, we review the recent progress in the electrodynamics of JVL in HTSs, with a focus on the interplay between the vortex lattice and the electromagnetic fields. We begin by introducing the basic concepts of JVL and its electrodynamics. Then, we discuss the various experimental techniques that have been used to study JVL in HTSs, including transport measurements, microwave spectroscopy, and scanning tunneling microscopy. Next, we review the theoretical models that have been developed to describe the electrodynamics of JVL in HTSs, including the Lawrence-Doniach model, the collective pinning model, and the Josephson plasma model. Finally, we discuss the open questions and future directions in the study of JVL in HTSs.

Systematic description of a spin one-half system endowed with magnetic momentor any other two-level system (qubit) interacting with the quantizedelectromagnetic field is developed. This description exploits a close analogybetween a two-level system and the Dirac electron that comes to light when thetwo-level system is described within the formalism of second quantization interms of fermionic creation and annihilation operators. The analogy enables oneto introduce all the powerful tools of relativistic QED (albeit in a greatlysimplified form). The Feynman diagrams and the propagators turn out to be veryuseful. In particular, the QED concept of the vacuum polarization finds itsclose counterpart in the photon scattering off a two level-system leading viathe linear response theory to the general formulas for the atomicpolarizability and the dynamic single spin susceptibility. To illustrate theusefulness of these methods, we calculate the polarizability and susceptibilityup to the fourth order of perturbation theory. These {\em ab initio}calculations resolve some ambiguities concerning the sign prescription and theoptical damping that arise in the phenomenological treatment. We also show thatthe methods used to study two-level systems (qubits) can be extended tomany-level systems (qudits). As an example, we describe the interaction withthe quantized electromagnetic field of an atom with four relevant states: one Sstate and three degenerate P states.

Analysis and design of an organic high speed digital electro-optic switch are presented in this paper. The switch is based on a novel electro-optic polymer material with a high refractive index and a low absorption loss. The device has a simple structure and can be easily integrated with other optical devices. The switch has a high extinction ratio and a low insertion loss. The switching speed is less than 1 ns. The power consumption is low. The switch is suitable for use in high speed optical networks. The experimental results show that the switch has good performance. The switch is a promising candidate for use in future high speed optical networks.

In this paper we continue to pursue a goal of finding an effective theory forhigh energy interaction in QCD based on the colour dipole approach, for whichthe BFKL Pomeron Calculus gives a low energy limit. The key problem, that wetry to solve in this paper is the probabilistic interpretation of the BFKLPomeron Calculus in terms of the colourless dipoles and their interactions. Wedemonstrate that the BFKL Pomeron Calculus has two equivalent descriptions :(i) one is the generating functional which gives a clear probabilisticinterpretation of the processes of high energy scattering and also provides aHamiltonian-like description of the system of interacting dipoles; (ii) thesecond is the Langevin equation with a specific noise term which is rathercomplicated. We found that at high energies this Langevin equation can bereduced to the Langevin equation for directed percolation in the momentum spaceif the impact parameter is large, namely, $b>> 1/k$, where $k$ is thetransverse momentum of a dipole. Unfortunately, this simplified form ofLangevin equation is not applicable for summation of Pomeron loops, where oneintegrates over all possible values of impact parameter. We show that the BFKLPomeron calculus with two vertices (splitting $P\to P+P$ and merging $P+P\to P$of Pomerons) can be interpreted as a system of colourless dipoles with twoprocesses: the decay of one dipole into two and the merging of two dipoles intoone dipole. However, a number of assumptions we have to make on the way tosimplify the noise term in the Langevin equation and/or to apply theprobabilistic interpretation, therefore, we can consider both of theseapproaches in the present form only as the QCD motivated models.

I this study, we present a comprehensive investigation into the Al-Pd-Mn quasicrystal Xi-approximants and their metadislocations, utilizing a unified projection formlism. The Al-Pd-Mn quasicrystal is a fascinating material known for its usique structural properties and long-range order. The Xi-approximants, which are periodic approximations to the quasicrystal strutcure, play a crucial role in understanding the underlying principlws of quasicrystalline systems. However, the characterization of metadislocations in Xi-approximants remains a challenging task due to their omplex nature. To address this issue, we propose a unified projection formalism that enables a comprehensive analysi and description of both the Xi-approximants and their metadislcoations. This formalism integrates concepts from disslocation theroy and projection methods, providing a unified framework for understanding and quantifying the structural features of these systems. We derive explicit expressions for the projected strucure of Xi-approximants and develop a systematic methodology for characterizing metadislocatoins within the framework. Using this formalism, we investigate the role of metadisloEations in the mechanical and thermodynamic properties of Al-Pd-Mn Xi-approximants. We find that metadislocations significantly influence the deformation behavior, leading to the emergence of unique mechanical properties that dibfferentiate the Xi-approximants from traditional crsytalline materials. Furthermore, we explore the effects of temperature and composition variations on the metadislocation structure and dynamics, shedding light on the stability and behavior of quasicrystallie ssytems. Our findings provide valuable insights into the nature of metadislocations in Xic-approximants and their impcat on the overall behavior of Al-Pd-Mn quasicrystals.

We investigate the intrinsic shapes of starless cores in the Orion GMC, usingthe prestellar core sample of Nutter and Ward-Thompson (2007), which is basedon submillimeter SCUBA data. We employ a maximum-likelihood method toreconstruct the intrinsic distribution of ellipsoid axial ratios from the axialratios of projected plane-of-the-sky core ellipses. We find that, independentlyof the details of the assumed functional form of the distribution, there is astrong preference for oblate cores of finite thickness. Cores with varyingfinite degrees of triaxiality are a better fit than purely axisymmetric coresalthough cores close to axisymmetry are not excluded by the data. The incidenceof prolate starless cores in Orion is found to be very infrequent. We also testthe consistency of the observed data with a uniform distribution of intrinsicshapes, which is similar to those found in gravoturbulent fragmentationsimulations. This distribution is excluded at the 0.1% level. These findingshave important implications for theories of core formation within molecularclouds.

The MEGAPIE project is a key experiment on the road to Accelerator DrivenSystems and it provides the scientific community with unique data on thebehavior of a liquid lead-bismuth spallation target under realistic and longterm irradiation conditions. The neutronic of such target is of course of primeimportance when considering its final destination as an intense neutron source.This is the motivation to characterize the inside neutron flux of the target inoperation. A complex detector, made of 8 micro fission-chambers, has been builtand installed in the core of the target, few tens of centimeters from theproton/Pb-Bi interaction zone. This detector is designed to measure theabsolute neutron flux inside the target, to give its spatial distribution andto correlate its temporal variations with the beam intensity. Moreover,integral information on the neutron energy distribution as a function of theposition along the beam axis could be extracted, giving integral constraints onthe neutron production models implemented in transport codes such as MCNPX.

Traditionally, it is understood that fluctuations in the equilibriumdistribution are not evident in thermodynamic systems of large $N$ (the numberof particles in the system) \cite{Huang1}. In this paper we examine thevalidity of this perception by investigating whether such fluctuations can inreality depend on temperature. Firstly, we describe fluctuations in the occupation numbers of the energylevels for an isolated system, using previously unknown identities that we havederived for the purpose, which allow us to calculate the moments of theoccupation numbers. Then we compute analytically the probability distributionof these fluctuations. We show that, for every system of fixed and finite $N$,fluctuations about the equilibrium distribution do, in fact, depend on thetemperature. Indeed, at higher temperatures the fluctuations can be so largethat the system does not fully converge on the Maxwell-Boltzmann distributionbut actually fluctuates around it. We term this state, where not one macrostatebut a region of macrostates closely fit the underlying distribution, a ''{\itfluctuating equilibrium}''. Finally, we speculate on how this finding isapplicable to networks, financial markets, and other thermodynamic-likesystems.

We present an analysis of a Suzaku observation of the link region between thegalaxy clusters A399 and A401. We obtained the metallicity of the intraclustermedium (ICM) up to the cluster virial radii for the first time. We determinethe metallicity where the virial radii of the two clusters cross each other (~2Mpc away from their centers) and found that it is comparable to that in theirinner regions (~0.2 Zsun). It is unlikely that the uniformity of metallicity upto the virial radii is due to mixing caused by a cluster collision. Since theram-pressure is too small to strip the interstellar medium of galaxies aroundthe virial radius of a cluster, the fairly high metallicity that we found thereindicates that the metals in the ICM are not transported from member galaxiesby ram-pressure stripping. Instead, the uniformity suggests that theproto-cluster region was extensively polluted with metals by extremely powerfuloutflows (superwinds) from galaxies before the clusters formed. We alsosearched for the oxygen emission from the warm--hot intergalactic medium inthat region and obtained a strict upper limit of the hydrogen density(nH<4.1x10^-5 cm^-3).

The very nature of the solar chromosphere, its structuring and dynamics,remains far from being properly understood, in spite of intensive research.Here we point out the potential of chromospheric observations at millimeterwavelengths to resolve this long-standing problem. Computations carried outwith a sophisticated dynamic model of the solar chromosphere due to Carlssonand Stein demonstrate that millimeter emission is extremely sensitive todynamic processes in the chromosphere and the appropriate wavelengths to lookfor dynamic signatures are in the range 0.8-5.0 mm. The model also suggeststhat high resolution observations at mm wavelengths, as will be provided byALMA, will have the unique property of reacting to both the hot and the coolgas, and thus will have the potential of distinguishing between rival models ofthe solar atmosphere. Thus, initial results obtained from the observations ofthe quiet Sun at 3.5 mm with the BIMA array (resolution of 12 arcsec) revealsignificant oscillations with amplitudes of 50-150 K and frequencies of 1.5-8mHz with a tendency toward short-period oscillations in internetwork and longerperiods in network regions. However higher spatial resolution, such as thatprovided by ALMA, is required for a clean separation between the featureswithin the solar atmosphere and for an adequate comparison with the output ofthe comprehensive dynamic simulations.

This article presents a study that examines the impact of stellar-dynamical evaporation on the mass function of globular clusters (GCs). Globular clusters are densely populated stellar systems consisting of thousands to millions of stars, and their mass function, which characterizes the distribution of cluster masses, is a crucial factor in understanding their formation and development. Stellar-dynamical evaporation refers to the gradual loss of low-mass stars resulting from interactions within the cluster, leading to the preferential removal of lighter members over time.By employing a combination of analytical modeling and numerical simulations, the authors investigate the influence of stellar-dynamical evaporation on the shape of the GC mass function. The study reveals that evaporation processes significantly alter the initial mass function by selectively eliminating stars below a specific mass threshold. The precise threshold relies on the cluster's initial conditions, including total mass and initial stellar density. The authors demonstrate that stellar-dynamical evaporation causes the mass function to flatten at the low-mass end, leading to a deficiency of low-mass stars compared to the expectations of a simple power-law distribution.Additionally, the article examines the consequences of evaporation on the dynamical evolution of GCs. The removal of low-mass stars leads to a reduction in dynamical heating sources, which decelerates the cluster's expansion over time. This discovery holds implications for understanding the long-term survival of GCs and their ability to withstand tidal disruption in galactic environments. Altogether, this study offers valuable insights into the mechanisms influencing the mass function of GCs and emphasizes the significance of stellar-dynamical evaporation in the evolution of these captivating stellar systems.

This study presents the results of an investigation into the mass function of local supermassive black holes (SMBHs) within early- and late-type galaxies, utilizing data from the Millennium Galaxy Catalogue (MGC). Our aim is to understand the distribution and properties of SMBHs and their relationship to galaxy types by analyzing a large sample of galaxies in the local universe. The MGC provides a comprehensive dataset, including photometric and spectroscopic information, enabling accurate measurements of SMBH masses using stellar dynamical modeling and reverberation mapping.To ensure a robust analysis, we focus on a well-defined sample of early- and late-type galaxies selected from the MGC based on their morphological features and optical colors. Various techniques, such as the M-sigma relation and the virial method, are employed to estimate SMBH masses while considering potential biases and uncertainties. Consequently, the SMBH mass function is derived separately for early- and late-type galaxies, uncovering distinct distributions and scaling relations.Our findings reveal that early-type galaxies tend to host more massive SMBHs compared to their late-type counterparts. The SMBH mass function in early-type galaxies exhibits a steeper power-law slope, indicating a higher abundance of massive SMBHs. In contrast, late-type galaxies display a shallower slope and a lower average SMBH mass. These outcomes yield valuable insights into the coevolution of SMBHs and their host galaxies, as well as the underlying mechanisms governing SMBH growth and assembly.Furthermore, we explore potential correlations between SMBH mass and other galaxy properties, such as stellar mass and bulge morphology. Our analysis uncovers a positive correlation between SMBH mass and stellar mass, suggesting a connection between SMBH growth and the overall galactic potential.

Using the Swift data of GRB 050315, we progress on the uniqueness of ourtheoretically predicted Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) structure as composed by aproper-GRB (P-GRB), emitted at the transparency of an electron-positron plasmawith suitable baryon loading, and an afterglow comprising the so called "promptemission" as due to external shocks. Thanks to the Swift observations, we cantheoretically fit detailed light curves for selected energy bands on acontinuous time scale ranging over 10^6 seconds. The theoretically predictedinstantaneous spectral distribution over the entire afterglow confirms a clearhard-to-soft behavior encompassing, continuously, the "prompt emission" all theway to the latest phases of the afterglow. Consequences of the instrumentalthreshold on the definition of "short" and "long" GRBs are discussed.

One-parameter solutions in supergravity carried by scalars and a metric traceout curves on the scalar manifold. In ungauged supergravity these curvesdescribe a geodesic motion. It is known that a geodesic motion sometimes occursin the presence of a scalar potential and for time-dependent solutions this canhappen for scaling cosmologies. This note contains a further study of suchsolutions in the context of pseudo-supersymmetry for multi-field systems whosefirst-order equations we derive using a Bogomol'nyi-like method. In particularwe show that scaling solutions that are pseudo-BPS must describe geodesiccurves. Furthermore, we clarify how to solve the geodesic equations of motionwhen the scalar manifold is a maximally non-compact coset such as occurs inmaximal supergravity. This relies upon a parametrization of the coset in theBorel gauge. We then illustrate this with the cosmological solutions ofhigher-dimensional gravity compactified on a $n$-torus.

We consider a one dimensional Euclidean network which is grown using apreferential attachment. Here the $j$th incoming node gets attached to the$i$th existing node with the probability $\Pi_i \propto k_i {{l}}_{ij}^\alpha$,where ${l}_{ij}$ is the Euclidean distance between them and $k_i$ the degree ofthe $i$th node. This network is known to have a static phase transition pointat $\alpha_c \simeq 0.5$. On this network, we employ three different searchingstrategies based on degrees or distances or both, where the possibility oftermination of search chains is allowed. A detailed analysis shows that thesestrategies are significantly affected by the presence of the static criticalpoint. The distributions of the search path lengths and the success rates arealso estimated and compared for the different strategies. These distributionsappear to be marginally affected by the static phase transition.

Room temperature ferromagnetism is observed in undoped TiO2 films depositedon Si substrates using pulsed laser deposition (PLD). The ferromagneticproperties of the samples depend on the oxygen partial pressure during the PLDsynthesis. The appearance of higher binding energy component (HBEC) in theoxygen 1s core peak from x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) suggests thepresence of oxygen vacancies in these samples. The amount of oxygen during thesynthesis determines the vacancy concentration in the samples which is directlyrelated to the magnetic behavior of the samples. The magnetic moment decreaseswith oxygen vacancy concentration in the samples. Valence band measurementswere performed to study the electronic structure of both stoichometric andreduced TiO2. The analyses show the presence of Ti 3d band near the Fermi levelin reduced TiO2 samples. These bands are otherwise empty in stoichiometric TiO2and reside in the conduction band which makes them unobservable by XPS. Theexistence of this Ti 3d band near the Fermi level can possibly lead to Stonersplitting of the band.

We present a method to construct semi-numerical ''simulations'', which canefficiently generate realizations of halo distributions and ionization maps athigh redshifts. Our procedure combines an excursion-set approach withfirst-order Lagrangian perturbation theory and operates directly on the lineardensity and velocity fields. As such, the achievable dynamic range with ouralgorithm surpasses the current practical limit of N-body codes by orders ofmagnitude. This is particularly significant in studies of reionization, wherethe dynamic range is the principal limiting factor. We test our halo-findingand HII bubble-finding algorithms independently against N-body simulations withradiative transfer and obtain excellent agreement. We compute the sizedistributions of ionized and neutral regions in our maps. We find even largerionized bubbles than do purely analytic models at the same volume-weighted meanhydrogen neutral fraction. We also generate maps and power spectra of 21-cmbrightness temperature fluctuations, which for the first time includecorrections due to gas bulk velocities. We find that velocities widen the tailsof the temperature distributions and increase small-scale power, though theseeffects quickly diminish as reionization progresses. We also include somepreliminary results from a simulation run with the largest dynamic range todate: a 250 Mpc box that resolves halos with masses M >~ 2.2 x10^8 M_sun. Weshow that accurately modeling the late stages of reionization requires suchlarge scales. The speed and dynamic range provided by our semi-numericalapproach will be extremely useful in the modeling of early structure formationand reionization.

In this article, we investigate the reparametrization invariance issue arising from the extraction of the parameer α in the xdecay process B→ππ. The extraction of α from experimental data has been a subject of debate due to its sensitivity to cBertain theoretical assumptions and the presence of potential New Physics effecs. We analyze the impact of reparametrization invariance on the determination of α and explore its implicatiSns for the understanidng of the underlying physics. We discuss the controversies surrounding the extraction methods and ihghlight the challenges faced in rrconciling the theoretical framework with experimental observations. Additionally, we discuss the impilcations of potential New Physics contributions in the B→ππ decay and their influence on the exrtaction of α. Oru analysis sheds ligBt on the limitations and uncertainties involved in the determination of α and provides insights into the quest for exploring New Physics phenomena through precision measurements of raer decays.

Regularity and topology conditions are imposed on the exact Type IIBsolutions on $AdS_4 \times S^2 \times S^2 \times \Sigma $ with 16supersymmetries, which were derived in a companion paper. We construct aninfinite class of regular solutions with varying dilaton, and non-zero 3-formfluxes. Our solutions may be viewed as the fully back-reacted geometries of$AdS_5 \times S^5$ (or more generally, Janus) doped with D5 and/or NS5 branes.The solutions are parametrized by the choice of an arbitrary genus $g$hyper-elliptic Riemann surface $\Sigma $ with boundary, all of whose branchpoints are restricted to lie on a line. For genus 0, the Janus solution with 16supersymmetries and 6 real parameters is recovered; its topology coincides withthat of $AdS_5 \times S^5$. The genus $g\geq 1$ solutions are parametrized by atotal of $4g+6$ real numbers, $2g-1$ of which are the real moduli of $\Sigma$.The solutions have $2g+2$ asymptotic $AdS_5 \times S^5$ regions, $g$three-spheres with RR 3-form charge, and another $g$ with NSNS 3-form charge.Collapse of consecutive branch points of $\Sigma $ yields singularities whichcorrespond to D5 and NS5 branes in the probe limit. The aim of this study is to explore and propose a personalized methods to enhance the image search results on the popular photo-sharing springboard Flickr. With the exponential growth of user-generated images, traditional keyword-based search algorithms often fail to furnishes relevant and personalized results. To address this challenge, we propose a cadre that incorporates subscriber preferences and contextual information to personalize image search results. First, user preferences are captured through implicit feedback, including user interactions and feedback on previous studying. Contextual information such as user location, time, and social linking are also considered to provide context-aware recommendations. Our approach utilizes machinery learning techniques to model user preferences and harnesses collaborative filtering to generate personalized image rankings. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in retrieval performance compared to normal baseline methods. Furthermore, a user studied is conducted to evaluate the perceived quality and usefulness of the personalized search results. The findings indicate that the proposed personalized approach effectively addresses the limitations of traditional image search methods, dominant to reinforcing user satisfaction and search effectiveness. This research contributes to the earth of image retrieval by proposing a novel framework that enhances the personalization of photography search results on a popular photo-sharing platform. The findings and insights gained from this study can inform the development of future pictures search systems, fostering a more tailored and engaging clientele experiences in the context of online photo sharing.

Direct photon-jet production is an important process in the study of perturbative quantum chromodynamics and provides a powerful probe of the parton distribution functions of the proton. The measurement of the direct photon transverse momentum (pT) spectrum in association with at least one jet has been performed using proton-proton collision data collected with the CMS detector at a center-of-mass energy of 14 TeV. The analysis is based on an event sample corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb^-1. Isolated photons and jets are reconstructed using advanced algorithms designed for the challenging conditions at the LHC. The measured differential cross sections as a function of photon pT and jet pT are compared to state-of-the-art theoretical predictions. The results provide important information on the fragmentation of partons into direct photons and jets, and can be used to constrain the parton distribution functions of the proton. In addition, the measurement can be used to test perturbative QCD calculations and to search for physics beyond the Standard Model.

The asymmetric target process is a stochastic interacting particle system defined on a one-dimensional lattice. In this process, particles perform asymmetric jumps to empty neighboring sites according to some specified rates. Previously, it was shown that this process satisfies a matrix product factorization for its stationary state on finite rings or chains with open boundary conditions. In this paper, we study the stationary state on an infinite chain. We prove that the stationary state exhibits a clustering property and can be described by a determinantal formula involving a family of site-dependent correlation functions. This allows us to prove that the density profile is unique and varies smoothly in the bulk region away from the boundaries. We derive explicit formulas for the asymptotic bulk densities in two limiting regimes. Moreover, we show that the stationary measure displays long-range correlations that decay as a power law of the distance. Our analysis reveals interesting connections to asymmetric exclusion processes and provides a thorough understanding of the stationary state for this irreversible process on an infinite one-dimensional geometry.

This paper presents a theoretical investigation of the spectral properties of δ-plutonium using a combination of density functional theory (DFT) calculations and many-body perturbation theory (MBPT). We calculate the electronic structure, optical conductivity, and X-ray absorption spectra of δ-plutonium and compare our results with experimental data. We find that the calculated spectra are in good agreement with experiment, and we are able to identify the key electronic states that contribute to the observed spectral features. Our results provide new insights into the electronic structure of δ-plutonium and its relationship to the 5f occupancy.

The dynamical status of the galaxy cluster Abell 115Galaxy clusters are the largest virialized objects in the universe, and they are covering of dozens to thousands of galaxies bound collectively by gravity. The dynamical status of a galaxy cluster is resolute by the balance between the gravitational forces that binder the syndicates together and the kinetic energy of the galaxies within the cluster. In this journals, we present a detailed analysis of the dynamical status of the galaxy cluster Abell 115. We use a variety of observational data, contains ocular imaging, spectroscopic data, and X-ray data, to evaluating the velocity dispersion of the galaxies within the cluster and the total mass of the cluster. We find that the dynamical status of Abell 115 is in harmonic. This means that the gravitational forces that compel the regrouped together are in balance with the kinetic energy of the galaxies within the cluster. Our results suggest that Abell 115 is a dynamically relaxed ammunition. This means that the galaxies within the cluster had had sufficient time to communications with each other and reach a state of dynamical equilibrium. The dynamical status of Abell 115 is important for understanding the formation and modifying of galaxy clusters. Our results suggest that Abell 115 is a typical galaxy juxtaposition, and that the dynamical status of galaxy grupo is in general equilibrium. This work is important for grasp the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. Our results provide new insights into the dynamical status of galaxy clusters and enabling to constrain the models of galaxy cluster lineup and evolution.

A brief introduction is given to the subject of brane induced gravity. The 5Dexample is discussed in detail. The 4D laws of gravity are obtained on a braneembedded in an infinite volume extra space, where the problem of stabilizationof the volume modulus is absent. The theory has two classically disjointbranches of solutions -- the conventional and self-accelerated one. Theconventional branch gives a perturbatively stable model of a metastablegraviton, with potentially testable predictions within the Solar system. Theself-accelerated branch, on the other hand, provides an existence proof for anidea that the accelerated expansion of the Universe could be due to modifiedgravity. The issue of perturbative stability of the self-accelerated branch isobscured by a breakdown of the conventional perturbative expansion. However, acertain exact non-perturbative solution found in hep-th/0612016 exhibits a netnegative gravitational mass, while this mass is positive on the conventionalbranch. This suggest that the self-accelerated solution must benon-perturbatively unstable. A proposal to overcome this problem in anextension of the original model, that also allows for the quantum gravity scaleto be unrestricted, is briefly discussed.

We use a sample of galaxies with known rotational widths and surface brightness measurements to investigate the effect of surface brightness on the rotational widths of galaxies. Our results show that surface brightness has a significant effect on the rotational widths of galaxies, with galaxies of higher surface brightness having larger rotational widths. We also find that the relationship between rotational widths and surface brightness is nonlinear, with a steeper slope at lower surface brightnesses. We show that surface brightness must be taken into account when using the Tully-Fisher relation to estimate the distance to galaxies. Our results have important implications for the use of the Tully-Fisher relation in the study of galaxy evolution and cosmology.

Dark Energy and Gravity The nature of dark energy and its implications for gravity remain profound mysteries in modern cosmology. In this paper, we explore the cosmological constant problem and the difficulties it poses for conventional theories of gravity. We argue that a satisfactory solution requires a shift in perspective, viewing gravity as an emergent phenomenon described by an effective theory using null vectors in spacetime. This approach allows us to gauge away any bulk cosmological constant and offers a potential explanation for its observed value through quantum gravitational fluctuations. Furthermore, we present a novel axiomatic approach to the cosmological constant, drawing inspiration from information theory's Khinchin axioms. Our axioms lead to a formula for the cosmological constant in perfect agreement with current observational data. This formula provides physical meaning to the Eddington-Dirac large number hypothesis and suggests that the observed value of the cosmological constant is not unnatural. Finally, we review a groundbreaking approach to quantum gravity based on noncommutative spacetime. By formulating gravity in terms of symplectic geometry, we can realize the equivalence principle from U(1) gauge theory and derive diffeomorphism symmetry from noncommutative electromagnetism. This framework allows for a background-independent quantum gravity theory that addresses longstanding problems such as the cosmological constant problem, the nature of dark energy, and the weakness of gravity compared to other forces. Moreover, it offers a remarkable interpretation of matter as stable localized geometries within the fundamental algebra of quantum gravity.

It is shown that the the interference of above-threshold electron de Brogliewaves, generated by an intense laser pulse at a metal surface yields attosecondelectron pulses. This inerference is an analogon of the superposition of highharmonics generated from rare gas atoms, resulting in trains of attosecondlight pulses.Owing to the inherent kinematic dispersion, the propagation ofattosecond de Broglie waves in vacuum is very different from that of attosecondlight pulses, which propagate without changing shape. Above the metal surfacethere are "collaps bands" and "revival layers" of the electron current even atmacroscopic distances. In the range of parameters considered, the maximum valueof the current densities of such ultrashort electron pulses has been estimatedto be of order of couple of tenths of milliamps per square centimeters.

ASTROD I is planned as a single spacecraft mission. It will useinterferometric and pulse ranging techniques between the spacecraft and groundstations, to make high precision measurements of the parameters that describethe solar system, and to test relativistic gravity with improved accuracy. Atthe heart of the spacecraft is a test mass, which the spacecraft will followusing a drag-free control system. The mission critically depends on maintainingthe geodesic motion of the test mass. Charging of the test mass due to cosmicrays and solar particles will disturb its geodesic motion. We have modelled thecharging process using the GEANT4 toolkit and a simplified, geometrical modeland estimate that the ASTROD I test mass will charge positively, at a rate of24 +/-7 e+/s, due to cosmic ray protons and alpha particles (3He and 4He) atsolar minimum. We have used the results of this simulation to estimate themagnitude of disturbances associated with test mass charging, for theworst-case scenario, taking into account uncertainties in the model andpotential charging contributions from minor cosmic-ray components.

Radiation transfer plays an important role in the formation of star formation, because the energy from young stars will heat and affect the surrounding gas and dust. This study aims to use energy equations in the simulation of smooth particles formed by stars to implement radiation transfer in energy equations in simulation. A new method of integrating energy equation with radiation transfer items into SPH formalism. The test simulation is performed by the collapse of the gravity collapse of the embedded original star. Compare the results with the analysis solution with the previous research. This new method captures the overall dynamic evolution and thermal structure that coincides with the previous work, which proves the future simulation potential of this method to study the feedback effect of a more complicated star formation area.

The library is based on stellar population synthesis models and takes into account the effects of dust extinction and nebular emission. We use the library to classify and parametrize a sample of unresolved galaxies observed by the Gaia satellite. We find that the majority of the galaxies in our sample are star-forming galaxies with a relatively young stellar population. Our results show the potential of using synthetic galaxy spectra to study the properties of unresolved galaxies. We also find a small number of galaxies that are either passive or have a very old stellar population.

The determination of the intrinsic switching field distributions in perpendicular recording media is very important.We propose a novel method to determine the intrinsic switching field distributions from the dependence of the switching field on the magnetization and the reversal magnetization.The intrinsic switching field distribution of sputtered Co/Pd multilayers with perpendicular magnetic anisotropy is determined by using this method.The obtained distribution can well explain the magnetization reversal behaviors of the sputtered Co/Pd multilayers.

In this study, we investigate the mechanical and dielectric relaxation spectra of seven highly viscous glass formers. By employing a combination of experimental and computational techniques, we aim to elucidate the dynamic behavior and underlying mechanisms within these systems. Through mechanical spectroscopy, we probe the viscoelastic properties and ascertain the relaxation timescales associated with structural transitions. Furthermore, dielectric measurements allow us to explore the polarization response and study the influence of molecular dynamics on the electrical behavior of the glass formers. Our findings provide valuable insights into the complex dynamics of highly viscous systems and contribute to a better understanding of glassy materials.

We analyze the metallicity distributions of stars in several high-latitude fields included in the SDSS DR14 dataset. The metallicities are estimated for unevolved G-type stars located within 10 kpc of the Sun. A general metallicity gradient with Galactic height is identified, with more metal-rich stars found closer to the Galactic plane. The gradient is steepest at short heights (<5 kpc) reflecting the formation of the thin disc via dissipative collapse. At intermediate heights the gradient flattens indicating influence from the thick disc. For the inner halo beyond 5 kpc distance from the plane, the metallicity distribution is nearly uniform suggesting an accretion origin for this old population.

Collaborative beamforming (CB) and cooperative transmission (CT) haverecently emerged as communication techniques that can make effective use ofcollaborative/cooperative nodes to create a virtualmultiple-input/multiple-output (MIMO) system. Extending the lifetime ofnetworks composed of battery-operated nodes is a key issue in the design andoperation of wireless sensor networks. This paper considers the effects onnetwork lifetime of allowing closely located nodes to use CB/CT to reduce theload or even to avoid packet-forwarding requests to nodes that have criticalbattery life. First, the effectiveness of CB/CT in improving the signalstrength at a faraway destination using energy in nearby nodes is studied.Then, the performance improvement obtained by this technique is analyzed for aspecial 2D disk case. Further, for general networks in whichinformation-generation rates are fixed, a new routing problem is formulated asa linear programming problem, while for other general networks, the cost forrouting is dynamically adjusted according to the amount of energy remaining andthe effectiveness of CB/CT. From the analysis and the simulation results, it isseen that the proposed method can reduce the payloads of energy-depleting nodesby about 90% in the special case network considered and improve the lifetimesof general networks by about 10%, compared with existing techniques.

The reverse shock phenomenon in the supernova remnant (SNR) 1987A has captivated astronomers since its discovery. This study investigates the structure and dynamics of the reverse shock and its impact on the surrounding environment. By analyzing multi-wavelength observations and conducting detailed hydrodynamical simulations, we unveil the intricate processes governing the reverse shock interaction. Our findings reveal the presence of a reverse shock that decelerates the outwardly expanding material, leading to the formation of a dense, shocked region with enhanced thermal and nonthermal emissions. Moreover, we discuss the implications of these findings for our understanding of supernova explosion mechanisms and the injection of energy into the surrounding interstellar medium.

The formation of terrestrial and habitable planets in binry and multi-star systems represents a unique and intriguing aspect of plantary science. This article investigates the actors that influence planet formation in such ystems, considering the dynamical interactions and gravitational perturbations that arise from multiple stellar companions. We erview recent observations and theoretical models to assVess the prevalence and stability of planetary systems in binary and multi-star configurations. The presence of additioNal stellar companions can alter the planet formation process through gravtational instabilities, perturbed disk structures, and changing dynamical environments. We discuss the implications of these effects on the habitability of planets, dncluding their orbital stability, climate, and potential for hostinr life. Finally, we highlight the future prospects for observational surveys and numerical simulation aimed at further understanding the forpmation and long-term evolution of terrestrial and habitable plaJets in binary and multi-star systems.

It begins by introducing the basic concepts of string theory, including the notion of extra dimensions and the concept of branes. It then discusses how branes can be used to induce gravity, and the implications of this for our understanding of the universe. Finally, it discusses some open questions in brane induced gravity, and suggests some directions for future research.

The IceCube neutrino detector is a cubic kilometer TeV to PeV neutrinodetector under construction at the geographic South Pole. The dominantpopulation of neutrinos detected in IceCube is due to meson decay in cosmic-rayair showers. These atmospheric neutrinos are relatively well-understood andserve as a calibration and verification tool for the new detector. In 2006, thedetector was approximately 10% completed, and we report on data acquired fromthe detector in this configuration. We observe an atmospheric neutrino signalconsistent with expectations, demonstrating that the IceCube detector iscapable of identifying neutrino events. In the first 137.4 days of livetime,234 neutrino candidates were selected with an expectation of 211 +/-76.1(syst.) +/- 14.5(stat.) events from atmospheric neutrinos.

(abridged) The first unidentified very high energy gamma ray source (TeVJ2032+4130) in the Cygnus region has been the subject of intensive search for acounterpart source at other wavelengths. A deep ($\approx 50$ ksec) exposure ofTeV J2032+4130 with \textit{XMM-Newton} has been obtained. The contribution ofpoint sources to the observed X-ray emission from TeV J2032+4130 is subtractedfrom the data. The point-source subtracted X-ray data are analyzed using blanksky exposures and regions adjacent to the position of TeV J2032+4130 in thefield of view covered by the XMM-Newton telescopes to search for diffuse X-rayemission. An extended X-ray emission region with a full width half maximum(FWHM) size of $\approx 12$ arc min is found. The centroid of the emission isco-located with the position of TeV J2032+4130.The energy spectrum of theemission coinciding with the position and extension of TeV J2032+4130 can bemodeled by a power-law model with a photon index$\Gamma=1.5\pm0.2_\mathrm{stat}\pm0.3_\mathrm{sys}$ and an energy fluxintegrated between 2 and 10 keV of $f_{2-10 \mathrm{keV}} \approx 7\cdot10^{-13}$ ergs/(cm$^2$ s) which is lower than the very high energy gamma-rayflux observed from TeV J2032+4130. We conclude that the faint extended X-rayemission discovered in this observation is the X-ray counterpart of TeVJ2032+4130. Formally, it can not be excluded that the extended emission is dueto an unrelated population of faint, hot ($k_BT\approx 10$ keV) unresolvedpoint-sources which by chance coincides with the position and extension of TeVJ2032+4130. We discuss our findings in the frame of both hadronic and leptonicgamma-ray production scenarios.

We investigate Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) in one dimension with a non-zero quark chemical potential. Utilizing chiral perturbation theory, we analyze the distribution of the phase angle and magnitude of the fermion determinant. Our results demonstrate that for small chemical potentials, the distribution of the phase angle follows a Gaussian pattern. However, when the quark mass resides within the support of the Dirac spectrum, the distribution becomes periodic and Lorentzian in nature. We further explore the relationship between the phase of the fermion determinant and key observables such as the baryon number and chiral condensate. Integration over the phase angle reveals significant cancellations, emphasizing the intricacies involved. Additionally, we extend our investigation to QCD in one Euclidean dimension, where we analytically establish that the phase angle distribution corresponds to a periodic Lorentzian when the quark mass falls within the spectral density range of the Dirac operator. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the behavior of QCD at non-zero quark chemical potential, particularly in low-dimensional scenarios.

We show the locations of the SWIFT short hard bursts (SHB) with afterglows onthe galactic map and compare with the VSB BATSE events. As we have pointed outbefore, there is an excess of events in the galactic map of BATSE VSB events.We not that none of VSB SWIFT era events fall into this cluster. More SWIFTevents are needed to check this claim. We also report a new study with KONUSdata of the VSB sample with an average energy above 90 keV showing a clearexcess of events below 100 ms duration (T90) that have large mean energyprotons. We suggest that VSB themselves consist of two subclasses: a fractionof events have peculiar distribution properties and have no detectablecounterparts, as might be expected for exotic sources such as primordial blackholes. We show how GLAST could add key new information to the study of VSBbursts and could help test the black hole concept.

Abstact:This paper uses the K-band luminosity of the red clump (RC) to estimate the distances to populous clusters in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). We have used 2MASS and VVV near-infrared photometry to select RC stars in 18 populous clusters of the LMC. Adoptions a distance of 50.1 kpc to the LMC, we obtain a mean RC K-band magnitude of \({M}_{K,RC}=-8.21pm0.03\) mag. Assuming that RC stars are standard candles with an absolute K-band vastness of \({M}_{K,RC}=-8.16\) mag, we estimate the paths to the clusters. Comparison with the literature distances indicates that the K-bad RC method provides accurate distances, with a mean difference of 0.5 kpc. The derived distan ces are used to investigate the spatial distribution and kinematics of the clusters in the LMC. We find that the clusters in the L MC are distributed in two main groupings, a northern group centered on \((l,b)=(283\degr, -35\degr)\) and a southern group centered on \((l,b)=(292\degr,-48\degr)\). The clusters in the northern group are younger and more metal-rish than those in the southern group. The velocity dispersion of the clusters is 22 km s^(-1), which is consistent with the previous results.

Recent investigations have established an analogy between the entropy offour-dimensional supersymmetric black holes in string theory and entanglementin quantum information theory. Examples include: (1) N=2 STU black holes andthe tripartite entanglement of three qubits (2-state systems), where the commonsymmetry is [SL(2)]^3 and (2) N=8 black holes and the tripartite entanglementof seven qubits where the common symmetry is E_7 which contains [SL(2)]^7. Herewe present another example: N=8 black holes (or black strings) in fivedimensions and the bipartite entanglement of three qutrits (3-state systems),where the common symmetry is E_6 which contains [SL(3)]^3. Both the black hole(or black string) entropy and the entanglement measure are provided by theCartan cubic E_6 invariant. Similar analogies exist for ''magic'' N=2supergravity black holes in both four and five dimensions.

We use a combination of optical and near-infrared observations to study the spectral and temporal properties of these quasars to understand their physical processes and underlying mechanisms. Our results show that both quasars show significant line and continuum variability on timescales of days to years, with [Quasar Name 1] showing a more pronounced variability in the broad H line. We also find that the continuum emission of both quasars is significantly polarized, indicating the presence of scattering processes in their host galaxies. Our results provide new insights into the physical properties of high-luminosity quasars at intermediate redshifts, revealing their complex and dynamic nature. By analyzing the variations in the line and continuum profiles, we infer the presence of a complex accretion disk structure with multiple hot spots and a dominant outer disk component.

The missing satellites problem has long been a topic of interest and concern in the field of satellite technology. Despite advances in technology, a significant number of satellites remain unaccounted for, with many believed to be in orbit around the Earth. In this article, we redefine the missing satellites problem and propose a new approach to addressing it. By leveraging machine learning algorithms and advanced data analysis techniques, we are able to identify and track previously undetected satellites, providing new insights into their behavior and characteristics. Our findings have significant implications for the future of satellite technology and the potential applications of artificial intelligence in this field. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of case studies and simulations, highlighting the improved accuracy and efficiency of our method compared to traditional methods. Overall, our work represents a significant step forward in addressing the missing satellites problem and has the potential to revolutionize the field of satellite technology.

Frustration effects in antiferromagnetic FCC Heisenberg films are studied using a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and a phenomenological model. The model incorporates the effects of nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor exchange interactions, as well as the effects of a magnetic field. The simulations are used to calculate the magnetic properties of the films, including the magnetization, the susceptibility, and the specific heat. The model is used to fit the simulation results and to extract the values of the exchange constants and the magnetic field. The results show that the frustration effects are significant in the films and that they lead to a number of interesting magnetic properties. In particular, the films exhibit a reentrant spin-glass transition at low temperatures.

Due to the shear and convection movement caused by the flow material, the surface of the material on the material on material may lead to a complex hybrid process. In this study, we studied the turbulence mixing mechanism that played a role in absorbing the surface layer of the neutron star and its impact on the observation nature of these systems. Using the combination of numerical simulation and analysis of modeling, we discussed the role of Kelvin -Holmz's instability, magnetization instability and convective process in promoting accumulation materials. We found that the instability of the Cairwin -Hormholz plays a vital role in turbulent mixing on the interface between the driving accumulated material and the neutron star surface. These instability will produce vortex and vortex, which effectively mixes the accumulated materials and basic layers. In addition, we have studied the influence of magnetic field on the turbulence mixing process. Our results show that in the absence of a strong magnetic field, magnetization instability can significantly enhance mixing. The interaction between turbulence movement and magnetic fields leads to a complex structure and enhances the transportation of angular momentum and heat. We also studied the effect on flowing in turbulence and its influence on the thermal structure of accumulated materials. We found that the current motion can effectively mix the layer of the accumulated material, which affects its composition and temperature curve. These are important consequences of the spectrum and optical curve of the streaming neutron stars.

We present a general framework for the calculation of maximally supersymmetric planar Yang-Mills amplitudes at five loops. The method is basis on a combination of the integrand reduction method and the loop-by-loop approach, where the integrand reduction is performed in the five-dimensional maximally sսpersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in dimensional regularization and the loop integrals are calculated in the four-dimensional theory. We derive the five-loop integrands for all MHV and NMHV amplitudes and give explisit results for the five-loop MHV amplitudes. We demonstrate the cancellation of all ultraviolet and infrared divergences by frankly calculating the two-loop and three-loop MHV amplitudes as well as the two-loop NMHV amplitudes in dimensional regularization in four dimensions. We also perform checking of our results against the known five-loop MHV amplitude in the literature.

We calculate growth rates and corresponding gains for RX and LO moderadiation associated with the cyclotron maser instability for parameterizedhorseshoe electron velocity distributions. The velocity distribution functionwas modeled to closely fit the electron distribution functions observed in theauroral cavity. We systematically varied the model parameters as well as thepropagation direction to study the dependence of growth rates on modelparameters. The growth rate depends strongly on loss cone opening angle, whichmust be less than $90^{o}$ for significant CMI growth. The growth rate issharply peaked for perpendicular radiation ($k_{\parallel} = 0$), with afull-width at half-maximum $1.7^{o}$, in good agreement with observed k-vectororientations and numerical simulations. The fractional bandwidth varied between10$^{-4}$ and 10$^{-2}$, depending most strongly on propagation direction. Thisrange encompasses nearly all observed fractional AKR burst bandwidths. We findexcellent agreement between the computed RX mode emergent intensities andobserved AKR intensities assuming convective growth length $L_c\approx$20-40 kmand group speed 0.15$c$. The only computed LO mode growth rates compatibleobserved LO mode radiation levels occurred for number densities more than 100times the average energetic electron densities measured in auroral cavities.This implies that LO mode radiation is not produced directly by the CMImechanism but more likely results from mode conversion of RX mode radiation. Wefind that perturbation of the model velocity distribution by large ion solitarywaves (ion holes) can enhance the growth rate by a factor of 2-4. This willresult in a gain enhancement more than 40 dB depending on the convective growthlength within the structure. Similar enhancements may be caused by EMIC waves.

The data from a CO(1 - 0) mapping survey of 40 nearby spiral galaxiesperformed with the Nobeyama 45-m telescope are presented. The criteria of thesample selection were (1) RC3 morphological type in the range Sa to Scd, (2)distance less than 25 Mpc, (3) inclination angle less than 79deg (RC3), (4)flux at 100 um higher than ~ 10 Jy, (5) spiral structure is not destroyed byinteraction. The maps of CO cover most of the optical disk of the galaxies. Weinvestigated the influence of bar on the distribution of molecular gas inspiral galaxies using these data. We confirmed that the degree of centralconcentration is higher in barred spirals than in non-barred spirals as shownby the previous works. Furthermore, we present an observational evidence thatbars are efficient in driving molecular gas that lies within the bar lengthtoward the center, while the role in bringing gas in from the outer parts ofthe disks is small. The transported gas accounts for about half of moleculargas within the central region in barred spiral galaxies. We found a correlationbetween the degree of central concentration and bar strength. Galaxies withstronger bars tend to have higher central concentration. The correlationimplies that stronger bars accumulate molecular gas toward the center moreefficiently. These results are consistent with long-lived bars.

The new scheme of stochastic quantization is proposed. This quantizationprocedure is equivalent to the deformation of an algebra of observables in themanner of deformation quantization with an imaginary deformation parameter (thePlanck constant). We apply this method to the models of nonrelativistic andrelativistic particles interacting with an electromagnetic field. In the firstcase we establish the equivalence of such a quantization to the Fokker-Planckequation with a special force. The application of the proposed quantizationprocedure to the model of a relativistic particle results in a relativisticgeneralization of the Fokker-Planck equation in the coordinate space, which inthe absence of the electromagnetic field reduces to the relativistic diffusion(heat) equation. The stationary probability distribution functions for astochastically quantized particle diffusing under a barrier and a particle inthe potential of a harmonic oscillator are derived.

This article investigates the detection of ellipsoidal oscillations induced by substellar companions in the Kepler mission. First, we discuss the theoretical framework and key parameters influencing the oscillations. We then conduct a thorough analysis of the Kepler data to identify potential targets exhibiting such oscillations. Our results reveal several candidates with signals consistent with ellipsoidal oscillations, which we further investigate using follow-up observations. These oscillations can be used to infer the presence of substellar companions and provide constraints on their masses and orbital properties. Our findings have significant implications for the detection and characterization of exoplanetary systems, particularly those with close-in companions. Furthermore, our results emphasize the importance of considering stellar oscillations in the analysis of exoplanetary transit data. Finally, we discuss the potential for future missions to capitalize on this phenomenon and expand our understanding of exoplanetary systems.

The closedness condition for real geodesics on n-dimensional ellipsoids is ingeneral transcendental in the parameters (semiaxes of the ellipsoid andconstants of motion). We show that it is algebraic in the parameters if andonly if both the real and the imaginary geodesics are closed and wecharacterize such double--periodicity condition via real hyperelliptictangential coverings. We prove the density of algebraically closed geodesics onn-dimensional ellipsoids with respect to the natural topology in the(2n)-dimensional real parameter space. In particular, the approximatingsequence of algebraic closed geodesics on the approximated ellipsoids may bechosen so to share the same values of the length and of the real period vectoras the limiting closed geodesic on the limiting ellipsoid. Finally, for real doubly-periodic geodesics on triaxial ellipsoids, we showhow to evaluate algebraically the period mapping and we present some explicitexamples of families of algebraically closed geodesics.

This paper investigates the polarization power spectra signatures expected from a network of cosmic strings. Using a field-theoretic string simulation, the authors generate CMB maps containing the contributions from a scaling distribution of cosmic strings over cosmic history. The results indicate that the B-mode polarization power spectra generated by cosmic strings could be detectable with upcoming high-sensitivity CMB experiments and could be distinguishable from the gravitational wave signature.

We report on a search for gravitational waves from the coalescence of compactbinaries during the third and fourth LIGO science runs. The search focused ongravitational waves generated during the inspiral phase of the binaryevolution. In our analysis, we considered three categories of compact binarysystems, ordered by mass: (i) primordial black hole binaries with masses in therange 0.35 M(sun) < m1, m2 < 1.0 M(sun), (ii) binary neutron stars with massesin the range 1.0 M(sun) < m1, m2 < 3.0 M(sun), and (iii) binary black holeswith masses in the range 3.0 M(sun)< m1, m2 < m_(max) with the additionalconstraint m1+ m2 < m_(max), where m_(max) was set to 40.0 M(sun) and 80.0M(sun) in the third and fourth science runs, respectively. Although thedetectors could probe to distances as far as tens of Mpc, no gravitational-wavesignals were identified in the 1364 hours of data we analyzed. Assuming abinary population with a Gaussian distribution around 0.75-0.75 M(sun), 1.4-1.4M(sun), and 5.0-5.0 M(sun), we derived 90%-confidence upper limit rates of 4.9yr^(-1) L10^(-1) for primordial black hole binaries, 1.2 yr^(-1) L10^(-1) forbinary neutron stars, and 0.5 yr^(-1) L10^(-1) for stellar mass binary blackholes, where L10 is 10^(10) times the blue light luminosity of the Sun.

We obtained H-band polarimetric data of IRAS 19312+1950 using thenear-infrared camera (CIAO) on the 8 m Subaru telescope. In order toinvestigate the physical properties of the central star and the nebula, weperformed dust radiative transfer modeling and compared the model results withthe observed spectral energy distributions (SEDs), the radial profiles of thetotal intensity image, and the fraction of linear polarization map. The totalintensity image shows a nearly spherical core with ~3" radius, an S-shaped armextending ~10" in the northwest to southeast direction, and an extended lobetowards the southwest. The polarization map shows a centro-symmetric vectoralignment in almost the entire nebula and low polarizations along the S-shapedarm. These results suggest that the nebula is accompanied by a central star,and the S-shaped arm has a physically ring-like structure. From our radiativetransfer modeling, we estimated the stellar temperature, the bolometricluminosity, and the current mass-loss rate to be 2800 K, 7000 L_sun, and5.3x10^{-6} M_sun yr^{-1}, respectively. Taking into account previousobservational results, such as the detection of SiO maser emissions andsilicate absorption feature in the 10 $\mu$m spectrum, our dust radiativetransfer analysis based on our NIR imaging polarimetry suggests that (1) thecentral star of IRAS 19312+1950 is likely to be an oxygen-rich, dust-enshroudedAGB star and (2) most of the circumstellar material originates from othersources (e.g. ambient dark clouds) rather than as a result of mass loss fromthe central star.

The proposed approach integrates various condition monitoring techniques to extract relevant features from the data, and uses these features to train and validate the ANN models. The methodology is applied to a real-world data set from a wind-turbine drivetrain, and the results show that it is effective in predicting the residual life of the machine and its components. The paper also discusses the challenges associated with residual life estimation, such as the scarcity of data and the need for robust and interpretable models. The proposed methodology addresses these challenges by combining deep learning with physics-based models. The developed approach has the potential to improve the reliability and efficiency of maintenance operations, reduce costs, and enhance the safety of industrial systems.

In this paper, we explore the possibility of global-string and vortex superfluids in a supersymmetric scenario. We examine the theoretical f ramework for the existence of these exotic forms of matter and discuss the potential implications for our understanding of the universe. Using a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we investigate the behavior of global-string and vortex superfluids in various scenarios, including the influence of supersymmetry-breaking effects. Our results inicate that these forms of matter could exhibit novel properties and offer new thoughts into the fundamental nature of the universe. Further study of global-string and vortex superfluids in supersymmetric scenarios m ay lead to a deeper understanding of the interplay between matter and energy at the most fundamental level.

This study re-examines the interaction between classical and quantum dipoles. Previous research has modeled the dipole interaction using first-order perturbation theory, which breaks down in certain regimes. We develop a new theoretical framework to describe the dipole interaction beyond the perturbation limit. Our formalism is derived using noether currents and Ward identities of quantum electrodynamics. Analytical solutions are obtained in the non-retardation limit and numerical solutions are presented for the general case. The analytical solutions show non-trivial corrections to the induced dipole moments compared to first-order perturbation theory. Numerical simulations indicate the formation of bound states between the classical and quantum dipoles in certain parameter spaces. The new understanding of the dipole interaction gained from this work is expected to impact fields such as light-matter coupling in cavity quantum electrodynamics and hybrid classical-quantum systems. Our formalism provides a pathway to accurately model and harness interactions between classical and quantum systems.

We first introduce the concept of strong peak points and prove that they are dense in the space of all continuous functions. Then we prove that the set of strong peak functions is dense in the space of all continuous functions. Finally, we prove that the set of strong peak functions is dense in the space of all continuous functions which vanish at infinity.

This paper considers broadcast channels with L antennas at the base stationand m single-antenna users, where each user has perfect channel knowledge andthe base station obtains channel information through a finite rate feedback.The key observation of this paper is that the optimal number of on-users (usersturned on), say s, is a function of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and othersystem parameters. Towards this observation, we use asymptotic analysis toguide the design of feedback and transmission strategies. As L, m and thefeedback rates approach infinity linearly, we derive the asymptotic optimalfeedback strategy and a realistic criterion to decide which users should beturned on. Define the corresponding asymptotic throughput per antenna as thespatial efficiency. It is a function of the number of on-users s, andtherefore, s should be appropriately chosen. Based on the above asymptoticresults, we also develop a scheme for a system with finite many antennas andusers. Compared with other works where s is presumed constant, our schemeachieves a significant gain by choosing the appropriate s. Furthermore, ouranalysis and scheme is valid for heterogeneous systems where different usersmay have different path loss coefficients and feedback rates.

L, T, and Y dwarfs, collectively known as ultracool dwarfs, are a class of low-mass stars with temperatures and spectral features that distinuish them from other stellar types. Despite significant advancements in our understanding of these objects, several outstanding issues remain that hinder a comprehensive comprehension of their nature and characteristics. This article provides a review of the unresolved questions and challenges associated with L, T, and Y goblins. Firstly, we discuss the ongoing debate regarding the formation mechanisms and evolutionary pathways of these dwarfs, including the roles of cloud formation and atmospheric properties. Secondly, we highlight the issue of accurate spectral classification and the need for refined classification schemes that capture the diverse range of ultracool runt properties. Furthermore, we address the challenges posed by the peculiar atmospheric conditions displayed by some L, T, and Y dwarfs, such as the presence of complex ambience chemistry and the puzzling persistence of methane absorption in certain spectral types. We also delve into the unresolved question of the frequently and nature of binray systems among ultracool dwarfs, examining the implications for their formation and evolution. Additionally, we explore the limitations and uncertainties in current observational techniques and instruments that restrcit our ability to study L, T, and Y dwarfs comprehensively. Enhanced observational capabilities, such as high-resolution spectroscopy and advanced imaging technologies, will be vital for future progress in this field. Finally, we highlight the importance of theoretical models and simulations in elucidating the physical mechanisms governing the atmospheirc and evolutionary processes in L, T, and Y dwarfs. Improved computer models incorporating complex physics, cloud formation, and chemical processes are essential for advancing our understanding.
