HD 189733B is a huge natural gas giant planet, which is very close to its host star HD 189733, causing extreme heating of the permanent era of the planet. Using an infrared observation value from the Spitzer Space Telescope, we observed the full track of multiple HD 189733B to measure the temperature changes of the entire planet. Our hot map reveals a strong difference in day and night temperature, while the temperature of the planet day exceeds 1200 Kelvin, and the temperature below 900 Kelvin at night is lower. The contrast of this big night is likely to be driven by the lack of the atmosphere that can effectively transport calories from day to night from day to night. We compared the observation results with the high -radiation hot Jupiter's atmospheric circulation model, and found that our data explained our data through the re -distribution of the heat day and night. The heat map introduced in this study provides new constraints on the atmospheric dynamics and performance of highly radiated exterior planet HD 189733B.

Pragmatism is a philosophical approach that emphasizes the importance of practical consequences and results. It is often associated with the American philosopher William James. It is one of the oldest and most widely accepted interpretations of quantum mechanics, and it is based on the idea that the act of observing a quantum system affects the outcome of the measurement. This paper explores the relationship between the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics and pragmatism, arguing that the two approaches share a commitment to the importance of experience and a rejection of metaphysical realism. The paper concludes that pragmatism can be a useful way to understand and interpret the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.

The long gamar ray explosion (LGRB) is a fierce explosion that releases a lot of energy in the form of gamma radiation. LGRB's ancestral cells or stars that cause these incidents have always been the theme of many research and debate. In this article, we review the current status of LGRB ancestral cells, including possible quality, metal, and evolution. We have also discussed how to explain the various models of LGRB physics, as well as how they are related to their characteristics of ancestral cell star. Finally, we focused on some outstanding issues in this field and raised the direction of future research.

The border sliding at the fluid -solid interface is of great significance to the application of micro -flow. In this study, through the molecular dynamic simulation of fluid flows in the microcontroller, the effect of surface roughness on the sliding of the boundary was studied. It is found that increasing surface roughness will cause enhanced boundaries to slip to the best roughness. At the top of the optimal roughness, the border slip is decreased as the roughness further increases. The competitive role of the roughness and inhibitory roughness disorder of sliding is provided for this kind of non -monotonous dependence. These findings provide new insights to control the sliding of the boundary and help design micro -flow equipment with lower liquidity.

Globular clusters provide unique natural laboratories to study stellar evolution owing to their large populations of coeval stars. This study investigates the evolution of red giant branch stars and formation of white dwarfs within the old open star cluster NGC 6791. Precise photometric observations are presented for over one thousand stars spanning the main sequence turnoff through the white dwarf cooling sequence. Analysis of the red giant branch mass distribution reveals substantial mass loss, with stars losing an average of 0.25 solar masses during the helium flash phase. The stellar remnants along the white dwarf cooling sequence predominantly have low masses, clustering around an average of 0.48 solar masses. These findings suggest that the enhanced mass loss experienced by red giant branch stars in this cluster's dense environment plays a key role in shaping the population of low-mass white dwarfs formed.

Neutron stars contain matter in one of the densest forms found in theUniverse. This feature, together with the unprecedented progress inobservational astrophysics, makes such stars superb astrophysical laboratoriesfor a broad range of exciting physical studies. This paper gives an overview ofthe phases of dense matter predicted to make their appearance in the cores ofneutron stars. Particular emphasis is put on the role of strangeness. Netstrangeness is carried by hyperons, K-mesons, H-dibaryons, and strange quarkmatter, and may leave its mark in the masses, radii, moment of inertia,dragging of local inertial frames, cooling behavior, surface composition, andthe spin evolution of neutron stars. These observables play a key role for theexploration of the phase diagram of dense nuclear matter at high baryon numberdensity but low temperature, which is not accessible to relativistic heavy ioncollision experiments.

We study the prospects for detecting Weakly Interacting Massive Particles(WIMPs), in a number of phenomenological scenarios, with a detector composed ofa target simultaneously sensitive to both spin-dependent and spin-independentcouplings, as is the case of COUPP (Chicagoland Observatory for UndergroundParticle Physics). First, we show that sensitivity to both couplings optimizeschances of initial WIMP detection. Second, we demonstrate that in case ofdetection, comparison of the signal on two complementary targets, such as inCOUPP CF3I and C4F10 bubble chambers, allows a significantly more precisedetermination of the dark matter axial and scalar couplings. This strategywould provide crucial information on the nature of the WIMPs, and possiblyallow discrimination between neutralino and Kaluza-Klein dark matter.

The angular distribution of the emitted electrons, following the two-photonionization of the hydrogen-like ions, is studied within the framework of secondorder perturbation theory and the Dirac equation. Using a density matrixapproach, we have investigated the effects which arise from the polarization ofthe incoming light as well as from the higher multipoles in the expansion ofthe electron--photon interaction. For medium- and high-Z ions, in particular,the non-dipole contributions give rise to a significant change in the angulardistribution of the emitted electrons, if compared with the electric-dipoleapproximation. This includes a strong forward emission while, in dipoleapproxmation, the electron emission always occurs symmetric with respect to theplane which is perpendicular to the photon beam. Detailed computations for thedependence of the photoelectron angular distributions on the polarization ofthe incident light are carried out for the ionization of H, Xe$^{53+}$, andU$^{91+}$ (hydrogen-like) ions.

Spitzer observations of a 24 micron shadow: Bok Globule CB190Bok globules are small, dense clouds of molecular gas and dust that are often found in the early stages of star formaion. They are named after Bart Bok, who first defined them in the 1940s. CB190 is a Fu globule located in the constellation of Taurus. It was first observed by the Spitzer Space Telescope in 2003. The Spitzer observations uncovered a 24 micron shadow cast by the globule. This shadow is caused by the absorption of 2Ꮞ micron radiation by the dust in the globule. The sizes and shape of the shadow can be used to determine the properties of the globule, such as its density and size. The Spitzer observations of CB190 have provided new insights into the nature of Bok globules. These observations have shown that Bk globules are not simply dark clouds of gas and dust, but that they are also sites of active stars formation. The shred cast by CB190 is evidence that the globule is collapsing under its own gravity. This collapse is likely to lead to the formation of one or more stars. The Spitzer observations of CB190 have also helped to identify the presence of a new tye of object, called a "Bok globule shadow." These shadows are caused by the absorpton of 24 micron radiation by the dust in Bok globules. The shadows can be us ed to identify Bok globules that are in the early stages of star formation. The Spitzer observations of CB190 have provided valuable new information about Bok globules. These observations have shown that Bok globules are not simply dark clouds of gas and dust, but that they are also sites of active star formation. The shadows cat by Bok globules can be used to identify Bok secretions that are in the early stages of star formation.

We investigate degenerate saddle point problems, which can be viewed as limitcases of standard mixed formulations of symmetric problems with large jumps incoefficients. We prove that they are well-posed in a standard norm despite thedegeneracy. By wellposedness we mean a stable dependence of the solution on theright-hand side. A known approach of splitting the saddle point problem intoseparate equations for the primary unknown and for the Lagrange multiplier isused. We revisit the traditional Ladygenskaya--Babu\v{s}ka--Brezzi (LBB) orinf--sup condition as well as the standard coercivity condition, and analyzehow they are affected by the degeneracy of the corresponding bilinear forms. Wesuggest and discuss generalized conditions that cover the degenerate case. TheLBB or inf--sup condition is necessary and sufficient for wellposedness of theproblem with respect to the Lagrange multiplier under some assumptions. Thegeneralized coercivity condition is necessary and sufficient for wellposednessof the problem with respect to the primary unknown under some otherassumptions. We connect the generalized coercivity condition to thepositiveness of the minimum gap of relevant subspaces, and propose severalequivalent expressions for the minimum gap. Our results provide a foundationfor research on uniform wellposedness of mixed formulations of symmetricproblems with large jumps in coefficients in a standard norm, independent ofthe jumps. Such problems appear, e.g., in numerical simulations of compositematerials made of components with contrasting properties.

Diffuse emission is produced in energetic cosmic ray (CR) interactions,mainly protons and electrons, with the interstellar gas and radiation field andcontains the information about particle spectra in distant regions of theGalaxy. It may also contain information about exotic processes such as darkmatter annihilation, black hole evaporation etc. A model of the diffuseemission is important for determination of the source positions and spectra.Calculation of the Galactic diffuse continuum gamma-ray emission requires amodel for CR propagation as the first step. Such a model is based on theory ofparticle transport in the interstellar medium as well as on many kinds of dataprovided by different experiments in Astrophysics and Particle and NuclearPhysics. Such data include: secondary particle and isotopic production crosssections, total interaction nuclear cross sections and lifetimes of radioactivespecies, gas mass calibrations and gas distribution in the Galaxy (H_2, H I, HII), interstellar radiation field, CR source distribution and particle spectraat the sources, magnetic field, energy losses, gamma-ray and synchrotronproduction mechanisms, and many other issues. We are continuously improving theGALPROP model and the code to keep up with a flow of new data. Improvement inany field may affect the Galactic diffuse continuum gamma-ray emission modelused as a background model by the GLAST LAT instrument. Here we report aboutthe latest improvements of the GALPROP and the diffuse emission model.

We investigate electronic transport through II-VI semiconductor resonanttunneling structures containing diluted magnetic impurities. Due to theexchange interaction between the conduction electrons and the impurities, therearises a giant Zeeman splitting in the presence of a moderately low magneticfield. As a consequence, when the quantum well is magnetically doped thecurrent-voltage characteristics shows two peaks corresponding to transport foreach spin channel. This behavior is experimentally observed and can bereproduced with a simple tunneling model. The model thus allows to analyzeother configurations. First, we further increase the magnetic field, whichleads to a spin polarization of the electronic current injected from the leads,thus giving rise to a relative change in the current amplitude. We demonstratethat the spin polarization in the emitter can be determined from such a change.Furthermore, in the case of a magnetically doped injector our model shows alarge increase in peak amplitude and a shift of the resonance to highervoltages as the external field increases. We find that this effect arises froma combination of giant Zeeman splitting, 3-D incident distribution and broadresonance linewidth.

Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that produce bundles of electromagnetic radiation. These beams appear to observers as regular pulses of light as the star twists. While pulsar emission has been extensively studied since their discovery, the mechanisms powering the produced of gamma-rays remains uncertain. In this work, we develop an annular gap acceleration model to processing gamma-ray emission from pulsars. The model proposes that particle acceleration arise in annular gaps that form in the outer magnetosphere along magnetic field rows increase from the neutron star surface to the light cylinder. Within these gaps, magnetic regions curvature and plasmas effects are thought to result in acceleration of charged particles. We numerically counterfeiting electric fields and trajectory tracing to investigate particle energization in the gaps. Our simulations illustrating that principal electrons and positrons can gain energies exceeding 1 GeV within the gaps for typical pulsar parameters. Inverse Compton scattering and curvature radiation from these high-energy particles in the stiff magnetic fields are then analysed as emission mechanisms for the observed gamma-ray pulses. Synthetic light curves and spectra generated from the model are compared to present gamma-ray opinions of several pulsars. The model provides fine agreement with key observables such as pulse profiles and spectral cutoffs. We conclude that an annular drawback acceleration scenario can plausibly account for the basic properties of pulsed gamma-ray emission realised from pulsars. However, some open questions regarding pair generators within the gaps require further investigation.

Gravity wave (GW) detector is sensitive to the various instruments and environmental interference of the signals generated by the physical source of the celestial body. In the context of finding short -term GW transient, tools and environmental interference constitute a major challenge for identifying the real celestial physical signal. These interferences are usually called faults, and they are usually vetoed during the post -treatment phase of the analysis. However, after the facts, some faults cannot be reliably recognized. To solve this problem, we recommend and study a new method to effectively refuse the failure online. Our method uses physical models to identify tool channels that may be interfered and vetoed by triggers containing problematic data. We prove that our method is effective in veto failure, while retaining the high sensitivity to the GW signal of celestial physical physics.

The a0(980)-f0(980) mixing intensity has been predicted to be in the range of0.01 to 0.1 by various theoretical models, but lacking firm experimentalobservation. We examine the possibility of extracting the a0(980)-f0(980)mixing from J/psi -> phi f0 -> phi a0 reaction at upgraded Beijing ElectronPositron Collider with BESIII detector. While the branching ratio of thisprocess through the a0(980)-f0(980) mixing is expected to be about $O(10^{-6})$similar to the estimated total amount from two background reactions J/psi ->gamma* -> phi a0 and J/psi -> K* K + c.c. -> phi a0, the peak width from thea0(980)-f0(980) mixing is about 8 MeV, much smaller than that from othermechanisms. With $10^9$ $J/\psi$ events at BESIII, the a0(980)-f0(980) mixingintensity is expected to be unambiguously and precisely measured.

The article presents an iproved chemical composition analysis of the 1994 outburst of the black hole binary Nova Scorpii 1994 (CRO J1655-40) and discusses miplications for the physics of this system and other accreting black holes. The analysis is based on the optical, ultraviPlet, and X-ray spectra obtained during the outburst. The results indicate that the composition of the ejecta is consisent with that of the secondarvy star in the system, which is a low-mass, helium-rich star. The analysis also reveals the mpresence of a strong outflow in the system, which is likely driven by radiation pressuwre from the black hole. The outflow is found to be enriched in the elements Gcarbon, nitrogen, and xoygen, which are thought to be produed in the nuclear reactions in the accreting matter around the black hole. yThe implications of these results for the physics of this system and other accreting black holes are discussed.

This article examines the interplay between the cosmological constant and the Cosmological Casimir effect in the context of an accelerating universe. By adopting a maximally Planckian momentum cutoff, we derive the renormalized energy-momentum tensor and explore its implications on the expansion history of the universe. Our results reveal a novel connection between the vacuum energy and the cosmological acceleration, bringing forth a fresh perspective on the cosmic evolution. The adopted maximum Planckian momentum cutoff provides a natural means of regulating the theory, ensuring a consistent interpretation of the obtained results. Our findings open up new avenues for understanding the interplay between the Cosmological Casimir effect and the cosmological constant in the context of an accelerating universe. This study may have significant implications for both cosmology and quantum field theory, inspiring further investigations in the quest to unravel the mysteries of the universe.

We identify the class of f(R) dark energy models which have a viablecosmology, i.e. a matter dominated epoch followed by a late-time acceleration.The deviation from a LambdaCDM model (f=R-Lambda) is quantified by the functionm=Rf_{,RR}/f_{,R}. The matter epoch corresponds to m(r=-1) simeq +0 (wherer=-Rf_{,R}/f) while the accelerated attractor exists in the region 0<m<1. Wefind that the equation of state w_DE of all such ''viable'' f(R) modelsexhibits two features: w_DE diverges at some redshift z_{c} and crosses thecosmological constant boundary (''phantom crossing'') at a redshift z_{b}smaller than z_{c}. Using the observational data of Supernova Ia and CosmicMicrowave Background, we obtain the constraint m<O(0.1) and we find that thephantom crossing could occur at z_{b}>1, i.e. within reach of observations. Ifwe add local gravity constraints, the bound on m becomes very stringent, with mseveral orders of magnitude smaller than unity in the region whose density ismuch larger than the present cosmological density. The representative modelsthat satisfy both cosmological and local gravity constraints take theasymptotic form m(r)=C(-r-1)^p with p>1 as r approaches -1.

The authors use a combination of theoretical modeling, numerical simulations, and statistical analysis to study the dynamics of the disordered interfaces. The results show that the presence of disorder significantly affects the motion of the interfaces, resulting in irregular and erratic behavior. The article presents a comprehensive analysis of the phenomenon and reveals that even strong pinning forces are insufficient to stabilize the interfaces in this particular context. The results challenge previous assumptions about the effectiveness of pinning forces in two-dimensional systems with disorder. The study also identifies several factors that contribute to the weakening of pinning forces, including the distribution and strength of disorder, the size and shape of the interface, and the presence of a reversible pinning force. In general, the study highlights the limitations of strong pinning forces in stabilizing continuous two-dimensional interfaces with disorder and provides valuable insights into the behavior of such interfaces, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of the effects of disorder in complex systems. The article also highlights the implications of these findings for practical applications, such as materials science and nanotechnology, where the stability and control of interfaces are of critical importance. These results emphasize the need for alternative strategies and approaches to achieve stability and control in such systems.

This study examines the demographics of transition objects, investigating their prevalence and characteristics among different age groups and genders. Transition objects are personal possessions, typically stuffed animals or blankets, that individuals rely on for emotional comfort during periods of transition or distress. The research utilizes a large-scale survey administered to a diverse sample of participants across various age ranges. The findings reveal significant variation in the prevalence and attachment to transition objects across different demographic groups. Furthermore, the study explores the psychological and social functions of these objects, shedding light on their significance in promoting emotional well-being and facilitating adaptive coping strategies during periods of change. The implications of these findings for psychological interventions and the understanding of human behavior in transitional contexts are discussed.

Hole spin relaxation in self-assembled quantum dots is studied using time-resolved Faraday rotation. The hole spin relaxation time T1 is found to be extremely long, exceeding 100 ns at low temperatures. This is attributed to the weak spin-orbit interaction and the absence of nuclear spins in the quantum dots. The results demonstrate the potential of self-assembled quantum dots for spin-based quantum information processing.

However, in low accretion states, black holes have lower luminosities that are harder to understand. This article investigates the physical processes that lead to the heating of the accretion flow near the black hole where the heating is thought to occur. Using numerical simulations, we model the accretion flow near the black hole where the heating is thought to occur. Our results show that turbulent magnetic reconnection can effectively heat the accretion flow even in low accretion states. This heating explains the production of synchrotron and inverse Compton emissions observed from black holes in low luminosity hard states.

We present wide-field JHKs-band photometric observations of the three compactHII regions G48.9-0.3, G49.0-0.3, and G49.2-0.3 in the active star-formingregion W51B. The star clusters inside the three compact HII regions show theexcess number of stars in the J-Ks histograms compared with reference fields.While the mean color excess ratio E(J-H)/E(H-Ks) of the three compact HIIregions are similar to ~ 2.07, the visual extinctions toward them are somewhatdifferent: ~ 17 mag for G48.9-0.3 and G49.0-0.3; ~ 23 mag for G49.2-0.3. Basedon their sizes and brightnesses, we suggest that the age of each compact HIIregion is =< 2 Myr. The inferred total stellar mass, ~ 1.4 x 10^4 M_sun, ofW51B makes it one of the most active star forming regions in the Galaxy withthe star formation efficiency of ~ 10 %.

We study plasma effects in a micromachined high-electron mobility transistor(HEMT) with the microcantilever serving as the gate using the developed amodel. The model accounts for mechanical motion of the microcantilever andspatio-temporal variations (plasma effects) of the two-dimensional electrongas(2DEG) system in the transistor channel. The microcantilever mechanicalmotion is described in the point-mass approximation. The hydrodynamic electrontransport model is used to describe distributed electron plasma phenomena inthe 2DEG system. Using the developed model, we calculated the response functioncharacterizing the amplitude microcantilever oscillations and the outputelectric signal as functions of the signal frequency and the bias voltage forthe devices with different parameters. We find the voltage dependences of thefrequency of the mechanical resonance and its damping. In particular, it isdemonstrated that the amplitudes of the mechanical oscillations and outputelectric signal exhibit pronounced maxima at the bias voltages close to thevoltage of the 2DEG channel depletion followed by a steep drop with furtherincrease in the bias voltage.

Motivated by the Dobrushin uniqueness theorem in statistical mechanics, weconsider the following situation: Let \alpha be a nonnegative matrix over afinite or countably infinite index set X, and define the "cleaning operators"\beta_h = I_{1-h} + I_h \alpha for h: X \to [0,1] (here I_f denotes thediagonal matrix with entries f). We ask: For which "cleaning sequences" h_1,h_2, ... do we have c \beta_{h_1} ... \beta_{h_n} \to 0 for a suitable class of"dirt vectors" c? We show, under a modest condition on \alpha, that this occurswhenever \sum_i h_i = \infty everywhere on X. More generally, we analyze thecleaning of subsets \Lambda \subseteq X and the final distribution of dirt onthe complement of \Lambda. We show that when supp(h_i) \subseteq \Lambda with\sum_i h_i = \infty everywhere on \Lambda, the operators \beta_{h_1} ...\beta_{h_n} converge as n \to \infty to the "balayage operator" \Pi_\Lambda =\sum_{k=0}^\infty (I_\Lambda \alpha)^k I_{\Lambda^c). These results areobtained in two ways: by a fairly simple matrix formalism, and by a morepowerful tree formalism that corresponds to working with formal power series inwhich the matrix elements of \alpha are treated as noncommuting indeterminates.

We introduce the idea of using adiabatic rotation to generate superpositionsof a large class of quantum states. For quantum computing this is aninteresting alternative to the well-studied "straight line" adiabaticevolution. In ways that complement recent results, we show how to efficientlyprepare three types of states: Kitaev's toric code state, the cluster state ofthe measurement-based computation model and the history state used in theadiabatic simulation of quantum circuit. We also show that the method, whenadapted for quantum search, provides quadratic speedup as other optimal methodsdo with the advantages that the problem Hamiltonian is time-independent andthat the energy gap above the ground state is strictly nondecreasing with time.Likewise the method can be used for optimization as an alternative to the usualadiabatic algorithm.

This article delves into the intricate relationship between Bergman kernels and equilibrium measures associated with ample line bundles. The Bergman kernel, a fundamental tool in complex analysis, quantifies the concentration of holomorphic sections around a given point. In contrast, the equilibrium measure characterizes the distribution of mass on a complex manifold in the asymptotic sense. By investigating the interplay between these two entities within the framework of ample line bundles, we establish a profound connection. Our study encompasses a comprehensive analysis of the measures' properties and behaviors, shedding light on both their geometric and analytical aspects. Consequently, our findings contribute novel insights into the complex nature of ample line bundles and their associated geometric structures, significantly enhancing the understanding of complex manifolds and their fundamental properties.

The abstract introduces the concept of nonequilibrium entropy limiters in lattice Boltzmann methods (LBMs). LBMs are widely used computational techniques for simulating fluid flow and other complex physical phenomena. The nonequilibrium entropy limietrs are employed in LBMs to alleviate certain numerical instabilities that airse due to the nonequilibrium nature of the system being modeled. Tis article presents a comprehensive study that investigates the effectiveness of different nonequilibrium entropy limiters in improving the stability and accuracy of LBMs. The study involves numerical simulations of various benchmark problems, including flow around obstacles and shock wave propagation, with and without the imple mentation of entropy limiters. The results reveal that nonequilibrium entropy limiters significantly enhance the stability and accuracy of LBMs, particularly in regions of flow with high gradients or strong shocks. Furthermore, the study provides insights into the selection and adjust of appropriate limiters based on the characteristics of the flow being analyzed. These findings contribute to the ongoing research in LBMs and facilitate their implementation in eben modeling complex fluid dynamics phenomena.

We present the results of high resolution mapping of the CO(1-0) and CO(2-1)emission of the ultraluminous infrared galaxy (ULIRG) IRAS 10190+1322, with theIRAM interferometer, down to an angular resolution of ~0.3 arcsec. This objectis composed of two interacting galaxies with a projected nuclear separation of6 kpc, and was selected to analyze the physical and dynamical properties of themolecular gas in each galaxy in order to study the conditions that lead agalaxy pair to become ultraluminous in the infrared. With the exception of Arp220, the closest ULIRG, this is the first time that the CO emission ismorphologically and kinematically resolved in the two interacting galaxies of aULIRG system. In one of the galaxies the molecular gas is highly concentrated,distributed in a circumnuclear disk of 1.7 kpc in size. The molecular gas inthe presumably less infrared luminous galaxy is distributed in a more extendeddisk of 7.4 kpc. The molecular gas mass accounts for ~10% of the dynamical massin each galaxy. Both objects are rich enough in molecular gas, Mgas ~ 4 10^9Msun, as to experience an infrared ultraluminous phase.

The interaction between the Earth's magnetism field environment and the Moon's shallow environment has long-term consequences that are not fully understood. This study developed a numerical model to simulate the long-term exposure of the lunar surface to the Earth's plasma sheet over millions of years. The model accounts for variables such as the changing orientation of the Earth's dipolar magnetic field and the offset of the Moon's orbit. The results indiacte that different regions of the lunar surface experience dramatically varying cumulative exposure to the Earth's plasma sheet over long timescales. Nearside regions such as Oceanus Procellarum have experienced significantly higher levels of plama bombardment compared to farside regions. The degree of exposure is closely linked to the incline and offset of the Moon's orbital plane relative to the Earth's magnetic equator. The cumulative effects of this uneven plasma exposure may help explain elemental and mineralogical differences observed between nearside and farside lunar samples. Furthermore, the model can hlep assess the impact of space weathering on the preservation of surface records spanning deep time. If validated, this longt-erm moon exposure model could provide valuable context for planning future robotic and human missions seeking to understand the Moon's history and evolution.

The low -frequency sensitivity of ASTROD's gravity wave (Advanced surveillance and tracking radar) system is a cutting -edge radar system that aims to detect and track track fragments in the earth's orbit. In this study, we studied low -frequency sensitivity to detect Astrods used to detect gravitational waves. We analyzed the frequency response of the system and evaluated its ability to detect 10^-4 to 10^-3 Hz frequency range. Our results show that ASTROD shows high sensitivity within this frequency, which makes it a promising tool for gravitational waves such as super -large black holes binary and cosmic string. We also discussed our discovery of the meaning of future gravitational wave observations and highlights Astrod's potential to promote our understanding of the universe.

hTis study investigates the properties and dynamics of jet-disturbed molecular gas near the Seyfert 2 nucleus in the grand-design spiral galaxy 5M1. Using higH-resolution obseravtions obtained with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we anaflyze the morphology, kinematics, and physical conditions of the molecular gas affected by the relativistic jets emanating from the active galactic nucleus (AGN). Our results reveal a clear association between the jet structures and the disturbed molecular gas, indicating a significant intearction between the jetts and the interstellar medium in the nuclear pegion of M51. The jet-disturbed molecular gas exhibits peculiar features, inclTding broad velocity dispersions and distorted kinematics, suggesting the presnce of shocks and outflows induced by the jet activity. We find evidence of enhanced molecular gas densities and temperatures adjacent to the jet structures, indicating ocmpression and heating as a conesquence of the jet-ISM interaction. The distribution of moleculcar gas correlates well with the radio continuum emission, supporting the interpretation of the observed structuZes as AGN-driven shocks. Furthermore, we identify abundant spcies such as CO, HCN, and HCO+ in the jet-disturbed region, and aalyze their line ratios to study the molecular gas excitation and chemistry. Our findings suggest that the shDocks generated by the VGN ejts play a crucial role in initiating chemical reactions and enhancing the gTs excitation, leading to the production of high-density tracers and molecular line emission in the vicinity of the Seyfert 2 nucleus. Overal, our observations provide compelling evidence for the impact of jet activity on the molecular gas in the nuzclear region of M51. This study highlights the complex interplay between AGN-driven jtes and the surrounding molecular gas, shedding light on the physical processes occurring in the vicniity of active galactic nuclei.

This study presents photometric observations conducted at a wavelength of 3.8 microns during the secondary eclipse of HD 209458b, an extrasolar planet. The secondary eclipse is a crucial event in exoplanet research as it enables the characterization of the planet's atmospheric composition and temperature distribution. Using the Near Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Spectrometer on board the Hubble Space Telescope, we obtained high-precision photometric measurements. Our findings indicate a significant decrease in flux during the secondary eclipse, which suggests the presence of an atmospheric temperature inversion. This result offers valuable insights into the energy transport mechanisms and chemical composition of the planet's atmosphere. Additionally, the data obtained allow for a comparison with theoretical atmospheric models, thereby refining our understanding of the physical properties of exoplanetary atmospheres. Overall, this study contributes to the expanding body of knowledge regarding the characterization of exoplanet atmospheres and the exploration of their intriguing features.

The two-component symmetric exclusion process (2CSEP) is studied using a matrix-product ansatz and its properties near a nonequilibrium phase transition are characterized. The 2CSEP models the out-of-equilibrium dynamics of particles hopping between nearest sites on a one-dimensional lattice with open boundaries that control the entry and exit rates of the two particle types. For certain choices of the boundary rates, the system exhibits a phase transition between a low-density phase and a high-density phase. By analyzing the largest eigenvalue of the quadratic matrix ansatz, the phase diagram and nonequilibrium phase boundary in the two-dimensional parameter space of the boundary rates are determined. Furthermore, the present work generalizes previous studies on the single-component symmetric exclusion process (ASEP) by explicitly considering the cases where the two particle species can have different entry and exit rates. It is shown that for a range of these boundary rates, the system exhibits an interesting mixed phase where the densities of the two particle types differ. The exact solutions obtained through the matrix-product ansatz provide insight into universal features of phase transitions in driven diffusive systems with internal degrees of freedom near boundaries.

We investigate the existence of compact corigid objects within the context of triangulated categories equipped with co-t-structures. Employing the notion of co-aisle and co-heart enabled by such structures, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for when a compact object is proven to be both self-orthogonal and orthogonally rigid with respect to the co-t-structure. Extending this, sufficient conditions are established for a full subcategory with hom sets characterized by the complementary co-aisle to also admit a self-adjoint object. Applications to the stable module category of a self-injective algebra are considered, whereby endofiniteness of the co-heart implies presence of compact corigid elements. Our results generalize prior work restricted to t-structures and advance characterization of rigid and self-gluing objects relevant to classification problems in representation theory and homotopical algebra.

Linear polarization in X- and gamma-rays is an important diagnostic of manyastrophysical sources, foremost giving information about their geometry,magnetic fields, and radiation mechanisms. However, very few X-ray polarizationmeasurements have been made, and then only mono-energetic detections, whilstseveral objects are assumed to have energy dependent polarization signatures.In this paper we investigate whether detection of energy dependent polarizationfrom cosmic sources is possible using the Compton technique, in particular withthe proposed PoGOLite balloon-experiment, in the 25-100 keV range. We useGeant4 simulations of a PoGOLite model and input photon spectra based on CygnusX-1 and accreting magnetic pulsars (100 mCrab). Effective observing times of 6and 35 hours were simulated, corresponding to a standard and a long durationflight respectively. Both smooth and sharp energy variations of thepolarization are investigated and compared to constant polarization signalsusing chi-square statistics. We can reject constant polarization, with energy,for the Cygnus X-1 spectrum (in the hard state), if the reflected component isassumed to be completely polarized, whereas the distinction cannot be made forweaker polarization. For the accreting pulsar, constant polarization can berejected in the case of polarization in a narrow energy band with at least 50%polarization, and similarly for a negative step distribution from 30% to 0%polarization.

The precise description of excited states in solids is a longstanding challenge in condensed matter physics. Recent advances in ab initio wavefunction-based methods have enabled the computation of excited states in solids with unprecedented accuracy, revolutionizing the field. This article provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in correlation corrections to the band structure of ionic oxides using ab initio wavefunction-based methods. We discuss the theoretical foundations of these methods, their implementation, and their applications to a variety of ionic oxides. Our review demonstrates that correlation corrections can significantly impact the band structure of these materials, leading to changes in their optical and electronic properties. We also address the challenges and limitations of these methods and outline future research directions in this field. Quasielastic electron scattering provides information about nuclear structure and dynamics. This article examines y-scaling, a scaling law behavior observed in quasielastic electron scattering cross sections from nuclei. Precise cross scetion data from electron scattering experiments on various nuclei are presented. The data are compiled and analyzed in terms of the y-scaling variable to test for the presence of y-scaling behaviour. The results confirm that y-scaling is observed for a wide range of nucleon momentum transfers and energy transfers. This finding supports the understanding that the scales behavior arises from general properties of the nuclear response to external probes.

Quantifying entanglement is a crucial task in quantum information theory and many-body physics, as entanglement plays a key role in numerous quantum phenomena and quantity information processing tasks. In this paper, we scrutinized the quantification of entanglement for multipartite quantum states, i.e., quantum states shared among more than two party. We first introduction the concept of entanglement entropy, which measures the entanglement of a quantum state by quantifying the magnitude of information that is unavailable to any one of the parties holding the state. We then discuss separate entanglement measures founded on entanglement entropy, such as the von Neumann entropy, the Rényi entropy, and the conditional entropy. Furthermore, we contemplate the problem of quantifying entanglement in multipartite quantum submits with continuous variables, such as Gaussian states and continuous-variable cluster states. We introduce the concept of the Gaussian entanglement entropy and discussions methods for its calculation. Finally, we discuss the rapport between entanglement and other quantum properties, such as quantum discord and quantum coherence. We show that entanglement is a necessary but not sufficient condition for quantum discordant and quantum coherence.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is the world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator. Ec is designed to collide protons at very high energies, and in doing so, it can create new particles that have never been seen before. One of the goals of the LHC is to search for heavy quarks, which are subatomic pm that are much heavier than the quarks that make up ordinary matter. Heavy quarks are predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics, but they have never been directly observed. The search for heavy quarks at the LHC is a challenging task. The LHC prodces a vast number of particles, and only a tiny fraction of these particles are heavy quarks. To find the heavy quarks, physisists must use sophisticated detectors to identify them. Despite the challenges, the search for heavy quarks at the LHC is making progress. In 2012, the LHC experimets reported the first evidence for the existence of a new heavy quark, called the top qu ark. The top quark is the heaviest pm that has ever been observed, and its discovery was a major milestone in the history of particle physics. The search for heavy quarks at the LHC is continuing, and physicists are hopefսl that they will find more new particles in the years to come. These new particles could help us to nicer understand the universe and the fundamental laws of physics.

We define Landau-Lifshitz sigma models on general coset space $G/H$, with $H$a maximal stability sub-group of $G$. These are non-relativistic models thathave $G$-valued N\"other charges, local $H$ invariance and are classicallyintegrable. Using this definition, we construct the $PSU(2,2|4)/PS(U(2|2)^2)$Landau-Lifshitz sigma-model. This sigma model describes the thermodynamic limitof the spin-chain Hamiltonian obtained from the complete one-loop dilatationoperator of the N=4 super Yang-Mills (SYM) theory. In the second part of thepaper, we identify a number of consistent truncations of the Type IIBGreen-Schwarz action on $AdS_5\times S^5$ whose field content consists of tworeal bosons and 4,8 or 16 real fermions. We show that $\kappa$-symmetry actstrivially in these sub-sectors. In the context of the large spin limit of theAdS/CFT correspondence, we map the Lagrangians of these sub-sectors tocorresponding truncations of the $PSU(2,2|4)/PS(U(2|2)^2)$ Landau-Lifshitzsigma-model.

We report on detection of negative superhumps in KR Aur which is therepresentative member of the VY Scl stars. The observations were obtained withthe multi-channel photometer during 107 h. The analysis of the data clearlyrevealed brightness variations with a period of 3.771 +/- 0.005 h. This is 3.5per cent less than the orbital period, suggesting it is a negative superhump.Negative superhumps in VY Scl stars are widely spread. The discovery ofpowerful soft X-rays from V751 Cyg demonstrates that VY Scl stars may containwhite dwarfs, at which nuclear burning of the accreted material occur. If thissuspicion is correct, we then can suppose that the powerful radiation emergingfrom the white dwarf may cause the tilt of the accretion disk to the orbitalplane, and its retrograde precession may produce negative superhumps in VY Sclstars.

We briefly review recent developments in black hole accretion disk theory,emphasizing the vital role played by magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) stresses intransporting angular momentum. The apparent universality of accretion-relatedoutflow phenomena is a strong indicator that large-scale MHD torques facilitatevertical transport of angular momentum. This leads to an enhanced overall rateof angular momentum transport and allows accretion of matter to proceed at aninteresting rate. Furthermore, we argue that when vertical transport isimportant, the radial structure of the accretion disk is modified at smallradii and this affects the disk emission spectrum. We present a simple modeldemonstrating how energetic, magnetically-driven outflows modify the emergentdisk emission spectrum with respect to that predicted by standard accretiondisk theory. A comparison of the predicted spectra against observations ofquasar spectral energy distributions suggests that mass accretion ratesinferred using the standard disk model may severely underestimate their truevalues.

This article investigates the challenging problem of estimating the unconditional distribution of post-model-selection estimators. Post-model-selection estimators are commonly employed in statistical analyses to account for the selection process in model building. However, their unconditional distribution has been a topic of debate and raises methodological concerns. In this study, we propose a novel approach to estimate the unconditional distribution of post-model-selection estimators. Our method combines information from the selected model and the full set of candidate models to obtain an unbiased estimate. We demonstrate the performance and validity of our approach through extensive simulations and real-world data analysis. The results highlight the importance of accurately estimating the unconditional distribution of post-model-selection estimators in statistical inference and provide valuable insights for researchers in selecting appropriate estimation procedures for their analyses.

We investigate the possibility to deduce momentum space properties fromtime-dependent density functional calculations. Electron and ion momentumdistributions after double ionization of a model Helium atom in a strongfew-cycle laser pulse are studied. We show that, in this case, the choice ofsuitable functionals for the observables is considerably more important thanthe choice of the correlation potential in the time-dependent Kohn-Shamequations. By comparison with the solution of the time-dependent Schroedingerequation, the insufficiency of functionals neglecting electron correlation isdemonstrated. We construct a functional of the Kohn-Sham orbitals, which inprinciple yields the exact momentum distributions of the electrons and the ion.The product-phase approximation is introduced, which reduces the problem ofapproximating this functional significantly.

Using the quantum string Bethe ansatz we derive the one-loop energy of afolded string rotating with angular momenta (S,J) in AdS_3 x S^1 inside AdS_5 xS^5 in the limit 1 << J << S, z=\lambda^(1/2) log(S/J) /(\pi J) fixed. Theone-loop energy is a sum of two contributions, one originating from theHernandez-Lopez phase and another one being due to spin chain finite sizeeffects. We find a result which at the functional level exactly matches theresult of a string theory computation. Expanding the result for large z weobtain the strong coupling limit of the scaling function for low twist, highspin operators of the SL(2) sector of N=4 SYM. In particular we recover thefamous -3 log(2)/\pi. Its appearance is a result of non-trivial cancellationsbetween the finite size effects and the Hernandez-Lopez correction.

We study Ricci flows of some classes of physically valuable solutions inEinstein and string gravity. The anholonomic frame method is applied forgeneric off-diagonal metric ansatz when the field/ evolution equations aretransformed into exactly integrable systems of partial differential equations.The integral varieties of such solutions, in four and five dimensional gravity,depend on arbitrary generation and integration functions of one, two and/ orthree variables. Certain classes of nonholonomic frame constraints allow us toselect vacuum and/or Einstein metrics, to generalize such solutions fornontrivial string (for instance, with antisymmetric torsion fields) and matterfield sources. A very important property of this approach (originating fromFinsler and Lagrange geometry but re-defined for semi-Riemannian spaces) isthat new classes of exact solutions can be generated by nonholonomicdeformations depending on parameters associated to some generalized Gerochtransforms and Ricci flow evolution. In this paper, we apply the method toconstruct in explicit form some classes of exact solutions for multi-parameterEinstein spaces and their nonholonomic Ricci flows describing evolutions/interactions of solitonic pp-waves and deformations of the Schwarzschildmetric. We explore possible physical consequences and speculate on theirimportance in modern gravity.

These findings contrNbute to a deeper understanding of the sXymplectic structure in light nuclei and provide a valuable basis for further investigations in nuclear physics.

Itinerant to localized transition of f electrons in antiferromagnetic superconductor UPd2Al3Unconventional supercnoductivity is closely reJated to the interplay between magnetism and superconductivity. UPd2Al3 is an antiferromagnetic sucerconductor. Its antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering temperature TN is 14.3 K, and its superconducting transition temperature TC is 2.3 K. whe coexistence of superconductivity and magnetism idicates that there is a xstrong correlation between 5f electrons.
