We then generalize these results to more complex selction mechanisms, using a phenomenological approach that captureds the essence of the selection process without requiring a detailed mathematical model. COur results provide new insigths into the role of selection in shaping the ancetsry of a population, and demonstrate the power of combining exact and phenomenological methods in population genetics.

This study investigates the properties of exceedingly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model and their potential for large eddy simulation (LS). The LANS-alpha model is a widely used mathematical model for turbulent flows, but its solutions are typically not eminently turbulent. By introducing a novel numerical method, we are able to otain highly tumultuous solutions of the LANS-alpha model that exhibit features similar to those observed in real-world turbulent flows. Our results show that the highly t urbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model have a number of desirable properties for LES, including high levels of turbulent kinetic energy, large-scale motins, and a wide range of turbulent length scales. These properties suggest that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model may be s uitable for use as initial conditions in LS simulations of turbulent flows. To evaluate the performance of the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model in LES, we compare them to results from direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulent flows. Our resluts show that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model are able to capturing many of the key features of turbulent flows, including the statistical proeprties of the velocity area and the scaling behavior of the energy spectrum. However, we also finds that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model are not without limitations. In particular, they exhibit some differences in the small-scale properties of the velocity field compared to DNS results. Despite these limitations, our result suggest that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model have the potential to be useful for LES simulations of turbulent flows. Further investigation is needed to fully understand the strengths and limtiations of the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-aplha model in LES.

We introduce an exponential random graph model for networks with a fixeddegree distribution and with a tunable degree-degree correlation. We theninvestigate the nature of a percolation transition in the correlated networkwith the Poisson degree distribution. It is found that negative correlation isirrelevant in that the percolation transition in the disassortative networkbelongs to the same universality class of the uncorrelated network. Positivecorrelation turns out to be relevant. The percolation transition in theassortative network is characterized by the non-diverging mean size of finiteclusters and power-law scalings of the density of the largest cluster and thecluster size distribution in the non-percolating phase as well as at thecritical point. Our results suggest that the unusual type percolationtransition in the growing network models reported recently may be inheritedfrom the assortative degree-degree correlation.

We have surveyed a ~0.9-square-degree area of the W3 giant molecular cloudand star-forming region in the 850-micron continuum, using the SCUBA bolometerarray on the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. A complete sample of 316 denseclumps was detected with a mass range from around 13 to 2500 Msun. Part of theW3 GMC is subject to an interaction with the HII region and fast stellar windsgenerated by the nearby W4 OB association. We find that the fraction of totalgas mass in dense, 850-micron traced structures is significantly altered bythis interaction, being around 5% to 13% in the undisturbed cloud but ~25 - 37%in the feedback-affected region. The mass distribution in the detected clumpsample depends somewhat on assumptions of dust temperature and is not a simple,single power law but contains significant structure at intermediate masses.This structure is likely to be due to crowding of sources near or below thespatial resolution of the observations. There is little evidence of anydifference between the index of the high-mass end of the clump mass function inthe compressed region and in the unaffected cloud. The consequences of theseresults are discussed in terms of current models of triggered star formation.

A finite group $G$ is of central type (in the non-classical sense) if itadmits a non-degenerate cohomology class $[c]\in H^2(G,\C^ )$ ($G$ actstrivially on $\C^ $). Groups of central type play a fundamental role in theclassification of semisimple triangular complex Hopf algebras and can bedetermined by their representation theoretical properties. Suppose that a finite group $Q$ acts on an abelian group $A$ so that thereexists a bijective 1-cocycle $\pi\in Z^1(Q,\ach)$, where$\ach=\rm{Hom}(A,\C^ )$ is endowed with the diagonal $Q$-action. Under thisassumption, Etingof and Gelaki gave an explicit formula for a non-degenerate2-cocycle in $Z^2(G,\C^ )$, where $G:=A\rtimes Q$. Hence, the semidirectproduct $G$ is of central type. In this paper we present a more general correspondence between bijective andnon-degenerate cohomology classes. In particular, given a bijective class$[\pi]\in H^1(Q,\ach)$ as above, we construct non-degenerate classes$[c_{\pi}]\in H^2(G,\C^*)$ for certain extensions $1\to A\to G\to Q\to 1$ whichare not necessarily split. We thus strictly extend the above family of centraltype groups.

We consider processes with second order long range dependence resulting fromheavy tailed durations. We refer to this phenomenon as duration-driven longrange dependence (DDLRD), as opposed to the more widely studied linear longrange dependence based on fractional differencing of an $iid$ process. Weconsider in detail two specific processes having DDLRD, originally presented inTaqqu and Levy (1986), and Parke (1999). For these processes, we obtain thelimiting distribution of suitably standardized discrete Fourier transforms(DFTs) and sample autocovariances. At low frequencies, the standardized DFTsconverge to a stable law, as do the standardized sample autocovariances atfixed lags. Finite collections of standardized sample autocovariances at afixed set of lags converge to a degenerate distribution. The standardized DFTsat high frequencies converge to a Gaussian law. Our asymptotic results arestrikingly similar for the two DDLRD processes studied. We calibrate ourasymptotic results with a simulation study which also investigates theproperties of the semiparametric log periodogram regression estimator of thememory parameter.

The dynamics of the 14 Her planetary system are investigated using a symplectic integrator. The simulations show the system's stability over various initial conditions. The planets exhibit a hierarchical configuration, with the innermost planet, 14 Her b, in a nearly circular orbit around the central star. The outer planets, 14 Her c, d, and e, have more eccentric and inclined orbits. Periodic resonances causing angular momentum exchange between the planets are identified. These resonances explain the observed variations in the planets' orbital elements. The study provides new insights into the dynamics of the 14 Her planetary system.

This paper examines the collaboration between universities and companies in the framework of the European Union's fifth framework programme (FP5). Through in-depth interviews and document analysis, the authors studied 10 research networks funded by FP5 that involved several universities and companies. They found that effective networks facilitated frequent interactions between academic and industrial participants to share expertise and resources. These networks also helped to share knowledge and train students to meet industry needs, thereby demonstrating how university-industry collaboration can benefit both sectors.

The results of the spectral, energetical and temporal characteristics ofradiation in the presence of the photonic flame effect are presented.Artificial opal posed on Cu plate at the temperature of liquid nitrogen boilingpoint (77 K) being irradiated by nanosecond ruby laser pulse produces long-term luminiscence with a duration till ten seconds with a finely structuredspectrum in the the antistocks part of the spectrum. Analogous visibleluminescence manifesting time delay appeared in other samples of the artificialopals posed on the same plate. In the case of the opal infiltrated withdifferent nonlinear liquids the threshold of the luminiscence is reduced andthe spatial disribution of the bright emmiting area on the opal surface isbeing changed. In the case of the putting the frozen nonlinear liquids on theCu plate long-term blue bright luminiscence took place in the frozen species ofthe liquids. Temporal characteristics of this luminiscence are nearly the sameas in opal matrixes.

The E-theoretic descent functor for groupoids is a novel approach to studying the algebraic structure of groupoids, which are fundamental objects in modern algebra and geometry. This functor allows for the systematic study of groupoids and their relationship to other algebraic objects, such as groups and rings. By utilizing the E-theoretic descent functor, researchers can gain new insights into the structure and behavior of groupoids, and explore their connections to various branches of mathematics. This article introduces the E-theoretic descent functor for groupoids and demonstrates its applications and potential for advancing our understanding of algebraic structures.

The dust distribution in galaxies plays a crucial role in understanding their evolution, as it affects the star formation process and the energy balance of the interstellar medium. In this paper, we present V and K'-band images of a sample of edge-on galaxies observed with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Submillimeter Array (SMA). We use radiative transfer models to fit the observed spectral energy distributions and derive the dust distribution in these galaxies. Our results show that the dust is distributed in a thin layer in the disk of the galaxies, with a scale height of a few hundred parsecs. The dust distribution is also found to be asymmetric, with more dust on the side of the galaxy facing the observer. This asymmetry is likely due to the effects of stellar winds and radiation pressure from young stars. Our results provide new insights into the dust distribution in edge-on galaxies and its role in the star formation process.

The production of Tsallis entropy is investigated in the limit of weak chaos and a new indicator of chaoticity is proposed. We show that the Tsallis entropy production \(\dot{S}_q\) for \(q>0\) is always positive for a chaotic map and \(\dot{S}_q\) for \(q<0\) oscillates around zero. The sign of \(\dot{S}_q\) can be used to measure the degree of chaoticity. The larger \(|\dot{S}_q|\) is, the more chaotic the map is. We also find that \(\dot{S}_q\) decreases with increasing \(q\). These results are significant for understanding the role of chaos in the production of entropy and for quantifying the degree of chaoticity.

A spectral method is described for solving coupled elliptic problems on aninterior and an exterior domain. The method is formulated and tested on thetwo-dimensional interior Poisson and exterior Laplace problems, whose solutionsand their normal derivatives are required to be continuous across theinterface. A complete basis of homogeneous solutions for the interior andexterior regions, corresponding to all possible Dirichlet boundary values atthe interface, are calculated in a preprocessing step. This basis is used toconstruct the influence matrix which serves to transform the coupled boundaryconditions into conditions on the interior problem. Chebyshev approximationsare used to represent both the interior solutions and the boundary values. Astandard Chebyshev spectral method is used to calculate the interior solutions.The exterior harmonic solutions are calculated as the convolution of thefree-space Green's function with a surface density; this surface density isitself the solution to an integral equation which has an analytic solution whenthe boundary values are given as a Chebyshev expansion. Properties of Chebyshevapproximations insure that the basis of exterior harmonic functions representsthe external near-boundary solutions uniformly. The method is tested bycalculating the electrostatic potential resulting from charge distributions ina rectangle. The resulting influence matrix is well-conditioned and solutionsconverge exponentially as the resolution is increased. The generalization ofthis approach to three-dimensional problems is discussed, in particular themagnetohydrodynamic equations in a finite cylindrical domain surrounded by avacuum.

This reviewed utilizes near-infrared polarimetry to examine the bipolar nebula IRAS 19312+1950. The nebula, located in the constellation Auriga, is conceptions to be a proto-planetary nebula with a binary central star regimen. Near-infrared polarimetry allows for the discovers of dust grains and magnetic campo within the nebula, providing valuable information on its structure and evolution. Our observations reveal a complex magnetic field configuration, with evidence of magnetic fields adapts with the nebula's bipolar morphology. We also find that the magnetic field strength decreases with increasing distance from the central sing. The polarization data displays the presence of large dust grains, which may play a role in the nebula's formation and collimation. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper inkling of the physical treating at play in the formation and evolution of bipolar nebulae.

We investigate the effect of Pauli non-locality in the heavy-ion opticalpotential on sub-barrier fusion reactions. The S\~{a}o Paulo potential, whichtakes into account the Pauli non-locality and has been widely used in analyzingelastic scattering, has also recently been applied to heavy-ion fusion.However, the approximation employed in deriving the S\~{a}o Paulo potential,based on the Perey-Buck semi-classical treatment of neutron induced reactions,must be assessed for charged particles tunneling through a barrier. It is thepurpose of this note to look into this question. We consider the widely studiedsystem $^{16}$O + $^{208}$Pb at energies that span the barrier region from 10MeV below to 10 MeV above. It seems that the non-locality plays a minor role.We find the S\~{a}o Paulo potential to be quite adequate throughout the region.

In this article, we present a brainy approach to address the phenomenon of resonance saturation in large-Nc QCD. Resonance saturation refers to the dominance of own resonances in scattering processes, leading to the breakdown of perturbative methods. We propose a new framework based on rational approximations, which provide us to systematically account for the contributions of resonances in a checked manner. By analyzing the relevant diagrams in large-Nc QCD, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our nears in capturing the essential physics of resonating saturation. Moreover, we discuss the implications of our results for comprehend the dynamics of strong interactions at high energies and offered insights into the role of resonances in the emergence of confinement and chiral symmetry break phenomena. Overall, our rational approach supplying a valuable tool for investigates complex phenomena in large-Nc QCD and opens up avenues for further theoretical developments in the field.

Non-topological solitons arise as stable localized field configurations in a nmber of theories describing physical systems. In this article, we explore the existenc of non-topological solitons in field thoeries where the kinetic term of the fields contains self-interaction terms. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulation, we demonstrate the emergence of stable oscillating solitary wave solutions in such thheories. These solitary waveVs exist due to the balance between dispersive and nonlinear effects introduced through the nonlinear kinetic terms. We systematically investigate how the propertie of these solitary waves, such as their frequency and amplitude, depend on the nonlinear coefficients in the kinetic trms. Additionally, we study scattgering processes between these solitary waves and find both elastic and inelastic interactions can occur. Our wMork significantly expand the class of field theories supporting non-topological solitons and provides a novel means of controlling soliton properties and interactions through modification of kinetic terms. Overall, our results establish that kinetic sKlf-coupling can promote the existence of non-topological solitons in a diverse range of physical sytems.

Previous studies have demonstrated the inefficiency of utilizing a singular random walk for exploration and search algorithms. This study experimentally compares the performance of employing multiple concurrent random walks versus a lone random walk across diverse search problems. The findings indicate that implementing numerous random walks in parallel notably surpasses the effectiveness of a sole random walker, allowing the target to be identified more rapidly. By dispersing the search labor among many autonomous random procedures, multiple random walks are better able to thoroughly examine the search domain relative to a single walk, confirming that distributing exploration across more walks can be preferential to reliance on lone walker for numerous search queries.

The qtudy presented in this paper addresses the phenomenon of elasticity in materials with arbitrarily shaped inhomogeneities. Understanding the behavior of materials with irregular internal structures is of isgnificant importance in various fields of engineering and mateials science. This research aims to elucidate the key aspects of eladsticity in such complex materials through theoretical analysis and numerTical simulations. The investigation begins by establishing a mathematiJcal framework that accounts for the presence of arbitrary inhomogeneities witjhin an elastic material. A variety of inhomoAeneity shapes, including irregular geometries and varying material properties, are considered. The study then focuses on analyzing the stress and strain distribtions within the mRaterial and examining the effects of the inhomogeneities on its overall mechanical behavior. The Wresults of this research provide valuable insights into the elastic properties of complex maAerials and offer a foundation for further investigation in the field. The findings have potential applicatins in the design and optimization of materials for various engineering applications, such as structural engineering, compsoite materials, and biomedical engineering.

Moving gap solitons are a fascinating phenomenon that has garnered significant attention in recent years. In this article, we explore the behavior of moving gap solitons in periodic potentials, using a combination of analytical and numerical methods. We show that the presence of a periodic potential can significantly affect the dynamics of gap solitons, leading to the formation of stable moving solitons that can persist for long times. These moving solitons can exhibit complex spatial and temporal patterns, and we demonstrate their potential for use in various applications, including the control of nonlinear waves and the creation of novel optical effects. Our results provide new insights into the behavior of gap solitons in periodic potentials and have important implications for the study of nonlinear waves in a variety of physical systems.

The dtust distribution in edge-on galaxies. Radiative transfer fits of V and K'-band imagesWe present a sTudy of the dust distribution in edgeo-n galaxies using radiative transfer fits of V and K'-band images. Te sample consists of 12 nearby galaxies with a wide range of morphological types. We use a two-dimensional dust distribution model to fit the observed images, and we derive the dust opacty, scale height, and asymmetrs. eW find that the dust opacity is typically higher in the inner regYions of the galaxies, and that the scale height increases with radius. dhe dust distribusion is also found to be asymmetric in most of the galaxies, with the dust lane being shifted towards the north-east. We comIpare our results with those of previous studies, and we discuss the implications of our findings for the dust properties and evolution in edge-on galaies.

In this paper, we propose a game-theoretic approach to energy-efficient modulation in CDMA networks with delay QoS constraints. The proposed scheme takes into account the impact of modulation and coding scheme (MCS) selection on the energy consumption and delay performance of the network. The game-theoretic framework is formulated as a non-cooperative game among the users, where each user selects its MCS to minimize its own energy consumption, while considering the impact of its decision on the delay performance of the network. The existence and uniqueness of the Nash equilibrium (NE) in the game are analyzed, and an iterative algorithm is proposed to compute the NE. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme can significantly reduce the energy consumption of the network, while meeting the delay QoS constraints.

A consistent approach to Cosmology requires an explicit averaging of theEinstein equations, to describe a homogeneous and isotropic geometry. Such anaveraging will in general modify the Einstein equations. The averagingprocedure due to Buchert has attracted considerable attention recently since itoffers the tantalizing hope of explaining the phenomenon of dark energy throughsuch corrections. This approach has been criticized, however, on the groundsthat its effects may be gauge artifacts. We apply the fully covariant formalismof Zalaletdinov's Macroscopic Gravity and show that, after making someessential gauge choices, the Cosmological equations receive \emph{spacetimescalar} corrections which are therefore observable in principle, and further,that the broad structure of these corrections is \emph{identical} to thosederived by Buchert.

In this paper, we explore a new method to modeling plenary relativity, combining elements of mixed hyperbolic and second-order parabolic formulations. By leveraging the strengths of both frameworks, we procure a more accurate and efficient method for solving Einstein's equations. Our approach is validated through a series of simulations, showing improved approximation and accuracy compared to traditional formulations. We also discuss the theoretical foundations of our method and its potential applications in astrophysics and astronomy. Overall, this operating represents a grand advancement in our understanding of gravitational physics and has important implications for the study of complex spacetime phenomena.

The nitrogen-vacancy (N-V) center in diamond is promising as an electron spinqubit due to its long-lived coherence and optical addressability. The groundstate is a spin triplet with two levels ($m_s = \pm 1$) degenerate at zeromagnetic field. Polarization-selective microwave excitation is an attractivemethod to address the spin transitions independently, since this allowsoperation down to zero magnetic field. Using a resonator designed to producecircularly polarized microwaves, we have investigated the polarizationselection rules of the N-V center. We first apply this technique to N-Vensembles in [100] and [111]-oriented samples. Next, we demonstrate an imagingtechnique, based on optical polarization dependence, that allows rapididentification of the orientations of many single N-V centers. Finally, we testthe microwave polarization selection rules of individual N-V centers of knownorientation.

We report on the Scanning Tunneling Microscope (STM) observation of linearfringes together with spatially varying super-lattice structures on (0001)graphite (HOPG) surface. The structure, present in a region of a layer boundedby two straight carbon fibers, varies from a hexagonal lattice of 6nmperiodicity to nearly a square lattice of 13nm periodicity. It then changesinto a one-dimensional (1-D) fringe-like pattern before relaxing into apattern-free region. We attribute this surface structure to a shear straingiving rise to a spatially varying rotation of the affected graphite layerrelative to the bulk substrate. We propose a simple method to understand thesemoire patterns by looking at the fixed and rotated lattices in the Fouriertransformed k-space. Using this approach we can reproduce the spatially varying2-D lattice as well as the 1-D fringes by simulation. The 1-D fringes are foundto result from a particular spatial dependence of the rotation angle.

In this study, we present a photometric analysis of the intermediate-age star cluster BS 90 located in the star-forming region NGC 346 within the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). We utilized Hubble Space Telescope Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) observations to investigate the properties of BS 90 and its surrounding environment. The ACS data provide high-resolution imaging capabilities that allow us to study the cluster's structure and color properties in detail. We found that BS 90 has a age of approximately 200 million years, which places it in the intermediate-age range between young and old clusters. The cluster's color-magnitude diagram reveals a clear red giant branch, which suggests that the cluster has undergone significant evolution since its formation. We also identified a number of asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars, which are likely to be the precursors of planetary nebulae. The spatial distribution of the stars in BS 90 shows a centrally concentrated distribution, indicative of a dynamically evolved cluster. Moreover, we found that the cluster's morphology is consistent with a mass of approximately 10^4 solar masses. The study of BS 90 provides valuable insights into the star formation history of the SMC and the evolution of intermediate-age clusters. The results of this study can be used to inform future research on the formation and evolution of star clusters in external galaxies.

This article presents the design and implementation of the Infrared Cloud Monitor (ICM) for the MAGNUM robotic telescope at Haleakala, Maui. The ICM is a critical component of the telescope's automated observing system, responsible for detecting and tracking clouds to ensure efficient and safe observation scheduling. Utilizing a combination of infrared and visible light sensors, the ICM provides accurate and reliable cloud detection, even in conditions of high humidity and scattered light. The system's algorithms and software are described in detail, highlighting its ability to adapt to varying weather conditions and telescope operations. The ICM's performance is evaluated through a series of tests and observations, demonstrating its effectiveness in supporting the MAGNUM telescope's scientific goals. Overall, the ICM represents a significant advance in the field of robotic telescope technology, enabling optimal observation scheduling and improved data quality.

We have combined multi-wavelength observations of a selected sample ofstarforming galaxies with galaxy evolution models in order to compare theresults obtained for different SFR tracers and to study the effect that theevolution of the starforming regions has on them. We also aimed at obtaining abetter understanding of the corrections due to extinction and nuclear activityon the derivation of the SFR. We selected the sample from Chandra data for thewell studied region Chandra Deep Field South (CDFS) and chose the objects thatalso have UV and IR data from GALEX and GOODS-Spitzer respectively. Our main finding is that there is good agreement between the extinctioncorrected SFR(UV) and the SFR(X), and we confirm the use of X-ray luminositiesas a trustful tracer of recent star formation activity. Nevertheless, atSFR(UV) larger than about 5Msol/year there are several galaxies with an excessof SFR(X) suggesting the presence of an obscured AGN not detected in theoptical spectra. We conclude that the IR luminosity is driven by recent starformation even in those galaxies where the SFR(X) is an order of magnitudehigher than the SFR(UV) and therefore may harbour an AGN. One object showsSFR(X) much lower than expected based on the SFR(UV); this SFR(X) 'deficit' maybe due to an early transient phase before most of the massive X-ray binarieswere formed. An X-ray deficit could be used to select extremely young bursts inan early phase just after the explosion of the first supernovae associated withmassive stars and before the onset of massive X-ray binaries.

We consider a $SO(d)$ gauge theory in an Euclidean $d$-dimensionalspace-time, which is known to be renormalizable to all orders in perturbationtheory for $2\le{d}\le4$. Then, with the help of a space-time representation ofthe gauge group, the gauge theory is mapped into a curved space-time withlinear connection. Further, in that mapping the gauge field plays the role ofthe linear connection of the curved space-time and an effective metric tensorarises naturally from the mapping. The obtained action, being quadratic in theRiemann-Christoffel tensor, at a first sight, spoils a gravity interpretationof the model. Thus, we provide a sketch of a mechanism that breaks the $SO(d)$color invariance and generates the Einstein-Hilbert term, as well as acosmological constant term, allowing an interpretation of the model as amodified gravity in the Palatini formalism. In that sense, gravity can bevisualized as an effective classical theory, originated from a well definedquantum gauge theory. We also show that, in the four dimensional case, twopossibilities for particular solutions of the field equations are the de Sitterand Anti de Sitter space-times.

The origin of the so called 'detached shells' around AGB stars is not fullyunderstood, but two common hypotheses state that these shells form eitherthrough the interaction of distinct wind phases or an eruptive mass lossassociated with a He-shell flash. We present a model of the formation ofdetached shells around thermal pulse asymptotic giant branch (TP-AGB) stars,based on detailed modelling of mass loss and stellar evolution, leading to acombination of eruptive mass loss and wind interaction. The purpose of this paper is first of all to connect stellar evolution withwind and mass loss evolution and demonstrate its consistency with observations,but also to show how thin detached shells around TP-AGB stars can be formed.Previous attempts to link mass loss evolution with the formation of detachedshells were based on approximate prescriptions for the mass loss and have notincluded detailed modelling of the wind formation as we do here. (abridged)

We investigate the structure and properties of differentially rotating main-sequence stars in the mass range of 1-2 M☉. By employing analytical methods and numerical simulations, we examine the effects of differential rotation on the stellar structure, internal transport processes, and evolutionary tracks. Our results reveal that differential rotation induces significant changes in the stellar profiles, leading to variations in the equatorial and polar radii, effective temperatures, and chemical compositions. The thermal and chemical redistribution caused by differential rotation affects the structural characteristics of the stars, resulting in modified thermal gradients and surface abundance patterns. Moreover, we find that differential rotation plays a crucial role in the generation and transport of magnetic fields, which may impact convective processes and dynamos in these stars. Our findings highlight the importance of considering differential rotation when studying the evolution and internal dynamics of main-sequence stars in the 1-2 M☉ range.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a noninvasive technique used to visualize internal anatomical structures but conventional MRI requires expensive and sizable superconducting magnets generating over 0.5 Tesla. This paper presents a novel instrumentation approach for ultra-low-field magnetic resonance imaging (ULF-MRI) utilizing superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) as highly sensitive magnetometers. The design of a SQUID-based system for ULF-MRI is described, outlining key components and their respective functions. Preliminary images from a benchtop 0.01 Tesla MRI prototype employing a commercial array of low-critical temperature SQUID sensors are displayed, demonstrating the potential of this method. The results suggest that SQUID-based ULF-MRI could enable new applications such as portable or wearable MRI with significantly lower cost and size than traditional high-field systems. However, further improvements to SQUID sensor performance and array configurations will be necessary to match the image quality of clinical scanners. With continued advancement, SQUID-based ULF-MRI may present new opportunities for magnetic resonance imaging in point-of-care diagnosis and biomedical investigation.

Our prediction is based on the assumption of a non-universal Higgs mass term at the GUT scale, which leads to a modification of the spectrum of the MSSM. We find that the branching ratio of b -> s gamma can be significantly enhanced in our scenario, and can reach values that are consistent with recent experimental data. We also discuss the implications of our prediction for the constrained MSSM, and show that it can provide a natural explanation for the observed value of the Higgs mass.

The asymmetric target process is a nonequilibrium stochastic process with unique long-term dynamical properties. Previous research has investigated various aspects of this process through simulation and analysis but the underlying structure of its stationary state remains poorly understood. In this paper, we develop a theoretical framework to characterize the stationary state that the process converges to over long timescales. Our approach represents the joint distribution of particle positions and occupation times in terms of a set of orthogonal basis functions. We derive expressions for these basis functions and use them to extract quantitative predictions for key properties of the stationary state. Computer simulations confirm that the theoretical description provides an accurate representation of the simulated stationary state. Interestingly, we find the stationary state exhibits spatially asymmetric structure even though the underlying dynamical rules are spatially symmetric. This feature highlights the system's intrinsic inability to sustain detailed balance. More broadly, our work provides new insights into nonequilibrium steady states for stochastic spreading processes far from thermal equilibrium. Finally, the theoretical framework introduced here could potentially be extended to analyze other stochastic systems exhibiting anomalous nonequilibrium behavior.

Evolutionary game theory provides valuable insights into the dynamics of social behaviors and strategies. While many studies focus on well-mixed or structured populations, there is a growing interest in understanding the dynamics of evolutionary games on minimally structured populations. In this article, we explore the implications of such population structures on the evolution of cooperative and competitive strategies.Minimally structured populations involve a simple form of local interactions, where individuals only interact with their immediate neighbors. We investigate the effects of limited interaction range on the emergence and persistence of cooperation through analytical and computational methods. By analyzing various game scenarios, including the Prisoner's Dilemma and the Snowdrift Game, we uncover the conditions under which cooperation can thrive in minimally structured populations.Our findings reveal that the presence of limited interaction range creates spatial clusters of cooperation, as cooperative individuals tend to group together. Moreover, we observe the emergence of cooperation in more challenging scenarios where well-mixed populations would typically favor defection. Interestingly, we identify a critical interaction range beyond which cooperation diminishes, emphasizing the delicate balance between local interactions and global population dynamics.To further understand the evolutionary dynamics, we analyze the impact of mutation rates, different game payoffs, and population sizes on the prevalence of cooperative strategies. Additionally, we explore the robustness of cooperation against different environmental factors and perturbations in the interaction networks.Our study sheds light on the intricate dynamics of evolutionary games in minimally structured populations and provides valuable insights into the conditions that promote or hinder cooperation.

Motivated by a class of orbit problems in astrophysics, this paper considerssolutions to Hill's equation with forcing strength parameters that vary fromcycle to cycle. The results are generalized to include period variations fromcycle to cycle. The development of the solutions to the differential equationis governed by a discrete map. For the general case of Hill's equation in theunstable limit, we consider separately the case of purely positive matrixelements and those with mixed signs; we then find exact expressions, bounds,and working estimates for the growth rates. We also find exact expressions,estimates, and bounds for the infinite products of several $2 \times 2$matrices with random variables in the matrix elements. In the limit of sharplyspiked forcing terms (the delta function limit), we find analytic solutions foreach cycle and for the discrete map that matches solutions from cycle to cycle;for this case we find the growth rates and the condition for instability in thelimit of large forcing strength, as well as the widths of the stable/unstablezones.

We study two recently proposed equations of state (EOS) which are obtainedfrom high temperature QCD, and show how they can be adapted to use them formaking predictions for relativistic heavy ion collisions. The method involvesextracting equilibrium distribution functions for quarks and gluons from theEOS, which in turn will allow a determination of the transport and other bulkproperties of the quark gluon plasma. Simultaneously, the method also yields aquasi particle description of interacting quarks and gluons. The first EOS isperturbative in the QCD coupling constant and has contributions of $O(g^5)$.The second EOS is an improvement over the first, with contributions upto $O(g^6 ln(\frac{1}{g}))$; it incorporates the nonperturbative hard thermalcontributions. The interaction effects are shown to be captured entirely by theeffective chemical potentials for the gluons and the quarks, in both the cases.The chemical potential is seen to be highly sensitive to the EOS. As anapplication, we determine the screening lengths which are, indeed the mostimportant diagnostics for QGP. The screening lengths are seen to behavedrastically differently depending on the EOS considered., and yield, therefore,a way to distinguish the two equations of state in heavy ion collisions.

High order convergent muligrid methods on domains containing holes for black hole initial dataIn this paper, we present high order convergent multigrid methods for solving elliptic equations on domains containing holes. The methods are based on a combination of a high order finite element discretization and a multigrid solver. We prvoe that the methods are convergent with optimal rates for smooth solutions and nearly optimal rates for solutions with singularities. We also present numerical results that confirm the theoretical results. The methods are applied to the problem of computing black hole initial dtaa. We show that the methods can be used to compute accurate solutions to this problem on domains containing holes. The methods are also efficient, and can be used to compute solutions on large domains.

The non-mesonic humble decay of Lambda hypernuclei receipts dominantly through the addressing where a Lambda particle embedded in a nucleus is converted into a proton and a pion. Previous theoretical studies of this decay methodology have typically included only one-pion-exchange processes. About this work, for the first time, two-pion-exchange processes are also taken into account to better understand their impact. A theoretical framework is developed to calculate the transition matrix factored and decay rates arising from two-pion-exchange processes pillars on an effective weak Hamiltonian and Lagrangian. The results specify that two-pion exchanges provide a non-negligible contribution to the overall non-mesonic decay grandeur, especially for heavier hypernuclei. More precise comparison with experimental measurements and implications for the suppression of s-wave pion emission gonna be discussed.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the study of network structure across various disciplines. This research aims to examine the impact of node deletion on network structure, with a specific focus on social networks. By systematically removing nodes from a given network, we analyze the resulting changes in the overall structure, connectivity, and functionality of the network. Through empirical analysis, we utilize several network metrics, including degree centrality, betweenness centrality, and clustering coefficient, to measure the effects of node deletion. Our findings reveal that the removal of highly connected nodes significantly disrupts the network structure, leading to network fragmentation and increased clustering. Additionally, we identify a non-linear relationship between node deletion and the network's resilience to disintegration. Specifically, we observe an initial gradual decline in network connectivity, followed by a sudden structural collapse once a critical threshold of node removal is surpassed. This study enhances our understanding of network dynamics and provides valuable insights for enhancing robustness and implementing targeted interventions in real-world networks, such as social, transportation, and communication systems.

This paper describes the Wide Field Spectrograph (WiFeS) under constructionat the Research School of Astronomy and Astrophysics (RSAA) of the AustralianNational University (ANU) for the ANU 2.3m telescope at the Siding SpringObservatory. WiFeS is a powerful integral field, double-beam, concentric,image-slicing spectrograph designed to deliver excellent thoughput, wavelengthstability, spectrophotometric performance and superb image quality along withwide spectral coverage throughout the 320-950 nm wavelength region. It providesa 25x38 arcsec. field with 0.5 arcsec. sampling along each of twenty five 38X1arcsec slitlets. The output format is optimized to match the 4096x4096 pixelCCD detectors in each of two cameras individually optimized for the blue andthe red ends of the spectrum, respectively. A process of "interleavednod-and-shuffle" will be applied to permit quantum noise-limited skysubtraction. Using VPH gratings, spectral resolutions of 3000 and 7000 areprovided. The full spectral range is covered in a single exposure at R=3000,and in two exposures in the R=7000 mode. The use of transmissive coated optics,VPH gratings and optimized mirror coatings ensures a throughput (includingtelescope atmosphere and detector) > 30% over a wide spectral range. Theconcentric image-slicer design ensures an excellent and uniform image qualityacross the full field. To maximize scientific return, the whole instrument isconfigured for remote observing, pipeline data reduction, and the accumulationof calibration image libraries.

We establish a one-to-one correspondence between one-sided and two-sidedregular systems of conditional probabilities on the half-line that preservesthe associated chains and Gibbs measures. As an application, we determineuniqueness and non-uniqueness regimes in one-sided versions of ferromagneticIsing models with long range interactions. Our study shows that the interplaybetween chain and Gibbsian theories yields more information than that containedwithin the known theory of each separate framework. In particular: (i) AGibbsian construction due to Dyson yields a new family of chains with phasetransitions; (ii) these transitions show that a square summability uniquenesscondition of chains is false in the general non-shift-invariant setting, and(iii) an uniqueness criterion for chains shows that a Gibbsian conjecture dueto Kac and Thompson is false in this half-line setting.

The thermal and ionization structure of an HII region, which is formed due to the presence of a yoJung star, is affected by the distribution of the ionizinig radiaiton in the region. A young star emits photons that ionize the surrounding gs and create an HII region. This leads to a decVease in the temperature of the gas due to the process of recombination. Howevepr, the temperature structure of the HII jegion is affected by the distribution of the ionizing sources, which may not be uniform throughout the region. Therefore, the study of the effects of spatially distributed ionization sources on the temperature strutcure of HII regions is mportant. In this paper, we aim to investigate the effeces of the distribution of ionization sources on the temperature structure of HII regLons. We present a model that takes into account the spatial distribution of the ionizing osurces and calculate the temperature structure of the HIi region. We ssow that the temperature structure of the HII region is affecetd by the distribution of the ionization osurces, and that the temperature gradient is steeper when the ionization sources are centrally concentrated. We also discuOs the implications of our results for the study of HII regions. Our results suggest that it is important to consider the distribution of ionization sources when studying the temperature structure of HII regcons, and that a uniform distribution of ionization soZurces amy not be a good approximation in all cases.

Solar coronal mass ejections (CMEs) show a large variety in their kinematicproperties. CMEs originating in active regions and accompanied by strong flaresare usually faster and accelerated more impulsively than CMEs associated withfilament eruptions outside active regions and weak flares. It has been proposedmore than two decades ago that there are two separate types of CMEs, fast(impulsive) CMEs and slow (gradual) CMEs. However, this concept may not bevalid, since the large data sets acquired in recent years do not show twodistinct peaks in the CME velocity distribution and reveal that both fast andslow CMEs can be accompanied by both weak and strong flares. We presentnumerical simulations which confirm our earlier analytical result that aflux-rope CME model permits describing fast and slow CMEs in a unified manner.We consider a force-free coronal magnetic flux rope embedded in the potentialfield of model bipolar and quadrupolar active regions. The eruption is drivenby the torus instability which occurs if the field overlying the flux ropedecreases sufficiently rapidly with height. The acceleration profile depends onthe steepness of this field decrease, corresponding to fast CMEs for rapiddecrease, as is typical of active regions, and to slow CMEs for gentledecrease, as is typical of the quiet Sun. Complex (quadrupolar) active regionslead to the fastest CMEs.

This academic article investigates the concept and applicability of sparse estimators and their relationship to the oracle property, with a particular focus on the revival of Hodges' Estimator. The oralce property refers to the ideal scenario where an estimator accomplishes the same accuracy as if the true model were known. Sparse estimators, known for their ability to identify and exploit the underlying structure of high-dimensional data, have gained significant attention in recent years. This study provides a somprehensive analysis of various sparse estimators and their performance in different statistical scenarios. Additionally, it explores the conditions under which Hodges' Estimator, an earlier proposal widely regarded as a benchmark for sparse estimation, can be effectively employed. The investigation is supported by theoretical derivations, simulation studies, and real-world data applications. The conclusions offer insights into the practical utility of sparse estimators and their potential implications for statistical modelled and inference in the era of big data.

The peculiar velocities of supernovae are the deviations from the mean expansion velocities of supernovae caused by their local gravitational interactions. To determine the impact of the peculiar velocities, we analyze a sample of local SNe Ia and compare their observed velocities with the predictions based on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) frame. SNe Ia are important cosmological probes, but their apparent magnitudes are influenced by the peculiar velocities, which leads to uncertainties in the cosmological parameters. We find that a significant fraction of SNe Ia have peculiar velocities that deviate from the CMB dipole. This observation suggests the presence of local gravitational structures, such as superclusters or voids, which affect the observed velocities. We also investigate the relationship between the peculiar velocities and cosmological parameters, such as the Hubble constant (H0) and the matter density (m). Our results show that accounting for the peculiar velocities is essential for accurate cosmological studies. Failure to account for them can lead to underestimation or overestimation of H0 and m, which could bias our understanding of the expansion history of the universe and the nature of dark energy. By simulating the SNe Ia data with varying cosmological parameters, we determine the biases introduced by the peculiar velocities in the H0-m plane. In conclusion, this study highlights the importance of understanding and reducing the impact of the peculiar velocities on cosmological studies using local SNe Ia. Future cosmological studies involving SNe Ia should include a comprehensive model that includes the peculiar velocities to improve the precision of cosmological parameter estimation.

Parameter learning and Monte Carlo optimization are two basic technologies in machine learning and optimization research. This article discusses the integration of these two methods to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the learning and optimization process. The parameter learning framework provides a strong foundation for complex system modeling by defining a set of parameters of control system behavior. However, when it is applied to large -scale problems, traditional parameter learning methods are usually plagued by high computing costs and convergence issues. Instead, Monte Carlo optimizes the use of random sampling to explore solution space and estimate the target function. This random method can identify the hopeful areas in the search space, but it may encounter fusion restrictions and lack of accuracy. By combining parameters with Monte Carlo optimization, we have proposed a new way to solve each technical limitations. We use the flexibility and performance of the parameter learning model to capture the complex relationships in the data, and at the same time use Monte Carlo optimization to effectively explore the solution space and improve the model. By conducting a large number of experiments on various data sets and optimization issues, we proved the effectiveness of the methods we put forward. Compared with the traditional parameter learning and Monte Carlo optimization method, we have observed a higher convergence rate, improved accuracy, and reduced calculation costs. In addition, we have comprehensively analyzed the basic mechanism and characteristics of the integrated framework. We have studied different parameter learning models, the impact of Monte Carlo sampling strategy and convergence standards on the overall performance.

Air fluorescence detectors measure the energy of ultra-high energy cosmicrays by collecting fluorescence light emitted from nitrogen molecules along theextensive air shower cascade. To ensure a reliable energy determination, thelight signal needs to be corrected for atmospheric effects, which not onlyattenuate the signal, but also produce a non-negligible background componentdue to scattered Cherenkov light and multiple-scattered light. The correctionrequires regular measurements of the aerosol attenuation length and the aerosolphase function, defined as the probability of light scattered in a givendirection. At the Pierre Auger Observatory in Malargue, Argentina, the phasefunction is measured on an hourly basis using two Aerosol Phase Function (APF)light sources. These sources direct a UV light beam across the field of view ofthe fluorescence detectors; the phase function can be extracted from the imageof the shots in the fluorescence detector cameras. This paper describes thedesign, current status, standard operation procedure, and performance of theAPF system at the Pierre Auger Observatory.

We find that the gamma-ray spectrum of the burst is significantly evolving during the prompt phase, displaying a complex and non-monotonic behavior. The initial burst spectrum is characterized by a hard spectral index, which gradually softens before the onset of the afterglow phase. Using multi-wavelength observations from X-rays to radio, we investigate the temporal behavior and spectral properties of the burst emissions. In the afterglow phase, the broad-band spectrum shows a characteristic broken power-law shape. The observed evolution suggests the involvement of particle acceleration processes and the presence of multiple emission components. We also investigate the evolution of the spectral peak energy during the prompt and afterglow phases. We find a significant shift in the spectral peak energy between these two phases, which implies a significant change in the underlying physical processes responsible for the emission. The results indicate the dominance of synchrotron radiation as the dominant emission mechanism during this phase. The observed spectral behavior suggests the involvement of diverse emission mechanisms, such as synchrotron radiation and high-energy particle acceleration, in shaping the observed spectra. These results constrain theoretical models and shed light on the physical processes occurring in gamma-ray burst sources.

We present a novel experiment with the capacity to independently measure boththe electron density and the magnetic field of the solar corona. We achievethis through measurement of the excess Faraday rotation due to propagation ofthe polarised emission from a number of pulsars through the magnetic field ofthe solar corona. This method yields independent measures of the integratedelectron density, via dispersion of the pulsed signal and the magnetic field,via the amount of Faraday rotation. In principle this allows the determinationof the integrated magnetic field through the solar corona along many lines ofsight without any assumptions regarding the electron density distribution. Wepresent a detection of an increase in the rotation measure of the pulsarJ1801$-$2304 of approximately 160 \rad at an elongation of 0.95$^\circ$ fromthe centre of the solar disk. This corresponds to a lower limit of the magneticfield strength along this line of sight of $> 393\mu\mathrm{G}$. The lack ofprecision in the integrated electron density measurement restricts this resultto a limit, but application of coronal plasma models can further constrain thisto approximately 20mG, along a path passing 2.5 solar radii from the solarlimb. Which is consistent with predictions obtained using extensions to theSource Surface models published by Wilcox Solar Observatory

The maximum number density of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGNs), as deduced fromX-ray studies, occurs at z<~1, with lower luminosity objects peaking at smallerredshifts. Optical studies lead to a different evolutionary behaviour, with anumber density peaking at z~2 independently of the intrinsic luminosity, butthis result is limited to active nuclei brighter than the host galaxy. Aselection based on optical variability can detect low luminosity AGNs (LLAGNs),where the host galaxy light prevents the identification by non-stellar colours.We want to collect X-ray data in a field where it exists an optically-selectedsample of "variable galaxies'', i.e. variable objects with diffuse appearance,to investigate the X-ray and optical properties of the population of AGNs,particularly of low luminosity ones, where the host galaxy is visible. Weobserved a field of 0.2 deg^2 in the Selected Area 57, for 67ks withXMM-Newton. We detected X-ray sources, and we correlated the list with aphotographic survey of SA 57, complete to B_J~23 and with availablespectroscopic data. We obtained a catalogue of 140 X-ray sources to limitingfluxes 5x10^-16, 2x10^-15 erg/cm^2/s in the 0.5-2 keV and 2-10 keVrespectively, 98 of which are identified in the optical bands. The X-raydetection of part of the variability-selected candidates confirms their AGNnature. Diffuse variable objects populate the low luminosity side of thesample. Only 25/44 optically-selected QSOs are detected in X-rays. 15% of allQSOs in the field have X/O<0.1.

We test the theory that lenticular (S0) galaxies form from spirals whose starformation has been shut down. We use the globular cluster specific frequencyS_N, defined as the number of globular clusters normalised by the galaxyluminosity as a diagnostic. NTT/EMMI long-slit spectroscopic observations of 11S0 galaxies at z < 0.006 are used to measure the absorption-line indices,Hdelta, Hgamma, Mgb, Fe5270 and Fe5335 within the central r_e/8. By invertingsingle-stellar population models, luminosity-weighted mean ages, metallicitiesand alpha-element abundance ratios are derived. We estimate the amount offading a galaxy has undergone by comparing each galaxy's S_N with its deviationfrom the mean spiral S_N. Galaxies with higher S_N have older stellarpopulations. Moreover, we find that the zero-point and amount of fading isconsistent with a scenario where lenticulars are formed by the quenching ofstar formation in spiral galaxies. Our data also rule out any formation methodfor S0s which creates a large number of new globular clusters. We confirm thatprevious results showing a relationship between S_N and color are driven by theS_N - Age relation. Five galaxies show detectable Hbeta, [OIII], Halpha or[NII] emission lines. However, only in the two youngest galaxies is thisemission unambiguously from star formation. Our results are consistent with thetheory that S0 galaxies are formed when gas in normal spirals is removed,possibly as a result of a change in environment. The on-going star formation inthe youngest galaxies hints that the timescale of quenching is ~< 1 Gyr. Wespeculate, therefore, that the truncation of star formation is a rather gentleprocess unlikely to involve a rapid burst of star formation.

Statistical mechanics is used to analyze the performance of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) Gaussian channels. The analysis provides a framework for understanding the performance of LDPC codes in MIMO channels and for designing LDPC codes that are well-suited for MIMO channels. The analsis is based on the retort method, which is a powerful technique for analyzing the statistical mechanics of disordered systems. The replica method is used to derive a set of equations that describe the performance of LDPC codes in MIMO channels. These equations can be solved numerically to obtain the performance of LDPC codes in MIMO channels. The analysis provides a number of insights into the performance of LDPC codes in MIMO channels. First, the analysis shows that the performance of LDPC codes in MIMO channels is significantly affected by the number of transmit and receive antennas. Second, the analysis shows that the performance of LDPC codes in MIMO channels is also affected by the code rate. Third, the analysis shows that the fulfilment of LDPC codes in MIMO channels can be improved by using a higher code rate.

We consider a nano-system connected to measurement probes via non interactingleads. When the electrons interact inside the nano-system, the coefficient|ts(E_F)|^2 describing its effective transmission at the Fermi energy E_Fceases to be local. This effect of electron-electron interactions upon|ts(E_F)|^2 is studied using a one dimensional model of spinless fermions andthe Hartree-Fock approximation. The non locality of |ts(E_F)|^2 is due to thecoupling between the Hartree and Fock corrections inside the nano-system andthe scatterers outside the nano-system via long range Friedel oscillations.Using this phenomenon, one can vary |ts(E_F)|^2 by an Aharonov-Bohm fluxthreading a ring which is attached to one lead at a distance Lc from thenano-system. For small distances Lc, the variation of the quantum conductanceinduced by this non local effect can exceed 0.1 (e^2/h).

This article explores the extraction of the $\bar q q$ condensate for light quarks beyond the chiral limit in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) models. The authors introduce a novel approach that enables the calculation of the condensate in the light quark mass regime, where previous methods have encountered difficulties. The approach combines lattice QCD and effective field theory techniques, and its reliability and accuracy are demonstrated through numerical simulations. The results offer valuable insights into the behavior of the $\bar q q$ condensate in the light quark regime, with significant implications for understanding the strong interaction and the structure of hadrons.

If a quark-nova occurs inside a collapsar, the interaction between thequark-nova ejecta (relativistic iron-rich chunks) and the collapsar envelope,leads to features indicative of those observed in Gamma Ray Bursts. Thequark-nova ejecta collides with the stellar envelope creating an outward movingcap (Gamma ~ 1-10) above the polar funnel. Prompt gamma-ray burst emission frominternal shocks in relativistic jets (following accretion onto the quark star)become visible after the cap becomes optically thin. Model features include:(i) precursor activity (optical, X-ray, gamma-ray), (ii) prompt gamma-rayemission, and (iii) afterglow emission. We discuss SN-less long duration GRBs,short hard GRBs (including association and non-association with star formingregions), dark GRBs, the energetic X-ray flares detected in Swift GRBs, and thenear-simultaneous optical and gamma-ray prompt emission observed in GRBs in thecontext of our model.

We use an effective field theory (EFT) which contains only short-rangeinteractions to study the dependence of a variety of three-nucleon observableson the pion mass. The pion-mass dependence of input quantities in our''pionless'' EFT is obtained from a recent chiral EFT calculation. To the orderwe work at, these quantities are the 1S0 scattering length and effective range,the deuteron binding energy, the 3S1 effective range, and the binding energy ofone three-nucleon bound state. The chiral EFT input we use has the inverse 3S1and 1S0 scattering lengths vanishing at mpi_c=197.8577 MeV. At this''critical'' pion mass, the triton has infinitely many excited states with anaccumulation point at the three-nucleon threshold. We compute the bindingenergies of these states up to next-to-next-to-leading order in the pionlessEFT and study the convergence pattern of the EFT in the vicinity of thecritical pion mass. Furthermore, we use the pionless EFT to predict how doubletand quartet nd scattering lengths depend on mpi in the region between thephysical pion mass and mpi=mpi_c.

We analyze a probabilistic cellular automaton describing the dynamics ofcoexistence of a predator-prey system. The individuals of each species arelocalized over the sites of a lattice and the local stochastic updating rulesare inspired on the processes of the Lotka-Volterra model. Two levels ofmean-field approximations are set up. The simple approximation is equivalent toan extended patch model, a simple metapopulation model with patches colonizedby prey, patches colonized by predators and empty patches. This approximationis capable of describing the limited available space for species occupancy. Thepair approximation is moreover able to describe two types of coexistence ofprey and predators: one where population densities are constant in time andanother displaying self-sustained time-oscillations of the populationdensities. The oscillations are associated with limit cycles and arise througha Hopf bifurcation. They are stable against changes in the initial conditionsand, in this sense, they differ from the Lotka-Volterra cycles which depend oninitial conditions. In this respect, the present model is biologically morerealistic than the Lotka-Volterra model.

We systematically explore the evolution of the merger of two carbon-oxygen(CO) white dwarfs. The dynamical evolution of a 0.9 Msun + 0.6 Msun CO whitedwarf merger is followed by a three-dimensional SPH simulation. We use anelaborate prescription in which artificial viscosity is essentially absent,unless a shock is detected, and a much larger number of SPH particles thanearlier calculations. Based on this simulation, we suggest that the centralregion of the merger remnant can, once it has reached quasi-static equilibrium,be approximated as a differentially rotating CO star, which consists of aslowly rotating cold core and a rapidly rotating hot envelope surrounded by acentrifugally supported disc. We construct a model of the CO remnant thatmimics the results of the SPH simulation using a one-dimensional hydrodynamicstellar evolution code and then follow its secular evolution. The stellarevolution models indicate that the growth of the cold core is controlled byneutrino cooling at the interface between the core and the hot envelope, andthat carbon ignition in the envelope can be avoided despite high effectiveaccretion rates. This result suggests that the assumption of forced accretionof cold matter that was adopted in previous studies of the evolution of doubleCO white dwarf merger remnants may not be appropriate. Our results imply thatat least some products of double CO white dwarfs merger may be considered goodcandidates for the progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. In this case, thecharacteristic time delay between the initial dynamical merger and the eventualexplosion would be ~10^5 yr. (Abridged).

Did time begin at a Big Bang? Will the present expansion of the universe lastfor a finite or infinite time? These questions sound philosophical but arebecoming, now in the twenty-first century, central to the scientific study ofcosmology. The answers, which should become clarified in the next decade ortwo, could have profound implications for how we see our own role in theuniverse. Since the original publication of Stephen Hawking's {\it A BriefHistory of Time} in 1988, the answers to these questions have progressed as aresult of research by the community of active theoretical physicists includingmyself. To present the underlying ideas requires discussion of a wide range oftopics in cosmology, especially the make up of the energy content of theuniverse. A brief summary of my conclusions, that of three differentpossibilities concerning the history and future of time, the least likely isthe conventional wisdom (time began and will never end) and most likely is acyclic model (time never begins or ends), is in the short final Chapter whichcould be read first. To understand the reasoning leading to my conclusionscould encourage reading of my entire book. My hope in writing this, my firstpopular book, is that it will engender reflection about time. Many anon-scientist may already hold a philosophical opinion about whether timebegins and ends. This book's aim is to present some recently discoveredscientific facts which can focus the reader's consideration of the two shortquestions in my title.

In this examines, we investigate the phenomenon of spontaneous Lorentz violation in the context of non-Abelian gauge fields. We propose a novel mechanism where non-Abelian gauge fields can behave as pseudo-Goldstone vector bosons, preeminent to the emergence of Lorentz symmetry breaking in a unintended manner. We explore the implications of this mechanism in both theoretical and flyboy aspects. We start by discussing the theoretical framework of non-Abelian gauge fields and their subject to the symmetry breaking patterns. We show that through a practical choice of the meters group and the Higgs potential, the non-Abelian gauge sector acquire a pseudo-Goldstone boson nature, similar to what occurs in the Higgs mechanism. Furthermore, we analyze the consequences of such Lorentz rapes in particle physics and cosmology. We investigate the modifications to the dispersion connecting and the associated particle properties for the pseudo-Goldstone vector bosons. Moreover, we explore the potential observational signing of spontaneous Lorentz violation in astrophysical and laboratory experiments. This study barns light on a new avenue for understanding the fundamental symmetries of the universe and the role of non-Abelian gauge fields in Lorentz symmetry sprain. The proposed mechanism paves the way for further theoretical and experimental investigations and provides a unique perspective on the interplay between gauge fields and unintentional symmetry outage.
