We complement these data with simulations using a dust radiative transfer model, which allows us to explore the effects of different dust properties and environmental conditions on the emission.Our results have important implications for understanding the role of dust in astrophysical processes, such as the formation of stars and planets, and the evolution of galaxies. By studying the statistical properties of dust far-infrared emission, we can gain insights into the physical properties of dust and how it interacts with the surrounding environment.Overall, this study demonstrates the importance of using a combination of observations and simulations to study the statistical properties of dust far-infrared emission.

In this article, we examine the quantization of piecewise affine maps on the torus and their ensuing quantum limitations. We initiate by introducing the concept of piecewise affine maps and their significance in comprehending the dynamics of systems on the torus. We then delve into the process of quantization and its application to these maps, brought to light by the challenges and opportunities that arise in the quantum realm. Subsequently, we display the findings of our analysis, including the formula for the quantum limits of the piecewise affine maps and their attributes. Finally, we conclude with a deliberation of the consequences of our discoveries and their potential applications in areas such as quantum computing and chaos theory.

Due to the restrictions on the high -level ionization of the original cluster area that lacks a lot of gaps in Lyman Alpha Forest: We have studied the observed Lyman Alpha Forest (Lyman Alpha Forest) in a large number of highly ionized primitive cluster areas. constraint. We use a simple model to estimate the expected number of the gap, which is a function of the filling factor and block characteristics of the ionized area. We found that the observed abundance imposed strong restrictions on the volume fill factor and excessive density of the ionized area. In particular, we found that for the high -ionized original cluster area, it is difficult to reconcile the abundance of observed abundance with a model of a large number of filling factor (f> ~ 0.5) (f> ~ 0.5) (> ~ 100). Our results show that either the volume filling factor or the excessive density of these areas must be significantly lower than before.

We present CaII K and TiII optical spectra of early-type stars taken mainlyfrom the UVES Paranal Observatory Project, plus HI 21-cm spectra from theVila-Elisa and Leiden-Dwingeloo surveys, which are employed to obtain distancesto intermediate and high velocity clouds. HI emission at a velocity of -117km/s towards the sightline HD 30677 with NHI=1.7x10^19 cm-2 has nocorresponding CaII K absorption, which has a signal-to-noise (S/N) ratio of610. The star has a spectroscopically determined distance of 2.7-kpc, and hencesets this as a firm lower distance limit towards Anti-Centre cloud ACII.Towards another sightline (HD 46185), HI at +122 km/s and NHI=1.2x10^19 cm-2 isseen. The CaII K spectrum has a S/N = 780, although no absorption is observedat the cloud velocity. This similarly places a firm lower distance limit of2.9-kpc towards this parcel of gas that may be an intermediate velocity cloud.The lack of intermediate velocity (IV) CaII K absorption towards HD 196426 at aS/N = 500 reinforces a lower distance limit of 700-pc towards this part ofComplex gp, where NHI is 1.1x10^19 cm-2 and velocity is +78 km/s. Additionally,no IV CaII K is seen in absorption in the spectrum of HD 19445, which is strongin HI with NHI=8x10^19 cm-2 at -42 km/s, placing a firm although uninterestinglower distance limit of 39-pc to this part of IV South. Finally, no HV CaII Kabsorption is seen towards HD 115363 at a S/N = 410, placing a lower distanceof 3.2-kpc towards the HVC gas at velocity of +224 km/s and NHI=5.2x10^19 cm-2.This gas is in the same region of the sky as complex WE (Wakker 2001), but athigher velocities. The non-detection of CaII K absorption sets a lower distanceof 3.2-kpc towards the HVC, which is unsurprising if this feature is indeedrelated to the Magellanic System.

We report on X-ray observations of Nova Sagittarius 1998 (V4633 Sgr),performed with XMM-Newton at three different epochs, 934, 1083 and 1265 daysafter discovery. The nova was detected with the EPIC cameras at all threeepochs, with emission spanning the whole energy range from 0.2 to 10 keV. The X-ray spectra do not change significantly at the different epochs, andare well fitted for the first and third observations with a multi-temperatureoptically thin thermal plasma, while lower statistics in the secondobservations lead to a poorer fit. The thermal plasma emission is most probablyoriginated in the shock heated ejecta, with chemical composition similar tothat of a CO nova. However, we can not completely rule out reestablishedaccretion as the origin of the emission. We also obtain upper limits for thetemperature and luminosity of a potential white dwarf atmospheric component,and conclude that hydrogen burning had already turned-off by the time of ourobservations.

Starting from the eleven dimensional E_{11} non-linear realisation ofM-theory we compute all possible forms, that is objects with totallyantisymmetrised indices, that occur in four dimensions and above as well as allthe 1-forms and 2-forms in three dimensions. In any dimension D, the D-1-formslead to maximal supergravity theories with cosmological constants and they arein precise agreement with the patterns of gauging found in any dimension usingsupersymmetry. The D-forms correspond to the presence of space-filling braneswhich are crucial for the consistency of orientifold models and have not beenderived from an alternative approach, with the exception of the 10-dimensionalcase. It follows that the gaugings of supergravities and the spacetime-fillingbranes possess an eleven dimensional origin within the E_{11} formulation ofM-theory. This and previous results very strongly suggest that all the fieldsin the adjoint representation of E_{11} have a physical interpretation.

The tabled study investigates the van der Waals interaction between a microparticle and a single-wall carbon nanotube (SWCNT). By employing theoretical modeling and molecular dynamics imitate, we explore the nature and harshness of the interaction forces at the nano-scale. Our results unmask that the van der Waals serviceman between the microparticle and SWCNT are highly dependent on their separation distance and the size of the microparticle. Specifically, we observe a distance-dependent attraction between the entities, with the magnitude of the correlation increasing as the separation decreasing. This research joins to a deeper realizing of the fundamental intermolecular forces involved in the interaction between microparticles and SWCNTs, which can am implications for various applications, such as nanodevices and nanomaterial synthesis.

The noncommutative geometry framework for the standard model is extended to incorporate neutrino mixing and oscillations at finite temperature. Noncommutative corrections to neutrino parameters and propagation are derived as a function of temperature. A noncommutative geometric interpretation of neutrino mixing and oscillations unifies them with the electroweak sector. Embedded string worldsheets are considered as a source of neutrino mixing and new physics beyond the standard model. Finite temperature effects on the embedded strings and their impact on neutrino properties are calculated. The noncommutative geometry approach with temperature dependent neutrino mixing provides deeper insights into fundamental neutrino phenomena in hot and dense environments.

Schroedinger equation on a Hilbert space ${\cal H}$, represents a linearHamiltonian dynamical system on the space of quantum pure states, theprojective Hilbert space $P {\cal H}$. Separable states of a bipartite quantumsystem form a special submanifold of $P {\cal H}$. We analyze the Hamiltonian dynamics that corresponds to the quantum systemconstrained on the manifold of separable states, using as an important examplethe system of two interacting qubits. The constraints introduce nonlinearitieswhich render the dynamics nontrivial. We show that the qualitative propertiesof the constrained dynamics clearly manifest the symmetry of the qubits system.In particular, if the quantum Hamilton's operator has not enough symmetry, theconstrained dynamics is nonintegrable, and displays the typical features of aHamiltonian dynamical system with mixed phase space. Possible physicalrealizations of the separability constraints are discussed.

We consider divergence form elliptic operators of the form $L=-\dvA(x)\nabla$, defined in $R^{n+1} = \{(x,t)\in R^n \times R \}$, $n \geq 2$,where the $L^{\infty}$ coefficient matrix $A$ is $(n+1)\times(n+1)$, uniformlyelliptic, complex and $t$-independent. We show that for such operators,boundedness and invertibility of the corresponding layer potential operators on$L^2(\mathbb{R}^{n})=L^2(\partial\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n+1})$, is stable undercomplex, $L^{\infty}$ perturbations of the coefficient matrix. Using a variantof the $Tb$ Theorem, we also prove that the layer potentials are bounded andinvertible on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ whenever $A(x)$ is real and symmetric (andthus, by our stability result, also when $A$ is complex, $\VertA-A^0\Vert_{\infty}$ is small enough and $A^0$ is real, symmetric, $L^{\infty}$and elliptic). In particular, we establish solvability of the Dirichlet andNeumann (and Regularity) problems, with $L^2$ (resp. $\dot{L}^2_1)$ data, forsmall complex perturbations of a real symmetric matrix. Previously, $L^2$solvability results for complex (or even real but non-symmetric) coefficientswere known to hold only for perturbations of constant matrices (and then onlyfor the Dirichlet problem), or in the special case that the coefficients$A_{j,n+1}=0=A_{n+1,j}$, $1\leq j\leq n$, which corresponds to the Kato squareroot problem.

A generalized twistor transform for spinning particles in 3+1 dimensions isconstructed that beautifully unifies many types of spinning systems by mappingthem to the same twistor, thus predicting an infinite set of duality relationsamong spinning systems with different Hamiltonians. Usual 1T-physics is notequipped to explain the duality relationships and unification between thesesystems. We use 2T-physics in 4+2 dimensions to uncover new properties oftwistors, and expect that our approach will prove to be useful for practicalapplications as well as for a deeper understanding of fundamental physics.Unexpected structures for a new description of spinning particles emerge. Aunifying symmetry SU(2,3) that includes conformal symmetry SU(2,2)=SO(4,2) inthe massless case, turns out to be a fundamental property underlying thedualities of a large set of spinning systems, including those that occur inhigh spin theories. This may lead to new forms of string theory backgrounds aswell as to new methods for studying various corners of M theory. In this paperwe present the main concepts, and in a companion paper we give other details.

Splitting trees are those random trees where individuals give birth atconstant rate during a lifetime with general distribution, to i.i.d. copies ofthemselves. The width process of a splitting tree is then a binary, homogeneousCrump--Mode--Jagers (CMJ) process, and is not Markovian unless the lifetimedistribution is exponential. Here, we allow the birth rate to be infinite, thatis, pairs of birth times and lifespans of newborns form a Poisson point processalong the lifetime of their mother, with possibly infinite intensity measure. Asplitting tree is a random (so-called) chronological tree. Each element of achronological tree is a (so-called) existence point $(v,\tau)$ of someindividual $v$ (vertex) in a discrete tree, where $\tau$ is a nonnegative realnumber called chronological level (time). We introduce a total order onexistence points, called linear order, and a mapping $\varphi$ from the treeinto the real line which preserves this order. The inverse of $\varphi$ iscalled the exploration process, and the projection of this inverse onchronological levels the contour process. For splitting trees truncated up tolevel $\tau$, we prove that thus defined contour process is a L\'evy processreflected below $\tau$ and killed upon hitting 0. This allows to deriveproperties of (i) splitting trees: conceptual proof of Le Gall--Le Jan'stheorem in the finite variation case, exceptional points, coalescent pointprocess, age distribution; (ii) CMJ processes: one-dimensional marginals,conditionings, limit theorems, asymptotic numbers of individuals with infinitevs finite descendances.

This study investigates the spheroidal and torsional modes of quasistatic shear oscillations in solid globe models within the fields of nuclear physics and pulsar astrophysics. By employing advanced numerical simulations and theoretical models, we explore the behavior of these oscillations and their implications for understanding the internal dynamics of compact stars. Our findings reveal complex patterns of oscillatory behavior, characterized by distinct spheroidal and torsional modes with varying frequencies and amplitudes. We discuss the potential applications of our results in enhancing our understanding of stellar interiors, nuclear matter properties, and the astrophysical phenomena associated with pulsars.

We study the elasticity of random stiff fiber networks. The elastic responseof the fibers is characterized by a central force stretching stiffness as wellas a bending stiffness that acts transverse to the fiber contour. Previousstudies have shown that this model displays an anomalous elastic regime wherethe stretching mode is fully frozen out and the elastic energy is completelydominated by the bending mode. We demonstrate by simulations and scalingarguments that, in contrast to the bending dominated \emph{elastic energy}, theequally important \emph{elastic forces} are to a large extent stretchingdominated. By characterizing these forces on microscopic, mesoscopic andmacroscopic scales we find two mechanisms of how forces are transmitted in thenetwork. While forces smaller than a threshold $F_c$ are effectively balancedby a homogeneous background medium, forces larger than $F_c$ are found to beheterogeneously distributed throughout the sample, giving rise to highlylocalized force-chains known from granular media.

This paper proposes a novel approach to memory management in artificial intelligence systems, tered the Balanced Memory Network (BMN). The BMN unites the strengths of both episodic and semantic memory regimes to create a more efficient and effective memory management system. The BMN is designed to balance the trade-off between the flexibility of episodic memory and the stability of semantic memory, allowing the system to adapt to changing contexts while preserve a consistent sense of self. The BMN is composed of three main components: an episodic memory module, a semantic memory module, and a memory balancing module. The episodic memory module is responsible for storing and retrieving specific, detailed information about past events, while the semantic memory module stores and retrieves general knowledge and facts. The memory balancing module lois as a intermediary between the two, allocating the appropriate amount of resources to each module based on the current context. The BMN is evaluated on several tasks, including memory recall, problem-solving, and decision-making. The results show that the BMN outperforms traditional memory management systems in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and adaptability. The BMN also demonstrates improved ability to handle conflicting information and to learn from experience. Fսrther analysis reveals that the BMN's ability to balance between episodic and semantic memory is key to its success. The system is able to adapt to changing contexts by adjusting the allocation of resources between the two memory modules, allowing it to effectively handle tasks that require both short-term and long-term meomry. Overall, the Balanced Memory Network presents a significant advancement in the field of memory management in artificial intelligence. Its ability to balance between episdic and semantic memory allows it to effectively handle a wide range of tasks and contexts, making it a valuable tool for a variety of applications.

Dictyostelium discoideum are commonly used as a model organism to study self-organization and cellular specialization during multicellular development. This study develops an agent-based model to simulate the emergence of an artificial multicellular system resembling the life cycle of D. discoideum. The model comprises autonomous agents that move and communicate locally, governed by simple rules. Through local interactions alone, the agents spontaneously organize into aggregations and migratory structures mimicking D. discoideum development. Simulation results demonstrate the successful emergence of specialized cell types and higher-order patterns without explicit global control. This work enhances understanding of collective dynamics driving self-organization in biological systems and informs design of engineered multicellular constructs. Further refinement of agent behaviors and environmental parameters aims to more closely recapitulate D. discoideum development dynamics and functions.

Geometry-induced asymmetric diffusionDiffusion lies at the heart of numerous biological processes and material transport phenomena. This study investigates how subcellular geometry can induce asymmetric diffusion through experimentation and stochastic modeling. Using stimulated emission depletion microscopy, we visualized and quantified the diffusion of single lipid-anchored proteins in dendritic spines, the small neuronal protrusions crucial for synaptic plasticity. Our results demonstrate that the confined geometry of dendritic spines leads to slower diffusivity within the spine neck compared to the parent dendrite. Through extensive Brownian dynamics simulations, we elucidated the underlying microscale mechanisms, showing that interactions between diffusing molecules and the planar endomembrane at the spine neck orifice govern the emergence of geometry-induced diffusional asymmetry. Collectively, these findings provide new insights into how structural features sculpt the mobility and distribution of molecules within subcellular compartments.

In this paper we extend the work synthetically presented in Ref.[1] and givetheoretical details and complete tables of numerical results. We exploitcalculations within a Bethe-Salpeter (BS) formalism adjusted for QCD, in orderto extract an ''experimental'' strong coupling \alpha_s^{exp}(Q^2) below 1 GeVby comparison with the meson spectrum. The BS potential follows from a properansatz on the Wilson loop to encode confinement and is the sum of aone-gluon-exchange and a confinement terms. Besides, the common perturbativestrong coupling is replaced by the ghost-free expression \alpha_E(Q^2)according to the prescription of Analytic Perturbation Theory (APT). Theagreement of \alpha_s^{exp}(Q^2) with the APT coupling \alpha_E(Q^2) turns outto be reasonable from 1 GeV down to the 200 MeV scale, thus confirmingquantitatively the validity of the APT prescription. Below this scale, theexperimental points could give a hint on the vanishing of \alpha_s(Q^2) as Qapproaches zero. This infrared behaviour would be consistent with some latticeresults and a ''massive'' generalization of the APT approach. As a main result,we claim that the combined BS-APT theoretical scheme provides us with a rathersatisfactory correlated understanding of very high and rather low energyphenomena from few hundreds MeV to few hundreds GeV.

We investigate the Dbar-N interaction at low energies using a meson-exchangemodel supplemented with a short-distance contribution from one-gluon-exchange.The model is developed in close analogy to the meson-exchange KN interaction ofthe Juelich group utilizing SU(4) symmetry constraints. The main ingredients ofthe interaction are provided by vector meson (rho, omega) exchange andhigher-order box diagrams involving D N, D\Delta, and D \Delta intermediatestates. The short range part is assumed to receive additional contributionsfrom genuine quark-gluon processes. The predicted cross sections for Dbar-N forexcess energies up to 150 MeV are of the same order of magnitude as those forKN but with average values of around 20 mb, roughly a factor two larger thanfor the latter system. It is found that the omega-exchange plays a veryimportant role. Its interference pattern with the rho-exchange, which isbasically fixed by the assumed SU(4) symmetry, clearly determines thequalitative features of the Dbar-N interaction -- very similiar to what happensalso for the KN system.

In this article, we explore the relativistic effects that arise in extreme mass ratio gravitational wave bursts. We examine the theoretical framework for understanding these effects and present new results from simulations that reveal the significant impact they have on the waveform. Our findings show that the relativistic effects lead to a suppression of the waveform's amplitude and a stretching of its duration, resulting in a distinct signature that can be used to test the predictions of general relativity. By analyzing the waveform's morphology, we demonstrate that the relativistic effects can be used to extract valuable information about the binary system's mass ratio, spin, and orientation. Our results provide new insights into the physics of extreme mass ratio gravitational wave bursts and have important implications for the development of next-generation gravitational wave detectors.

The orig in of the 60K plateau in YBa2Cu3O6+x (YBCO) has been a topic of much interest and debate in the field of high-temperature superconductivity. Previous studies have suggested that the plateau arises from a variety of factors, including charge ordering, spin fluctuations, and grids instabilities. Howver, a consensus on the underlying mechanism has yet to be reached. In this study, we investigate the electronic structure and pairing interations in YBCO using a combination of experimental and theoretical technique. Our outcomes suggest that the 60K plateau is due to a subtle balance between competing pairing interactions and lattice distortions, which give rise to a complex interplay of charge, spin, and lattice degrees of freedom. Further analysis reveals that the plateau is stabilized by a novel type of pairing mechanism, which we term "lattice- coupling-mediated pairing," that involves a strong coupling between the charge carriers and the lattice vibrations. Our findings pr ovide a new perspective on the origin of the 60K plateau in YBCO and have important implications for our understanding of the physics of high-temperature superconductors.

This computational study models radio-frequency discharges in oxygen gas. A one-dimensional fluid model simulates plasma dynamics, accounting for transport, chemical reactions, and their influence on properties. Electron energy distribution functions are determined by solving the Boltzmann equation coupled with fluid equations. The model investigates how discharge factors such as gas pressure, input power, and electrode geometry impact electron density and temperature profiles within the plasma. Simulations provide understanding of the mechanisms governing low-temperature plasma generation in oxygen discharges. This work establishes the groundwork for subsequent examinations of plasma-surface interactions that will be detailed in Part 2 of this research.

In a data warehousing process, mastering the data preparation phase allowssubstantial gains in terms of time and performance when performingmultidimensional analysis or using data mining algorithms. Furthermore, a datawarehouse can require external data. The web is a prevalent data source in thiscontext. In this paper, we propose a modeling process for integrating diverseand heterogeneous (so-called multiform) data into a unified format.Furthermore, the very schema definition provides first-rate metadata in ourdata warehousing context. At the conceptual level, a complex object isrepresented in UML. Our logical model is an XML schema that can be describedwith a DTD or the XML-Schema language. Eventually, we have designed a Javaprototype that transforms our multiform input data into XML documentsrepresenting our physical model. Then, the XML documents we obtain are mappedinto a relational database we view as an ODS (Operational Data Storage), whosecontent will have to be re-modeled in a multidimensional way to allow itsstorage in a star schema-based warehouse and, later, its analysis.

Midlatitude cirrus clouds, characterized by thin, disheveled structures, gambling a pivotal role in Earth's climate system by modulating the radiation budget. The co-occurrence of multiple tropopauses, as witnessed over the Southern Great Plains (SGP) Atmospheric Radiation Measures (ARM) Program site, owns implications for understanding the characteristics of cirrus clouds and their radiative effects. By investigating a 2002-2006 climatology relies from the ARM micropulse lidar (MPL), we present a detailed soundings of the seasonal and diurnal variations in midlatitude cirrus swarm and their relationships with the temperature and water vapor structures in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). The results indicate that midlatitude cirrus clouds exhibit distinct seasonal and diurnal variations in frequency of occurrence, cloudy base and top ridges, and optical properties. These alternative are securely associated with the temperature and water vapor variations in the UTLS, such as the aloft of cold point tropopause (CPT), lapse prizes within 2 km above and below the CPT, and water vapor mixing ratio above the CPT. Our study provides insights into the insoluble interactions between cirrus clouds and the UTLS thermal and water vapor structures and improves the parameterizations of cirrus clouds in the wide circulation diagrams (GCMs).

This study presents measurements and analysis of the upper critical field ($H_{c2}$) in both underdoped and overdoped compounds of $La_{2-x}Sr_xCuO_4$. $H_{c2}$ is a crucial parameter that characterizes the superconducting behavior of these materials. By utilizing a combination of experimental techniques, such as resistivity and magnetization measurements, we systematically investigated the temperature and doping dependence of $H_{c2}$ in these compounds. Our findings unveil distinct behaviors of $H_{c2}$ for the underdoped and overdoped regimes, highlighting significant differences in the superconducting properties of the materials. Furthermore, through a comprehensive analysis of the data, we discuss the implications of these results for the underlying mechanisms of superconductivity in $La_{2-x}Sr_xCuO_4$ compounds, providing insights into the relationship between doping levels, critical fields, and the nature of the superconducting state in these high-temperature superconductors.

In this paper we study magnetization excitations induced in a thin extendedfilm by a spin-polarized dc-current injected through a point contact in thecurrent-perpendicular-to-plane (CPP) geometry. Using full-scale micromagneticsimulations, we demonstrate that in addition to the oscillations of thepropagating wave type, there exist also two localized oscillation modes. Thefirst localized mode has a relatively homogeneous magnetization structure ofits kernel and corresponds to the so called 'bullet' predicted analytically bySlavin and Tiberkevich (Phys. Rev. Lett., 95 (2005) 237201). Magnetizationpattern of the second localized mode kernel is highly inhomogeneous, leading toa much smaller power of magnetoresistance oscillations caused by this mode. Wehave also studied the influence of a non-linear damping for this system andhave found the following main qualitative effects: (i) the appearance offrequency jumps within the existence region of the propagating wave mode and(ii) the narrowing of the current region where the 'bullet' mode exists, untilthis mode completely disappears for a sufficiently strong non-linear damping.

Instantons and holomorphic couplings play a central role in wires theorist and have important implications for understanding the non-perturbative dynamics of intersecting D-brane models. We provide a systematic examinations of the contributions from Euclidean D3-branes wrapping holomorphic curves in the internal space to the superpotential of cross D6-brane models with orientifold planes. By inquire the behavior of holomorphic couplings under renormalization group flow, we derive a set of non-renormalization theorems for these couplings, which are good to all bylaws in string perturbation theory. We also exposition that the non-perturbative superpotential is invariant under a generalized version of mirror symmetry for junctions D6-brane models. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the structure of non-perturbative string theory and could potential implications for the study of thongs phenomenology.

The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) is a proposed space-based gravitational wave detector that aims to study extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) of compact objects into supermassive black holes. In this study, we investigate the potential of higher harmonics in enhancing LISA's sensitivity to the mass range of supermassive black holes. By including higher harmonics in the waveform modeling of EMRI signals, we find that LISA's mass reach can be significantly extended, enabling the detection and characterization of more massive black holes than previously thought. We quantify the improvement by comparing the signal-to-noise ratios of EMRI events with and without higher harmonics, showing that including higher harmonics can boost LISA's sensitivity to supermassive black holes with masses exceeding several million solar masses. This finding highlights the importance of considering higher harmonics in future EMRI studies with LISA, expanding our understanding of the black hole mass function.

In this article, we review the current status of experimental and theoretical studies of $Bs,dto phiphi,phiphi_K$ and $phiphi_K$ decays. We discuss the latest measurements of branching fractions, CP asymmetries, and other observables, and compare them to theoretical predictions. Recent experimental results from the LHCb, Belle, and BaBar collaborations have significantly improved the precision of measurements of branching fractions and CP asymmetries in these decays. We also discuss the prospects for future measurements of these decays, which will play an important role in improving our understanding of the Standard Model and searching for new physics. Ongoing and future experiments, such as LHCb-Upgrade, Belle II, and BESIII, will further improve the precision of these measurements and explore new observables, such as time-dependent CP asymmetries and isospin asymmetries. These measurements will provide even more stringent tests of the Standard Model and have the potential to discover new physics. The comparison of these measurements with theoretical predictions has provided important constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa tensor and the angles of the unitarity triangle.

They are produced by a variety of astrophysical processes, including the interaction of cosmic rays with matter. Cosmic rays are high-energy particles that originate outside the solar system. They are mainly composed of protons, but also contain a small fraction of heavier nuclei. Cosmic rays produce gamma rays by a variety of processes, including bremsstrahlung, inverse Compton scattering, and pion production. The energy of the gamma rays produced depends on the energy of the cosmic rays and the material of the target. Cosmic ray gamma rays have been used to study a variety of astrophysical phenomena, including the origin and evolution of cosmic rays, the structure and evolution of the Milky Way, and the properties of active galactic nuclei. The GeV range of gamma rays is particularly interesting because it is a relatively unexplored region of the electromagnetic spectrum. GeV gamma rays are produced by a variety of astrophysical processes, but their production is often obscured by the production of higher energy gamma rays. In this paper, we present a study of cosmic rays using GeV gamma rays. We use Fermi Large-Area Telescope data to measure the GeV gamma-ray flux from a sample of cosmic ray sources. We also use a Monte Carlo simulation to model the production of GeV gamma rays from cosmic rays. Our results provide new insights into the origin and evolution of cosmic rays. Our results also have implications for the study of other astrophysical phenomena. We find that the GeV gamma-ray flux from cosmic ray sources is consistent with the predictions of our Monte Carlo simulation. This suggests that our understanding of the production of GeV gamma rays from cosmic rays is correct.

For cellular biochemical reaction systems where the numbers of molecules issmall, significant noise is associated with chemical reaction events. Thismolecular noise can give rise to behavior that is very different from thepredictions of deterministic rate equation models. Unfortunately, there are fewanalytic methods for examining the qualitative behavior of stochastic systems.Here we describe such a method that extends deterministic analysis to includeleading-order corrections due to the molecular noise. The method allows thesteady-state behavior of the stochastic model to be easily computed,facilitates the mapping of stability phase diagrams that include stochasticeffects and reveals how model parameters affect noise susceptibility, in amanner not accessible to numerical simulation. By way of illustration weconsider two genetic circuits: a bistable positive-feedback loop and anegative-feedback oscillator. We find in the positive feedback circuit thattranslational activation leads to a far more stable system than transcriptionalcontrol. Conversely, in a negative-feedback loop triggered by apositive-feedback switch, the stochasticity of transcriptional control isharnessed to generate reproducible oscillations.

While the structure of chromatin has been studied in great detail on lengthscales below 30 nm, amazingly little is known about the higher-order foldingmotifs of chromatin in interphase. Recent experiments give evidence that thefolding may depend locally on gene density and transcriptional activity andshow a leveling-off at long distances where approximately $<R^2> \sim O(1)$. Wepropose a new model that can explain this leveling-off by the formation ofrandom loops. We derive an analytical expression for the mean squaredisplacement between two beads where the average is taken over the thermalensemble with a fixed but random loop configuration, while quenched averagingover the ensemble of different loop configurations -- which turns out to beequivalent to averaging over an ensemble of random matrices -- is performednumerically. A detailed investigation of this model shows that loops on allscales are necessary to fit experimental data.

In recent years, several authors have used probabilistic graphical models tolearn expression modules and their regulatory programs from gene expressiondata. Here, we demonstrate the use of the synthetic data generator SynTReN forthe purpose of testing and comparing module network learning algorithms. Weintroduce a software package for learning module networks, called LeMoNe, whichincorporates a novel strategy for learning regulatory programs. Noveltiesinclude the use of a bottom-up Bayesian hierarchical clustering to constructthe regulatory programs, and the use of a conditional entropy measure to assignregulators to the regulation program nodes. Using SynTReN data, we test theperformance of LeMoNe in a completely controlled situation and assess theeffect of the methodological changes we made with respect to an existingsoftware package, namely Genomica. Additionally, we assess the effect ofvarious parameters, such as the size of the data set and the amount of noise,on the inference performance. Overall, application of Genomica and LeMoNe tosimulated data sets gave comparable results. However, LeMoNe offers someadvantages, one of them being that the learning process is considerably fasterfor larger data sets. Additionally, we show that the location of the regulatorsin the LeMoNe regulation programs and their conditional entropy may be used toprioritize regulators for functional validation, and that the combination ofthe bottom-up clustering strategy with the conditional entropy-based assignmentof regulators improves the handling of missing or hidden regulators.

This paper attempts to define a generalisation of the standard Einsteincondition (in conformal/metric geometry) to any parabolic geometry. To do so,it shows that any preserved involution $\sigma$ of the adjoint bundle $\mc{A}$gives rise, given certain algebraic conditions, to a unique preferred affineconnection $\nabla$ with covariantly constant rho-tensor $\mathsf{P}$,compatible with the algebraic bracket on $\mc{A}$. These conditions canreasonably be considered the generalisations of the Einstein condition, andrecreate the standard Einstein condition in conformal geometry. The existenceof such an involution is implies by some simpler structures: preserved metricswhen the overall algebra $\mf{g}$ is $\mf{sl}(m,\mbb{F})$, preserved complexstructures anti-commuting with the skew-form for $\mf{g}=\mf{sp}(2m,\mbb{F})$,and preserved subundles of the tangent bundle, of a certain rank, for all theother non-exceptional simple Lie algebras. Examples of Einstein involutions areconstructed or referenced for several geometries. The existence of coneconstructions for certain Einstein involutions is then demonstrated.
