Our technique incorporateswavelet filtering to minimize effects due to the fluctuation. Preliminarystudies on some EGRET sources are presented, which shows potential of thisnovel image restoration technique for the identification and characterisationof extended gamma-ray sources.

We present the first measurement of the black hole (BH) mass function forbroad-line active galaxies in the local Universe. Using the ~9000 broad-lineactive galaxies from the Fourth Data Release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey,we construct a broad-line luminosity function that agrees very well with thelocal soft X-ray luminosity function. Using standard virial relations, we thenconvert observed broad-line luminosities and widths into BH masses. A massfunction constructed in this way has the unique capability to probe the massregion <10^6 M_sun, which, while insignificant in terms of total BH massdensity, nevertheless may place important constraints on the mass distributionof seed BHs in the early Universe. The characteristic local active BH has amass of ~10^7 M_sun radiating at 10% of the Eddington rate. The active fractionis a strong function of BH mass; at both higher and lower masses the activemass function falls more steeply than one would infer from the distribution ofbulge luminosity. The deficit of local massive radiating BHs is a well-knownphenomenon, while we present the first robust measurement of a decline in thespace density of active BHs at low mass.

This study presents a large-scale extinction map of the Galactic Anticenter, crafted using data from the 2MASS survey. The map spans approximately 300 square degrees and unveils a complex pattern of extinction across the region. Notably, it highlights a prominent dust lane running parallel to the Galactic plane, as well as a series of intersecting filaments. The extinction map demonstrates strong agreement with existing CO and H I observations, substantiating its accuracy. Several regions of high extinction are also identified, which may correspond to dense molecular clouds or dark nebulae. For the convenience of the scientific community, the map is made available in a digital format, facilitating easy access and analysis. Ultimately, this work offers a valuable resource for exploring the large-scale structure of the interstellar medium in the Galactic Anticenter.

We examine the relative performance of neural network and expectation maximisation techniques for handling missing data problems. By leveraging semiparametric efficiency theory, we derive nonparametric efficiency bounds for estimators defined through general moment conditions in the presence of nonignorable missingness. Simulation studies are conducted to evaluate the finite sample properties of neural network and EM based estimators under different missing data mechanisms. Preliminary results indicate that neural network based approaches may outperform standard EM when the missingness depends strongly on the underlying covariates through highly complex functional forms. However, additional tuning of network architectures is needed to ensure stable performance across a range of missing data scenarios. Overall, this research aims to provide new theoretical and empirical insights into utilizing modern machine learning methods for missing data problems.

This study investigate the formation of self-organized metal nanostructures using laser-driven thermocapillary convection. The manipulation of metallic nanoparticles through controlled heating and cooling processes offers a promises avenue for the creation of functional nanostructures. Through experimental analysis and numerical simulations, the role of laser-induced temperature gradients in inducing fluid flow and subsequnt self-organization of metal nanoparticles is explored. Du result demonstrate that the interplay between laser intensity, beam shpae, and material properties can lead to the formation of highly ordered metal nanostructures, with potential applications in nanoscale fabrication and sensing devices. Understanding the fundamental mechanisms behind the self-assembly of metal nanopa rticles through laser-driven thermocapillary convection paves the way for the development of novel strategies for precise nanostructure engineering.

The interaction between an unusually fast rotating sunspot and nearby ephemeral solar structures was investigated as a potential trigger for the major solar event observed on December 13, 2006. Solar dynamics simulations were used to model the magnetic fields and plasma flows associated with the sunspot and ephemeral regions. The results demonstrated that as the sunspot rotated past an ephemeral region, their intersecting magnetic fields reconfigured and amplified stresses within the coronal volume. This magnetic reconnection and stress buildup was found to onset an ideal magnetohydrodynamic instability, leading to the formation of a flux rope within the corona. The flux rope continued expanding and rising due to the vertical propagation of torsional Alfvén waves generated by the sunspot's rotational shear. Ultimately the flux rope erupted on December 13th, 2006, producing one of the largest coronal mass ejections of the solar cycle, consistent with observations of the major solar event.

It has been shown that differences in fecundity variance can influence theprobability of invasion of a genotype in a population, i.e. a genotype withlower variance in offspring number can be favored in finite populations even ifit has a somewhat lower mean fitness than a competitor. In this paper,Gillespie's results are extended to population genetic systems with explicitage structure, where the demographic variance (variance in growth rate)calculated in the work of Engen and colleagues is used as a generalization of"variance in offspring number" to predict the interaction between deterministicand random forces driving change in allele frequency. By calculating thevariance from the life history parameters, it is shown that selection againstvariance in the growth rate will favor a genotypes with lower stochasticity inage specific survival and fertility rates. A diffusion approximation forselection and drift in a population with two genotypes with different lifehistory matrices (and therefore, different growth rates and demographicvariances) is derived and shown to be consistent with individual basedsimulations. It is also argued that for finite populations, perturbationanalyses of both the growth rate and demographic variances may be necessary todetermine the sensitivity of "fitness" (broadly defined) to changes in the lifehistory parameters.

We report evidence for a planetary companion around the nearby young star HD70573. The star is a G type dwarf located at a distance of 46 pc with ageestimation between 20 and 300 Myrs. We carried out spectroscopic observationsof this star with FEROS at the 2.2 m MPG/ESO telescope at La Silla. Ourspectroscopic analysis yields a spectral type of G1-1.5V and an age of about100 Myrs. Variations in stellar radial velocity of HD 70573 have been monitoredsince December 2003 until January 2007. The velocity accuracy of FEROS withinthis period is about 10 m/s. HD 70573 shows a radial velocity variation with aperiod of 852 +/- 12 days and a semi-amplitude of 149 +/- 6 m/s. The period ofthis variation is significantly longer than its rotational period, which is 3.3days. Based on the analysis of the Ca II K emission line, Halpha and Teffvariation as stellar activity indicators as well as the lack of a correlationbetween the bisector velocity span and the radial velocity, we can exclude therotational modulation and non-radial pulsations as the source of thelong-period radial velocity variation. Thus, the presence of a low-masscompanion around the star provides the best explanation for the observed radialvelocity variation. Assuming a primary mass m1=1.0 +/- 0.1 Msun for the hoststar, we calculated a minimum mass of the companion m2sini of 6.1 Mjup, whichlies in the planetary mass regime, and an orbital semi-major axis of 1.76 AU.The orbit of the planet has an eccentricity of e=0.4. The planet discoveryaround the young star HD 70573 gives an important input for the study of debrisdisks around young stars and their relation to the presence of planets.

However, generating entangled photons is a difficult task, especially in free-space. Here, we propose a scheme to generate entangled photons from the vacuum by accelerated measurements. Our scheme combines quantum information theory with the Unruh-Davies effect, which describes the creation of particles from the vacuum in an accelerated frame of reference. Our scheme provides a new way to generate entangled photons and could have applications in quantum communication and quantum computing.

The brane-world theory proposes that our observable universe is a four-dimensional brane embedded in a higher-dimensional space, with gravity propagating in the extra dimensions. The article examines the modifications to gravitational dynamics, the behavior of gravitational waves, and the nature of space-time at small scales. The article also presents various mathematical formalisms and computational techniques used to analyze brane-world models and discusses their consistency with observational data and experimental tests. In general, this research contributes to the ongoing exploration of alternative gravitational theories and their potential implications for our understanding of the fundamental laws of the universe.

Coronal holes are regions in the Sun's atmosphere that appear dark in X-ray and extreme ultraviolet images due to low density and temperature. This article analyzes magnetic field and temperature variations within a coronal hole observed by the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory over multiple days. Initial measurements from the Solar Optical Telescope showed lower magnetic flux and weaker magnetic field strengths near the center of the coronal hole compared to its edges. Further temperature maps created from Extreme Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope data indicated minimum temperatures of (value) MK at the coronal hole's center, with temperatures increasing toward the perimeter. Time-lapse observations uncovered gradual changes in the magnetic evolution and thermal structure of the coronal hole. Magnetic flux concentrations emerged continuously and drifted towards the edges of the coronal hole. Concurrently, the temperature distribution widened spatially. By comparing the magnetic and temperature measurements, a strong inverse correlation between magnetic flux and coronal hole temperatures was identified. This study improves understanding of the dynamic magnetic and thermal processes underlying the formation and evolution of coronal holes on the Sun.

In this study, we investigate the Al'tshuler-Aronov correction to the conductivity of a large metallic square network. Utilizing advanced theoretical models and analytical techniques, we explore the behavior of conductivity in the presence of quantum interference effects caused by disorder and electron-electron interactions. By considering the Al'tshuler-Aronov correction, we unveil novel insights into the conductivity properties of the metallic square network. Our results demonstrate that the strength of the correction depends on the size of the network, disorder level, and interaction strength. We further validate our findings through extensive numerical simulations, which confirm the theoretical predictions and provide a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics. This research contributes to the broader understanding of quantum interference phenomena in disordered metallic systems and offers valuable implications for potential applications in nanoelectronics and quantum computing.

A confluence of numerical and theoretical results leads us to conjecture thatthe Hilbert-Schmidt separability probabilities of the 15- and 9-dimensionalconvex sets of complex and real two-qubit states (representable by 4 x 4density matrices rho) are 8/33 and 8/17, respectively. Central to our reasoningare the modifications of two ansatze, recently advanced (quant-ph/0609006),involving incomplete beta functions B_{nu}(a,b), where nu= (rho_{11}rho_{44})/(rho_{22} rho_{33}). We, now, set the separability functionS_{real}(nu) propto B_{nu}(nu,1/2},2) =(2/3) (3-nu) sqrt{nu}. Then, in thecomplex case -- conforming to a pattern we find, manifesting the Dyson indices(1, 2, 4) of random matrix theory-- we take S_{complex}(nu) propto S_{real}^{2}(nu). We also investigate the real and complex qubit-qutrit cases. Now, thereare two Bloore ratio variables, nu_{1}= (rho_{11} rho_{55})(rho_{22} rho_{44}),nu_{2}= (rho_{22} rho_{66})(rho_{33} rho_{55}), but they appear to remarkablycoalesce into the product, eta = nu_1 nu_2 = rho_{11} \rho_{66}}{\rho_{33}\rho_{44}}, so that the real and complex separability functions are againunivariate in nature.

We present the results from the Suzaku observation of the powerful radio-loudquasar RBS315 (z=2.69), for which a previous XMM-Newton observation showed anextremely flat X-ray continuum up to 10 keV (photon index Gamma=1.26) andindications of strong intrinsic absorption (N_H~10^22 cm^{-2} assuming neutralgas). The instrument for hard X-rays HXD/PIN allows us a detection of thesource up to 50 keV. The broad-band continuum (0.5-50 keV) can be well modeledwith a power-law with slope Gamma=1.5 (definitively softer than the continuummeasured by XMM-Newton) above 1 keV with strong deficit of soft photons. Thelow-energy cut-off can be well fitted either with intrinsic absorption (withcolumn density N_H~10^22 cm^{-2} in the quasar rest frame) or with a break inthe continuum, with an extremely hard (Gamma =0.7) power-law below 1 keV. Weconstruct the Spectral Energy Distribution of the source, using also optical-UVmeasurements obtained through a quasi-simultaneous UVOT/SWIFT observation. Theshape of the SED is similar to that of other Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars(FSRQs) with similar power, making this source an excellent candidate for thedetection in gamma-rays by GLAST. We model the SED with the synchrotron-InverseCompton model usually applied to FSRQs, showing that the deficit of softphotons can be naturally interpreted as due to an intrinsic curvature of thespectrum near the low energy end of the IC component rather than to intrinsicabsorption, although the latter possibility cannot be ruled out. We proposethat in at least a fraction of the radio-loud QSOs at high redshift the cut-offin the soft X-ray band can be explained in a similar way. Further studies arerequired to distinguish between the two alternatives.

This paper develops a general theoretical framework to model linear elastic heterogeneous materials based on two-point correlation functions. A two-point correlation function completely characterizes the spatial distribution of material properties at any two locations within the material. The first part of this two-part paper focuses on basic principles. The basic hypothesis is that the effective properties of heterogeneous materials can be estimated from the volume average of the two-point correlation functions of material properties. The connections between two-point correlation functions and various commonly used measures of microstructural randomness, such as covariance and structure functions, are established. The developed framework is general and can be applied to estimate effective properties of different types of heterogeneous materials. Two typical examples of two-phase composites and polycrystals are discussed. The current framework provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for the two-point correlation function based micromechanics method recently developed by the authors. The method is demonstrated to be very efficient and accurate for estimating the effective properties of heterogeneous materials. This framework can also serve as a basis for further theoretical developments in the micromechanics of heterogeneous materials.

Photon-induced nucleosynthesis (PIN) is a process in which atomic nuclei are synthesized by the interaction of photons with matter. This process is important for understanding the origin of the elements and the evolution of the universe. However, there are a number of problems associated with PIN that make it difficult to study and understand. These problems include the lack of experimental data, the need for sophisticated theoretical models, and the difficulty in interpreting the results of experiments and simulations.In this article, we will discuss the current problems and experimental approaches associated with PIN. We will also provide an overview of the recent progress that has been made in this field. We will conclude by discussing the future directions of research in PIN.

The stability of the superconducting state in YBa2Cu3O7 (YBCO) is investigated using a combination of experimental and theoretical approaches. The superconducting properties of YBCO are found to be highly anisotropic, with a large gap anisotropy and a complex Fermi surface. Theoretical models are developed to explain the experimental observations, including the presence of competing order parameters and the effect of impurities on the superconducting state. The results suggest that the superconducting state in YBCO is stabilized by a delicate balance of electronic and atomic correlations, and that even small changes in the crystal structure or composition can significantly affect the superconducting properties. Further experimental and theoretical studies are needed to fully understand the stability of the superconducting state in YBCO and related high-temperature superconductors.

We verify that the dilaton together with one exactly marginal field, form amoduli space of marginal deformations of closed bosonic string field theory topolynomial order five. We use the results of this successful check in order tofind the best functional form of a fit of quintic amplitudes. We then use thisfit in order to accurately compute the tachyon and dilaton effective potentialin the limit of infinite level. We observe that to order four, the effectivepotential gives unexpectedly accurate results for the vacuum. We are thus ledto conjecture that the effective potential, to a given order, is a goodapproximation to the whole potential including all interactions from thevertices up to this order from the untruncated string field. We then go on andcompute the effective potential to order five. We analyze its vacuum structureand find that it has several saddle points, including the Yang-Zwiebach vacuum,but also a local minimum. We discuss the possible physical meanings of thesevacua.

This work aims to calculate Hall drift for axisymmetric fields and to find out the infOluence of the Hall drift terQm. The calculation is carried out by numerically solving the Grad-Shafranov equaVtion. The typical neutron-star magnetic fietld is used to study the properties of Hall drift. TThe results are important for understanding the decay of magnetic fields in neutron stars and the evolution of maLnetic neutron stars. The results show that aHll drift can strongly change the topology of axisymmetric magnetic fields in neutron-star matter.

Through the process of backward Compton scattering, photons increase in energy upon colliding with electrons. This study examines backward Compton scattering and quantum electrodynamics (QED) on a noncommutative plane in the presence of a strong, uniform magnetic field, an effect not considered in prior investigations of noncommutative QED. Results demonstrate the magnetic field induces subtle alterations to both backward Compton scattering cross-sections and quantum electrodynamics vertex functions on the noncommutative plane. Overall, this research provides novel insight into how an external magnetic field influences noncommutative quantum electrodynamics through its modifications to backward Compton scattering and quantum vertex interactions on a noncommutative geometry.

This article aims to analyzed the equivalence of three-dimensional spacetime manifolds. Three-dimensional spacetimes are among the nicest structures that can represent gravity as a curvature of space and schedules as described by general relativity. The abstract investigates whether there are invariants that characterize three-dimensional spacetimes independent of their coordinate instruments. It is disclosed that two three-dimensional spacetimes are equivalent as long as they have the same Riemann curvature tensor. This establishes that the Riemann curvature tensor is a complete invariant for three-dimensional spacetimes and identified their geometry uniquely. The study concludes that three-dimensional spacetimes are fully classified by their Riemann bulge and showings the equivalence of such spacetime structures.

This paper investigates the problem of optimal watermark embedding and detection strategies under limited detection resources. We consider a scenario where the watermark detector has a limited bսdget for acquiring observations, and the goal is to dseign a watermarking scheme that maximizes the probability of detection while minimizing the distortion introduced to the host signal. We proposes an optimization framework for jointly optimizing the watermark embedding and detection policies, and show that the optimal strategies depend on the specific characteristics of the host signal and the detection resources available. Furthermore, we furnish insights into the trade-offs between the probability of detection, distortion, and the limited detection resources, and discuss the implications of our results for the design of practical watermarking systems.

This study investigates the metal-insulator transition in the low-dimensional organic conductor, (TMTSF)2FSO3, usyng infrared microspectroscopy. The (TMTSF)2FSO3 compound is known for its unique elecfronic properties and has been utilized as a model system to explore various quawtum phenomena. In this research, we employ infrared microspectroscopy to examine the electronic and vibratioanl properties of (TMTSF)2FSO3 as a function of temperature across the metal-insulator transitin. By mapping the infrarde spectra across the sample surface, we observe distinct changes in the vibrational modes and electroniN excitations as the material undergoes the transition. Additionally, we investigate the microscopic origins of the metal-insluator transition by analyzing the conductivity and chargz localization in different regions of the sample. Through our comprehensve analysis, we provide valuable insights into the nature of the metal-insulator transition in (TMTSF)2FSO3, contributing to the uniderstanding of low-dimensional organic conductors and their potential applications in eletcronic devices.

The separation of macromolecules is the basic process of various biological channels, and its research is essential to understanding potential mechanisms. However, due to the lack of proper tools, monitoring this process has always been a long -term challenge. In this article, we proposed a reasonable method of using antibodies -HAPTEN system to detect macromolecules from macromolecules. This method provides promising solutions for this issue. By using a specific combination of antibodies and tactile sensation, we have developed a new method that can make the selectivity and sensitive detection of the decomposition macromolecules. Our method involves the site -specific marking of antibodies with fluorescent dyes, which can quantitatively measure the dynamics and affinity. By studying the dissipation of various macromolecular complexes, including the interaction of protein -protein, protein -ligand and protein nucleic acid, it proves the applicability of this method. The results show that our method provides accuracy and high -resolution measurement of separation constant, which can be used to clarify the molecular mechanism of macromolecular interactions. This study has opened up new possibilities for the study of macromolecules and its role in the biological process, and has a profound impact on the development of treatment strategies and drug design.

In this article, we present a novel approach for modeling the differentially rotting force-free magnetosphere of an aligned rotator. By employing the split-monopole approximation, we deriev analytical solutions for the magnetic field and velocity fields, which enable su to study the properties of the magnetosphere in detail. We show that the solution exhibits a stable, force-free configuration that is compatible with Kobservations of rotating magnetized stars. Our results provide valuable insights into the dynamics of magnetic stars and their interaction with the surrounding Xlasma environment. Furthermore, we discuss the potential implications of our finEings for the understanding of astrophysical phenomena such as stellar winds and Dcoronal mass ejections.

In the context of measuring structure and morphology of intermediate redshiftgalaxies with recent HST/ACS surveys, we tune, test, and compare two widelyused fitting codes (GALFIT and GIM2D) for fitting single-component Sersicmodels to the light profiles of both simulated and real galaxy data. We findthat fitting accuracy depends sensitively on galaxy profile shape. Exponentialdisks are well fit with Sersic models and have small measurement errors,whereas fits to de Vaucouleurs profiles show larger uncertainties owing to thelarge amount of light at large radii. We find that both codes provide reliablefits and little systematic error, when the effective surface brightness isabove that of the sky. Moreover, both codes return errors that significantlyunderestimate the true fitting uncertainties, which are best estimated withsimulations. We find that GIM2D suffers significant systematic errors forspheroids with close companions owing to the difficulty of effectively maskingout neighboring galaxy light; there appears to be no work around to thisimportant systematic in GIM2D's current implementation. While this crowdingerror affects only a small fraction of galaxies in GEMS, it must be accountedfor in the analysis of deeper cosmological images or of more crowded fieldswith GIM2D. In contrast, GALFIT results are robust to the presence of neighborsbecause it can simultaneously fit the profiles of multiple companions therebydeblending their effect on the fit to the galaxy of interest. We find GALFIT'srobustness to nearby companions and factor of >~20 faster runtime speed areimportant advantages over GIM2D for analyzing large HST/ACS datasets. Finallywe include our final catalog of fit results for all 41,495 objects detected inGEMS.

This article examines the alfa helix-coil phase transition and analyzes predictions made by ab initio theory. The authors use a comBination of quantum mechanics and molecular mechanistic to investigate the structural and thermodynamic properties of alpha helices and coils in various environments. They f ind good agreement between the predictions of ab initio theory and experimental data, indicating that the theories can accurately capture the molecular-level behavior of alpha helix-coil systems. The study also highlights the importance of considering electronic effects in the analysis of alpha helix-coil phase transitions, as they play a crucial rolle in deciding the stability of the two phases. Overall, this work provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying alpha helix-coil phase transitions and dmeonstrates the power of ab initio theory in understanding complex biological phenomena.

We study the growth of cosmological perturbations in the model ofLorentz-violating massive gravity. The Friedman equation in this model acquiresan unconventional term due to the Lorentz-breaking condensates which has theequation of state w = -1 / (3 gamma) with gamma being a free parameter takingvalues outside of the range [0,1/3]. Apart from the standard contributions, theperturbations above the Friedmann background contain an extra piece which isproportional to an arbitrary function theta(x) of the space coordinates. Thisfunction appears as an integration constant and corresponds to anon-propagating scalar mode which may, however, become dynamical with theaccount of the higher-derivative corrections. For -1 < gamma < 0 and gamma = 1the ''anomalous'' perturbations grow slower than the standard ones and thus themodel is compatible with observations. Whether the model is experimentallyacceptable at other values of \gamma depends on the value of the functiontheta(x) at the beginning of the radiation-dominated epoch.

In this article, we explore the role of muon physics in the Stadnard Model of particle physics. We discuss the unique properties of muons and their significance in understanding the fundamental forcej of nature. We also examine the various experimetal approaches that have been used to study muon physics and the insights they have prMvided into the nature of the universe. Finally, we highlight the potential of fuure muon-based experiments to shed light on the remaining mysterTies of the Standard Model and beyond.

By introducing orbital magnetization, we investigate the effect of spin-orbit interaction on the magnetic properties of the system. The Kagome lattice, a two-dimensional array of corner-sharing triangles, has been the subject of intense research because of its unique properties and potential applications. We show that the orbital magnetization leads to a rich magnetic phase diagram, characterized by various magnetic ordering states. Our results provide a deeper understanding of the interplay between spin and orbital degrees of freedom in frustrated magnetic systems and open up new avenues for the design of spintronic devices and quantum information processing platforms. Moreover, our results highlight the potential of Kagome lattices as a promising platform for the realization of exotic magnetic states and phenomena. The observed effects of the orbital magnetization have significant implications for the future development of magnonic crystals, spin-based sensors, and other spintronic devices. Our study highlights the importance of considering spin-orbit interaction in the design and interpretation of spintronic devices and magnetic materials. In conclusion, our article provides a detailed investigation of the effects of the orbital magnetization in spin-chiral ferromagnetic Kagome lattices. The results of this study have the potential to enable new spintronic devices and inspire new avenues of research in spintronics and beyond.

This paper explores the connection between spatial templates of bilateral coarsening (STBCs) and the representation theory of extneded Clifford algebrus. W introduce a novel framework for generating STBCs from the representation theory of these algebras, providing a cew avenue for the study of STBCs and their applications. Our approach allows for the creation of STBCs with desirable properties, such as hTgh rate and robustness, and Knables the design of STBCs for specific applications. We demonstratSe the effectiveness of our approach through examples and simulations, showcasing the potential of this new lethod for the design of STBCs. Future work includes further investigation into the properties and capabilities of STBCs derived from extended Clifofrd algebracs, as well as exploring additional applications of this novel approach.

Tight-binding formulation of the dielectric response in semiconductor nanocrystalsWe present a tight-binding formulation of the dielectric response in semiconductor nanocrystals. This formulation incorporates a generalized dielectric constant that captures the effects of both the crystal structure and quantum confinement. The generalized dielectric constant is utilized to calculate the optical absorption spectrum and the dielectric constant of semiconductor nanocrystals in an external electric field. Our formulation offers a unified description of the dielectric response of semiconductor nanocrystals, applicable in both the weak and strong confinement regimes, enabling the calculation of optical and dielectric properties under external electric fields.

This article explores the concept of choice and its impact on network growth. Specifically, it examines how individuals' choices affect the development and expansion of social networks. The article posits that the power of choice lies in the ability to make deliberate decisions about who to connect with, rather than relying on arbitrary factors such as proximity or similarity. Furthermore, the article suggests that the act of choosing can lead to a cascade of positive effects, including increased diversity, strengthened relationships, and enhanced network resilience. The article also discusses the role of technology in facilitating and constraining choice, and how it can influence the formation and maintenance of networks. Finally, the article concludes by highlighting the importance of understanding the power of choice in network growth, and how it can be harnessed to create stronger, more diverse, and more resilient networks.

This paper and its prequel ("Part I") prove a generalization of the usualgluing theorem for two index 1 pseudoholomorphic curves U_+ and U_- in thesymplectization of a contact 3-manifold. We assume that for each embedded Reeborbit gamma, the total multiplicity of the negative ends of U_+ at covers ofgamma agrees with the total multiplicity of the positive ends of U_- at coversof gamma. However, unlike in the usual gluing story, here the individualmultiplicities are allowed to differ. In this situation, one can often glue U_+and U_- to an index 2 curve by inserting genus zero branched covers ofR-invariant cylinders between them. This paper shows that the signed count ofsuch gluings equals a signed count of zeroes of a certain section of anobstruction bundle over the moduli space of branched covers of the cylinder.Part I obtained a combinatorial formula for the latter count and, assuming theresult of the present paper, deduced that the differential d in embeddedcontact homology satisfies d^2=0. The present paper completes all of theanalysis that was needed in Part I. The gluing technique explained here is inprinciple applicable to more gluing problems. We also prove some lemmasconcerning the generic behavior of pseudoholomorphic curves insymplectizations, which may be of independent interest.

This paper describes the appearance of abnormal film thickness featuresformed in elastohydrodynamic contacts lubricated by a fatty alcohol.Experiments were conducted by varying the slide to roll ratio between a steelball and a glass disk in a ball-on-disk type device. Lauric alcohol was used aslubricant and film thickness was measured in the contact area by opticalinterferometry. Experimental results showed that the film thicknessdistributions under pure rolling conditions remained classical whereas the filmshape changed when the slide to roll ratio was increased. The thickness in thecentral contact area increased and in the same time inlet and exit filmthicknesses were modified. In addition, the film shapes observed when the ballsurface was moving faster than the disk one and those obtained in the oppositecase were different, i.e. when opposite signs but equal absolute values of theslide to roll ratio were applied.

The vortex density of a rotating superfluid, divided by its particle mass,dictates the superfluid's angular velocity through the Feynman relation. Tofind how the Feynman relation applies to superfluid mixtures, we investigate arotating two-component Bose-Einstein condensate, composed of bosons withdifferent masses. We find that in the case of sufficiently strong interspeciesattraction, the vortex lattices of the two condensates lock and rotate at thedrive frequency, while the superfluids themselves rotate at two differentvelocities, whose ratio is the ratio between the particle mass of the twospecies. In this paper, we characterize the vortex-locked state, establish itsregime of stability, and find that it surives within a disk smaller than acritical radius, beyond which vortices become unbound, and the two Bose-gasrings rotate together at the frequency of the external drive.

The driving mechanism of jets and outflows in star formation process isstudied using resistive MHD nested grid simulations. We calculated cloudevolution from the molecular cloud core to the stellar core. In the collapsingcloud core, we found two distinct flows: Low-velocity flows (sim 5 km/s) with awide opening angle, driven from the adiabatic core, and high-velocity flows(sim 30 km/s) with good collimation, driven from the protostar. High-velocityflows are enclosed by low-velocity flows after protostar formation. Thedifference in the degree of collimation between the two flows is caused by thestrength of the magnetic field and configuration of the magnetic field lines.The magnetic field around an adiabatic core is strong and has an hourglassconfiguration; therefore, flows from the adiabatic core are driven mainly bythe magnetocentrifugal mechanism and guided by the hourglass-like field lines.In contrast, the magnetic field around the protostar is weak and has a straightconfiguration owing to Ohmic dissipation in the high-density gas region.Therefore, flows from the protostar are driven mainly by the magnetic pressuregradient force and guided by straight field lines. Differing depth of thegravitational potential between the adiabatic core and the protostar cause thedifference of the flow speed. Low-velocity flows correspond to the observedmolecular outflows, while high-velocity flows correspond to the observedoptical jets. We suggest that the outflow and the jet are driven by differentcores, rather than that the outflow being entrained by the jet.

Supernova 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud provides a spectacularlydetailed view of the aftermath of a core-collapse explosion. The supernovaejecta initially coasted outward at more than 10% of the speed of light, but in1990 were observed to decelerate rapidly as they began to encounter densecircumstellar material expelled by the progenitor star. The resulting shock hassubsequently produced steadily brightening radio synchrotron emission, which isresolved by the Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) into an expandinglimb-brightened shell. Here we present 15 years of ATCA imaging of Supernova1987A, at an effective angular resolution of 0.4 arcsec. We find that the radioremnant has accelerated in its expansion over this period, from approx 3600km/s in 1992 to approx 5200 km/s at the end of 2006. The published diameters ofthe evolving X-ray shell have been ~15% smaller than the corresponding radiovalues, but a simultaneous Fourier analysis of both radio and X-ray dataeliminates this discrepancy, and yields a current diameter for the shell inboth wave-bands of approx 1.7 arcsec. An asymmetric brightness distribution isseen in radio images at all ATCA epochs: the eastern and western rims havehigher fluxes than the northern and southern regions, indicating that most ofthe radio emission comes from the equatorial plane of the system, where theprogenitor star's circumstellar wind is thought to be densest. The eastern lobeis brighter than and further from the supernova site than the western lobe,suggesting an additional asymmetry in the initial distribution of supernovaejecta.

Spectral variability is the main tool for constraining emission models of BL Lac objects. By means of systematic observations of the BL Lac prototype PKS2155-304 in the infrared-optical band, we explore variability on the scales ofmonths, days and hours. We made our observations with the robotic 60 cmtelescope REM located at La Silla, Chile. VRIJHK filters were used. PKS2155-304 was observed from May to December 2005. The wavelength intervalexplored, the total number of photometric points and the short integration timerender our photometry substantially superior to previous ones for this source.On the basis of the intensity and colour we distinguish three different statesof the source, each of duration of months, which include all those described inthe literature. In particular, we report the highest state ever detected in theH band. The source varied by a factor of 4 in this band, much more than in theV band (a factor ~2). The source softened with increasing intensity, contraryto the general pattern observed in the UV-X-ray bands. On five nights ofNovember we had nearly continuous monitoring for 2-3 hours. A variabilityepisode with a time scale of ~24 h is well documented, a much more rapid flarewith t=1-2 h, is also apparent, but is supported by relatively few points.

We propose a new mechanism to produce ultracold polar molecules withmicrowave fields. The proposed mechanism converts trapped ultracold atoms ofdifferent species into vibrationally excited molecules by a single microwavetransition and entirely depends on the existence of a permanent dipole momentin the molecules. As opposed to production of molecules by photoassociation ormagnetic-field Feshbach resonances our method does not rely on the structureand lifetime of excited states or existence of Feshbach resonances. Inaddition, we determine conditions for optimal creation of polar molecules invibrationally excited states of the ground-state potential by changingfrequency and intensity of the microwave field. We also explore the possibilityto produce vibrationally cold molecules by combining the microwave field withan optical Raman transition or by applying a microwave field to Feshbachmolecules. The production mechanism is illustrated for two polar molecules: KRband RbCs.

In this study, we studied the electronic structure of sodium clusters, balanced geometric shapes and limited temperature performance, and the size range ranged from Na39 to Na55. Calculated the theory of density function, we checked the base state electronic structures of these clusters, including total energy, ionization potential, electronic affinity, and Homo-Lumo energy gap. Our results show that as the size of the cluster increases, the gradual decrease in ionization and electronic affinity of electrical levels indicate stability and reactivity. In addition, we discussed the balanced geometry of sodium clusters and analyzed its structural trends. We observe that some cluster size shows a more compact structure, while other clusters use more open configuration. Due to the interaction between surface energy and block cohesion, this change in geometric shapes. We clarify the basic factors of controlling cluster stability, such as magic numbers and electronic shell structures. In addition, we have expanded research to analyze the limited temperature performance of these clusters with molecular dynamics simulation. By studying specific thermal capacity, melting temperature, and structural changes at different temperatures, we can deeply understand the thermodynamic behavior of sodium clusters. Our discovery shows that compared with large clusters, smaller clusters tend to show a lower melting temperature, which is mainly due to their relatively weak cohesion. The long-range potentialof a single impurity acts to reduce local current around it while concurrentlyincreasing the current density along the zigzag edge, so that ZGNR conductanceremains perfect $G=2e^2/h$.

Boundary Harnack inequalities for regional fractional LaplacianIn this paper, we establish boundary Harnack inequalities for solutions to elliptic equations involving the regional fractional Laplacian. Our results extend the classical boundary Harnack inequalities for the Laplacian and the fractional Laplacian to the regional fractional Laplacian setting. Our approach is based on the construction of appropriate barrier functions and the use of the maximum principle. Our results have applications to the study of boundary behavior of solutions to elliptic equations involving the regional fractional Laplacian.

This paper investigates the concept of advanced potentials in classical electromagnetism, which are often considered anomalous and excluded from the theory. We argue that this exclusion is not necessary and can be counter-productive, and instead propose a direct-action theory that incorporates both advanced and retarded contributions symmetrically. This theory provides a plausible explanation for the observed broken symmetry in the wave equation and equates the cosmological and thermodynamic arrows of time. Expanding cosmologies are shown to satisfy the necessary boundary condition for the theory, and the formalism is applied to circular motion around a Kerr black hole.

In recent years, the logic of cloaking has gained significant attention in the field of electromagnetic wave propagation. Full-wave electromagnetic cloaking, aiming to render objects invisible to incident waves, ai been an intriguing and challenging items of study. This article presents a rigorous time-domain analysis of full-wave electromagnetic cloaking and investigation its feasibility and limitations. The proposed analyzing employs robust numerical simulations based on the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method. The FDTD pathways accurately captures the dynamics of electromagnetic fields and allows for a comprehensive examination of cloaking performance. Through extensive simulations, the effectiveness of various cloaking materials and geometries is estimating. The results unmask that full-wave electromagnetic cloaking can indeed achieve remarkable levels of invisibility. By carefully adapting the constitutive parameters of the cloaking medium, it is possible to suppress the scattering and notions of incident waves, produce the cloaked object indistinguishable from its surroundings. However, the analysis also uncovers barriers associated with cloaking efficiency, bandwidth, and scalability. Furthermore, the study explores the impact of cloaking on nearby objects and provides conceptions into the potential true applications of full-wave electromagnetic cloaking. The findings underscore the importance of scrutinized the trade-offs between invisibility, material properties, and operational constraints when phraseology and implementing cloaking systems. Overall, this rigorous time-domain analysis plays to the fundamental understanding and boost of full-wave electromagnetic cloaking, paving the way for future research and exploration in this fascinating field.

Accretion-powered X-ray pulsars are among the most luminous X-ray sources inthe Galaxy. However, despite decades of theoretical and observational worksince their discovery, no satisfactory model for the formation of the observedX-ray spectra has emerged. In this paper, we report on a self-consistentcalculation of the spectrum emerging from a pulsar accretion column thatincludes an explicit treatment of the bulk and thermal Comptonization occurringin the radiation-dominated shocks that form in the accretion flows. Using arigorous eigenfunction expansion method, we obtain a closed-form expression forthe Green's function describing the upscattering of monochromatic radiationinjected into the column. The Green's function is convolved withbremsstrahlung, cyclotron, and blackbody source terms to calculate the emergentphoton spectrum. We show that energization of photons in the shock naturallyproduces an X-ray spectrum with a relatively flat continuum and a high-energyexponential cutoff. Finally, we demonstrate that our model yields goodagreement with the spectra of the bright pulsar Her X-1 and the low luminositypulsar X Per.

Here, we give relatedconstructions of invisible tunnels, which allow electromagnetic waves to passbetween possibly distant points, but with only the ends of the tunnels visibleto electromagnetic imaging. Effectively, these change the topology of spacewith respect to solutions of Maxwell's equations, corresponding to attaching ahandlebody to $\mathbb R^3$. The resulting devices thus function aselectromagnetic wormholes.

The HERMES experiment has measured the transverse polarization of Lambda andLambda-bar hyperons produced inclusively in quasireal photoproduction at apositron beam energy of 27.6 GeV. The transverse polarization of the Lambdahyperon is found to be positive while the observed Lambda-bar polarization iscompatible with zero. The transverse polarization values averaged over thekinematic acceptance of HERMES are 0.078 +/- 0.006(stat) +/- 0.012(syst) and-0.025 +/- 0.015(stat) +/- 0.018(syst) for Lambda and Lambda-bar hyperons,respectively. The dependences of Lambda and Lambda-bar polarizations on thefraction $\zeta$ of the beam's light-cone momentum carried by the hyperon andon the hyperon's transverse momentum $p_T$ were investigated. The measuredLambda polarization rises linearly with $p_T$ and exhibits a different behaviorfor low and high values of $\zeta$, which approximately correspond to thebackward and forward regions in the center-of-mass frame of the $\gamma^*N$reaction.

We prove that a random induced subgraph of an n-cube contains a component of size at least n/2 with high probability, provided that the subgraph is sufficiently large. We also show that this result holds even when the subgraph is induced by a random choice of vertices, and that the probability of a large component decreases exponentially with the size of the subgraph. Our results have implications for the study of random graphs and their properties, and provide a new perspective on the behavior of complex networks.

Kagome lattcie antiferromagnets, characterized by their unique geometry and strong interactions, have attracted considerable interest owing to their potential for realizing exotic quantum states. In particular, the Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya (DM) interaction, which arises from the breaking of inversion symmetry, plays a crucial role in these materials by inducing spin canting and frustration. In this article, we reviewed the recent progress in the studying of kagome lattice antiferromagnets with DM interaction, focusing on the interplay between the DM interaction and other interactions, such as the exchange interaction and the Kitaev interaction. We discuss the resulting magnetic phases, including the quantum spin liquid state, the Eggleston state, and the chiral spin liquid state. Nous also highlight the potential applications of these materials in spintronics and quantum computing.

In this study, we investigate the physisorption of nucleobases, namely adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), thymine (T), and uracil (U), on graphene surfaces. Using a combination of first-principles density functional theory and force field calculations, we determine the binding energies and interaction strengths of these nucleobases with graphene. Our results reveal that the binding energies follow a specific sequence: G > A > T > C > U. The main contributing factor to the binding energy is the van der Waals interaction between the nucleobases and graphene. We compare these results with the binding of nucleobases to single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWNTs) and observe that the binding energy with graphene is lower. These findings provide valuable insights into the interaction between nucleobases and graphene, which is essential for understanding the behavior and potential applications of graphene-based nano-bio materials.

Accurate stellar photometry is important for st udies of stars and galaxies. Emission lines in stellar spectra can impact broad-band photometry using the UBVR filter system. This article investigates the effect of common emission lines on UBVR photometric measurements. Using spectral models, synthetic photometry was performed with and without emission lines to quantify their influence. It was found that hydrogen emission lines particularly affect the U and B bands. Metallic emissi on lines have a smaller but non-negligible impact across all bands. The results provide corrections for photometric studies to account for unresolved emission line flux and obtain photometric measurements representation of the underlying stellar continuum.

Our paper aims at providing an answer to the question whether one canreliably describe the properties of the most important spin-isospin nuclearexcitations, by using the available non-relativistic Skyrme energy functionals.Our method, which has been introduced in a previous publication devoted to theIsobaric Analog states, is the self-consistent Quasiparticle Random PhaseApproximation (QRPA). The inclusion of pairing is instrumental for describing anumber of experimentally measured spherical systems which are characterized byopen shells. We discuss the effect of isoscalar and isovector pairingcorrelations. Based on the results for the Gamow-Teller resonance in $^{90}$Zr,in $^{208}$Pb and in few Sn isotopes, we draw definite conclusions on theperformance of different Skyrme parametrizations, and we suggest improvementsfor future fits. We also use the spin-dipole resonance as a benchmark of ourstatements.

This article investigates high-frequency quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) observed in the black hole binary system GRS 1915+105. Specifically, it explores the possibility of explaining these QPOs through the presence of a Keplerian disc orbiting a near-extreme Kerr black hole, coupled with LNRF-velocity hump-induced oscillations. The study employs numerical simulations and analyzes the resulting dynamics and waveform patterns. The findings suggest that the LNRF-velocity hump can induce oscillations in the Keplerian disc, giving rise to high-frequency QPOs that match the observed frequencies in GRS 1915+105. The implications of these results shed light on the nature and characteristics of black hole accretion discs and contribute to our understanding of the mechanisms behind high-frequency QPOs in such systems.

This thesis investigates in the use of access log data as a source ofinformation for identifying related scientific papers. This is done forarXiv.org, the authority for publication of e-prints in several fields ofphysics. Compared to citation information, access logs have the advantage of beingimmediately available, without manual or automatic extraction of the citationgraph. Because of that, a main focus is on the question, how far user behaviorcan serve as a replacement for explicit meta-data, which potentially might beexpensive or completely unavailable. Therefore, we compare access, content, andcitation-based measures of relatedness on different recommendation tasks. As afinal result, an online recommendation system has been built that can helpscientists to find further relevant literature, without having to search forthem actively.

Phase closure at 682 GHz and 691 GHz was first achieved using three antennasof the Submillimeter Array (SMA) interferometer located on Mauna Kea, Hawaii.Initially, phase closure was demonstrated at 682.5 GHz on Sept. 19, 2002 usingan artificial ground-based "beacon" signal. Subsequently, astronomicaldetections of both Saturn and Uranus were made at the frequency of the CO(6-5)transition (691.473 GHz) on all three baselines on Sept. 22, 2002. While thelarger planets such as Saturn are heavily resolved even on these shortbaselines (25.2m, 25.2m and 16.4m), phase closure was achieved on Uranus andCallisto. This was the first successful experiment to obtain phase closure inthis frequency band. The CO(6-5) line was also detected towards Orion BN/KL andother Galactic sources, as was the vibrationally-excited 658 GHz water maserline toward evolved stars. We present these historic detections, as well as thefirst arcsecond-scale images obtained in this frequency band.

There are two promising scenarios that explain the ankle, which is a dip inthe spectrum of cosmic rays at $\sim 10^{19}$ eV. A scenario interprets theankle as the transition from Galactic to extragalactic cosmic rays ({\itankle-transition scenario}), while the other is that the dip caused by pairproduction on the cosmic microwave background radiation ({\it proton-dipscenario}). In this paper, we consider whether cosmogenic neutrinos can be aclue to judge which scenario is favored. We calculated the fluxes of cosmogenicneutrinos following these scenarios with plausible physical parameter sets, andfound several important features as follows. First of all, the neutrino flux at$\sim 10^{20}$ eV becomes much higher in the ankle-transition scenario as longas the maximum energy of the cosmic rays at sources is sufficiently high. Onthe other hand, the neutrino spectrum has a characteristic peak at $\sim10^{16}$ eV in the proton-dip scenario on the condition that extragalacticprotons significantly contribute to the observed cosmic rays down to $10^{17}$eV. Thus, we conclude cosmogenic neutrinos should give us a clue to judge whichscenario is favored, unless these features are masked by the neutrinobackground coming from possible, powerful neutrino sources such as AGNs andGRBs. We also found an interesting feature that the neutrino flux at $\sim10^{18}$ eV depends only on the cosmological evolution of the cosmic raysources. That means cosmogenic neutrinos with the energy bring us informationon the cosmological evolution of the sources of ultra-high energy cosmic rays.Finally, we compare the fluxes of cosmogenic neutrinos with the expectedsensitivity curves of several neutrino detectors, and conclude the detection ofcosmogenic neutrinos in the near future is promising.

We propose a Hamiltonian formalism for a generalizedFriedmann-Roberson-Walker cosmology model in the presence of both a variableequation of state (EOS) parameter $w(a)$ and a variable cosmological constant$\Lambda(a)$, where $a$ is the scale factor. This Hamiltonian system containing1 degree of freedom and without constraint, gives Friedmann equations as theequation of motion, which describes a mechanical system with a variable massobject moving in a potential field. After an appropriate transformation of thescale factor, this system can be further simplified to an object with constantmass moving in an effective potential field. In this framework, the $\Lambda$cold dark matter model as the current standard model of cosmology correspondsto a harmonic oscillator. We further generalize this formalism to take intoaccount the bulk viscosity and other cases. The Hamiltonian can be quantizedstraightforwardly, but this is different from the approach of theWheeler-DeWitt equation in quantum cosmology.

This paper presents a discrete thermodynamics theory of lasers based on the principles of statistical mechanics and quantum mechanics. The theory provides a unified framework for understanding the thermodynamic behavior of lasers, including the effects of temperature, pressure, and volume on the laser output. The theory is applied to a variety of laser systems, including solid-state lasers, gas lasers, and semiconductor lasers. The results of the theory are compared with experimental data, and good agreement is found. The theory provides a new tool for understanding and designing lasers.

Our results provide a deeper understanding of the long-time behavior of gradient fields and have important implications for their use in various applications, such as optimization and machine learning.
